analysis_markdown_en:
The study addresses the soil-structure degradation caused by alternate wetting and drying irrigation (IAWD), which fragments macroaggregates and reduces nitrogen availability in paddy fields. By synthesizing nano-clinoptilolite loaded with ammonium, the authors created a slow-release nitrogen carrier that simultaneously acts as a cementing agent for soil particles. The field trial demonstrates that replacing 20% of urea with this nano-zeolite fertilizer (Z2N8) under IAWD yields the best trade-off: it restores aggregate stability lost to wet-dry cycles, boosts effective tillering, and raises both irrigation water use efficiency and nitrogen use efficiency without sacrificing yield. Higher zeolite ratios (Z4N6) further improve aggregate metrics but do not consistently increase chlorophyll or tillering, indicating a fertilization threshold. The approach offers a practical pathway for Northeast China's water-saving rice systems, though long-term field-scale validation and cost analysis of nano-clinoptilolite production remain necessary before broad adoption.

### Abstract

Nano-colloidal particles are fundamental units of soil aggregates, critically supporting aggregate stability and water-fertilizer utilization. To evaluate the regulatory effects of nano-clinoptilolite-based nitrogen fertilizer (ZN) on soil aggregate structure, rice physiological traits, nitrogen utilization, and yield formation in water-saving irrigated paddy fields, a field split-plot experiment was conducted in 2021–2022. Main plots received conventional flooded irrigation (ICF) or alternate wetting and drying irrigation (IAWD); subplots received three fertilization regimes: 100% urea (Z0N10), 20% ZN + 80% urea (Z2N8), and 40% ZN + 60% urea (Z4N6). Results showed that under identical fertilization, IAWD-induced wet-dry cycles fragmented macroaggregates (>0.25 mm) into microaggregates (<0.25 mm), reducing aggregate stability. Increasing ZN application ratio significantly improved aggregate structure and stability while elevating soil inorganic nitrogen concentration. Z2N8 performed best in effective tillering rate, chlorophyll content, irrigation water use efficiency (IWUE), nitrogen use efficiency (NUE), and yield. ZN increased the inflection point accumulated temperature during key growth stages, significantly raising plant nitrogen accumulation thresholds and enhancing sustained nitrogen supply and uptake. Structural equation modeling indicated that ZN improved yield through a pathway of soil aggregate structure optimization, effective tillering promotion, and increased nitrogen accumulation. Integrating soil structure improvement and crop growth responses, applying 20% ZN + 80% urea under IAWD achieved the best synergy between soil amelioration and crop production. These findings provide a scientific basis for rational ZN application in water-saving paddy fields of Northeast China.

## Nano-Clinoptilolite Synthesis and Nitrogen Loading Chemistry

Nano-clinoptilolite was prepared by dispersing raw clinoptilolite in distilled water and applying ultrasonic pulverization. The supernatant was collected and dried for at least 48 hours to obtain nano-sized particles. These were then mixed with ammonium chloride solution and allowed to adsorb for 2 hours, after which the supernatant was separated. The resulting nano-clinoptilolite-based nitrogen fertilizer (ZN) was dried for more than 48 hours until completely dry. Elemental analysis (Table 1) showed that nitrogen loading increased the N content from 0% in raw clinoptilolite (NC) to 1.06% in ZN, while carbon decreased from 0.28% to 0.15% and hydrogen increased from 1.51% to 1.97%, confirming successful ammonium exchange within the zeolite framework.

The fertilization regimes (Table 2) applied a total nitrogen rate of 86.25 kg·hm⁻² for all treatments, with ZN supplying 0, 17.25, or 34.50 kg·hm⁻² for Z0N10, Z2N8, and Z4N6, respectively. Phosphorus (32.75 kg·hm⁻²) and potassium (51.75 kg·hm⁻²) were applied uniformly. The ZN fraction was incorporated into the basal fertilizer, while urea was split across basal, tillering, and panicle stages. This design allowed isolation of the nano-zeolite effect from total nutrient input, ensuring that observed differences in soil aggregation and nitrogen dynamics could be attributed to the carrier material rather than to varying nitrogen rates.

## Aggregate Size Distribution and Stability under IAWD and ZN Ratios

Soil aggregate composition (Table 3) was dominated by >0.25 mm macroaggregates (83.38–92.66%). IAWD significantly reduced 2–<3 mm aggregates by 31.25% and increased <0.5 mm microaggregates by 18.79% compared to ICF, with geometric mean diameter (GMD) declining by 4.67%. Increasing ZN proportion progressively shifted the distribution toward larger sizes: Z4N6 achieved the highest >5 mm fraction (53.14%) and the lowest <0.25 mm fraction (7.34%), both significantly different from Z2N8 and Z0N10 (P<0.01). ZN application raised the >0.25 mm proportion (R0.25) by 6.26–11.13% and reduced microaggregates by 31.42–55.85% relative to Z0N10.

Aggregate stability parameters responded strongly to ZN. Mean weight diameter (MWD) increased by 6.60% (Z2N8) and 16.96% (Z4N6) versus Z0N10, while GMD rose by 6.95% and 17.72%, respectively. The ANOVA confirmed that both irrigation mode and ZN ratio significantly affected R0.25 and GMD (P<0.01 for ZN; P<0.01 for irrigation on R0.25). These results indicate that nano-clinoptilolite acts as a binding agent that counteracts the disruptive effects of wet-dry cycles, promoting the formation and stabilization of macroaggregates even under IAWD.

## Soil Inorganic Nitrogen Dynamics and Rice Physiological Responses

Soil NH4⁺-N and NO3⁻-N concentrations (Tables 4 and 5) were monitored across five growth stages in both years. ZN application significantly elevated both nitrogen forms at all stages (P<0.01). In 2021, Z2N8 produced the highest NH4⁺-N at tillering (5.50 mg·kg⁻¹) and panicle initiation (2.32 mg·kg⁻¹), while Z4N6 led at grain filling (2.67 mg·kg⁻¹) and maturity (2.40 mg·kg⁻¹). For NO3⁻-N, Z2N8 peaked at tillering (1.30 mg·kg⁻¹) and panicle initiation (0.85 mg·kg⁻¹), whereas Z4N6 showed higher values at later stages (0.67 and 0.84 mg·kg⁻¹). This pattern suggests that ZN prolongs nitrogen availability, with higher zeolite ratios extending supply into grain filling.

Rice tillering (Table 6) was significantly affected by ZN ratio (P<0.01), but not by irrigation alone. In 2021, Z2N8 increased effective tiller number by 25.29% and reduced ineffective tillers by 64.65% compared to Z0N10, raising the effective tiller rate by 28.76%. In 2022, the corresponding increases were 33.33% and 30.94%, with a 31.21% rise in effective tiller rate. Chlorophyll content (Table 7) was highest under Z2N8, which exceeded Z0N10 by 28.97% at most stages, while Z4N6 showed no further increase or even a decline, indicating a threshold effect beyond 20% ZN substitution.

## Nitrogen Accumulation Kinetics and Yield/Water-Nitrogen Efficiency Outcomes

Logistic modeling of plant nitrogen accumulation (Table 8) revealed that ZN increased both the accumulation potential (a) and the inflection point accumulated temperature (c). Under IAWD, Z2N8 achieved the highest a (133.209 kg·hm⁻² in 2021; 125.180 kg·hm⁻² in 2022) and c (712.07 °C in 2021; 693.32 °C in 2022), with maximum growth rate Vmax of 0.194 and 0.190 kg·hm⁻²·°C⁻¹, respectively. The model fit was strong (R² = 0.933 in 2021 and 0.974 in 2022 for IAWDZ2N8). These parameters indicate that ZN extends the duration of nitrogen uptake and shifts the accumulation peak to higher accumulated temperatures, supporting sustained nitrogen supply during critical growth phases.

Yield and efficiency metrics (Table 9) showed that ZN significantly improved irrigation water use efficiency (IWUE) and nitrogen use efficiency (NUE). In 2021, Z2N8 and Z4N6 increased IWUE by 35.36% and 42.47% over Z0N10, respectively. NUE under Z2N8 rose by 18.70% in 2021 and 14.59% in 2022. Yield was also significantly higher under ZN treatments, with Z2N8 consistently outperforming other regimes. Structural equation modeling confirmed that the yield benefit under IAWDZ2N8 flowed through a pathway of improved aggregate structure, enhanced effective tillering, and increased nitrogen accumulation, establishing 20% ZN + 80% urea as the optimal combination for balancing soil improvement and crop productivity.

## Boundary Constraints and Industrial Scaling of Nano-Clinoptilolite Fertilizer

- The study was conducted over only two growing seasons (2021–2022) at a single field site; long-term effects on soil health and cumulative nitrogen dynamics remain unverified.

- Nano-clinoptilolite production requires ultrasonic pulverization and 48-hour drying steps, which may limit scalability and increase energy costs for industrial manufacturing.

- The optimal ZN ratio of 20% was identified under specific IAWD cycles; performance under different soil textures, climates, or irrigation thresholds is not established.

- Yield and efficiency gains were measured against urea-only controls; comparison with other slow-release fertilizers or zeolite carriers is absent.

analysis_markdown_en:
Late-laying hens suffer declining antioxidant and immune function, reducing egg production and shell quality. This 8-week trial in 480 Hy-Line Brown hens tested a pure (≥99.0%) lemairamin (WGX-50) powder at 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 mg/kg. The 1.0 mg/kg dose cut feed-to-egg ratio by 4.65% (2.15 to 2.05) and raised serum T-AOC by 49.4% (4.47 to 6.68 U/mL), while MDA fell from 10.38 to 8.76 nmol/mL. IL-1β dropped 33.4% (12.41 to 8.27 ng/L) and FSH rose from 2.24 to 3.19 mIU/mL. Total ovarian follicles increased from 52.33 to 65.17.

The additive is a natural cinnamoyl amide with no drug residue, fitting green production. The effective dose is low (1.0–2.0 mg/kg), so inclusion cost is minimal relative to feed. However, production gains (laying rate +3.82% at 1.0 mg/kg) were not statistically significant, and immune globulins (IgA, IgG, IgM) were unchanged. The trial used 60-week-old hens over 8 weeks; longer studies and dose-response beyond 2.0 mg/kg are needed. The mechanism likely involves antioxidant enzyme upregulation and NF-κB pathway inhibition, but this was inferred, not directly measured.

### Abstract

## Boundary Constraints and Industrial Scaling of WGX-50 in Late-Laying Hen Diets

- The trial used 60-week-old Hy-Line Brown hens over only 8 weeks; effects on persistency beyond 68 weeks of age are not established.

The industrial bottleneck addressed is the trade-off between high-speed automated transplanting and seedling damage in labor-intensive chrysanthemum production. Conventional two- or four-needle claws concentrate forces at non-coincident points, causing tilting, root tearing, and substrate loss. The three-needle symmetric arrangement converges force lines to a single point, improving grasping consistency without additional actuation complexity.

The design uses a pneumatic cylinder driving a slider-crank mechanism with geometric constraints (base width 32 mm, needle spacing ≥5 mm, bend angle 167°). The EDEM-RecurDyn co-simulation, validated within 8.16 percentage points, enables parameter optimization before field trials. ### Abstract

To address unstable grasping and severe seedling damage during seedling extraction in greenhouse chrysanthemum transplanters, a three-needle concentrating seedling-picking claw was designed. A three-dimensional complex root system model of chrysanthemum plug seedlings was generated using L-system theory, incorporating root reinforcement effects typically neglected in substrate-only models. An EDEM-RecurDyn coupling model of the root-substrate-claw system was constructed and validated against extraction tests. The effects of needle configuration, extraction depth, extraction speed, and push-plate stroke on mechanical characteristics and damage were analyzed. Response surface methodology established multivariate regression equations for substrate breakage rate and seedling integrity, yielding optimal working parameters. Results show that extraction depth, extraction speed, and push-plate stroke significantly affect seedling damage. At an extraction depth of 20 mm, extraction speed of 200 mm/s, and push-plate stroke of 5 mm, seedling integrity was optimal, with an extraction success rate of 84.3% and substrate integrity of 93.10%. Compared with the initial parameters (stroke 5 mm, depth 25 mm, speed 200 mm/s), the optimized settings reduced Bond breakage count by 510 and increased seedling integrity by 8.48 percentage points. The three-needle claw exhibited superior grasping stability and interference resistance versus two- and four-needle configurations under center offset conditions. Field trials validated the optimization, providing a reference for automatic seedling-picking mechanism design in chrysanthemum transplanters.

## Three-Needle Concentrating Claw Geometry and Slider-Crank Kinematics

The claw comprises a pneumatic cylinder, base, push rod, push plate, and three seedling needles arranged with central symmetry. Unlike the four-needle configuration whose force lines converge at two collinear points, the three-needle layout directs all force action lines to a single point, enabling synchronous concentrating clamping. Geometric constraints fix the base width at η=32 mm, needle installation at 5 mm from the base periphery (l2=21 mm), push plate radius l5=21 mm, and bend angle β=167° derived from the plug tray slope of 77°. Needle minimum spacing is set to 5 mm to avoid root damage, yielding l4=88.7 mm and l3=23.6 mm with a 10 mm safety clearance below the 100 mm average seedling height.

The claw is modeled as a slider-crank linkage with the base fixed and needles rotating in-plane. MATLAB kinematic simulation of the end-effector trajectory under maximum push-plate stroke determines a maximum extraction depth of 30 mm, constrained by the requirement that the opened claw span m remain smaller than the plug cell gap n. Operating ranges are set as: push-plate stroke 5–10 mm (below 5 mm ineffective clamping; above 10 mm limited by cylinder stroke), extraction depth 20–30 mm (below 20 mm insufficient clamping stability), and extraction speed 200–400 mm/s.

## L-System Root Modeling and EDEM-RecurDyn Coupled Validation

Chrysanthemum root architecture was generated via the Rootbox platform, an open-source L-system model implemented in MATLAB. Input parameters include a 15-day cultivation period, plug space of 32×32 mm top, 14×14 mm bottom, 40 mm height, main root initial elongation rate 3 mm/d and diameter 0.8±0.1 mm, lateral root elongation 2 mm/d, mean diameter 0.5±0.1 mm, branching angle 60±10°, and root hair zone length 10 mm. Validation against 10 measured seedlings showed relative errors below 10% for main root length (4.1%), main root diameter (9.1%), lateral root average length (5.7%), and lateral root average diameter (8.3%).

The EDEM-RecurDyn co-simulation assigned material properties: substrate particles (Poisson ratio 0.424, density 0.6205 g/cm³, shear modulus 1.366×10⁶ Pa), claw (0.269, 7.89 g/cm³, 7.7×10¹⁰ Pa), and plug tray (0.35, 1.05 g/cm³, 1.25×10⁹ Pa). Contact parameters included particle-particle static friction 0.65, dynamic 0.273, restitution 0.19; particle-tray 0.415, 0.245, 0.32; particle-claw 0.424, 0.283, 0.68. Substrate particles were 0.8 mm spheres. The coupled model achieved an average error of 8.16 percentage points versus grasping tests, validating its predictive capability for damage assessment.

## Response Surface Optimization of Extraction Parameters

A three-factor, three-level Box-Behnken design (17 runs) varied push-plate stroke X1 (5–10 mm), extraction depth X2 (20–30 mm), and extraction speed X3 (200–400 mm/s). Bond breakage count Y1 ranged from 3,520 to 5,824, and seedling integrity Y2 from 37.96% to 86.5%. Regression models were highly significant (P<0.0001) with lack-of-fit P values of 0.2831 and 0.4451, indicating good fit. For Y1, X2, X1², and X2² were extremely significant; X1X3 and X2X3 significant. For Y2, X2, X3, X2X3, X1², X2², and X3² were extremely significant.

Design Expert optimization identified push-plate stroke 5 mm, extraction depth 20 mm, and extraction speed 200 mm/s as optimal, predicting Bond breakage count 3,608 and seedling integrity 94.36%. Compared with initial parameters (stroke 5 mm, depth 25 mm, speed 200 mm/s), Bond breakage decreased by 510 counts and integrity increased by 8.48 percentage points. Field trials under these settings achieved average extraction success rate 84.3% and average substrate integrity 93.10%, confirming the optimization's effectiveness.

## Needle Configuration Robustness Under Center Offset

Extraction configuration tests compared two-, three-, and four-needle claws under center offset conditions. As offset increased, seedling integrity declined for all configurations, with substrate loosening and root exposure. The three-needle claw maintained structural integrity with minimal substrate loss at 0–2 mm offset and remained stable at 3 mm offset despite some deformation. In contrast, two- and four-needle claws showed rapid integrity decline and substantial substrate detachment, with the two-needle claw most sensitive.

Quantitative analysis indicated that the three-needle claw exhibited minimal mass loss variation across offset conditions, demonstrating significantly superior interference resistance. This robustness is attributed to the concentrating force path that maintains synchronous clamping even under positional misalignment, whereas non-converging force paths in alternative configurations amplify local pressure and damage.

# Performance Analysis and Optimization of a Three-Needle Concentrating Seedling-Picking Claw for Greenhouse Chrysanthemum Transplanters

---

**DOI:** `10.11975/j.issn.1002-6819.202506116` | **Journal:** Transactions of the Chinese Society of Agricultural Engineering (Transactions of the Chinese Society of Agricultural Engineering (农业工程学报)) | **Published:** 2026 (Vol 46 6)  
**Authors:** WANG Lihong, LUO Zhitao, ZHAN Yixiang, ZHENG Dan, ZHENG Enlai, CHEN Long, DONG Jinyu, WANG Xiaochan  
**Institution:** College of Engineering, Nanjing Agricultural University  
**Portal:** `https://sinoagritech.com/paper/performance-analysis-and-optimization-of-a-three-needle-concentrating-seedling-picking-claw-for-126851`

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

To address unstable grasping and severe seedling damage during seedling extraction in greenhouse chrysanthemum transplanters, a three-needle concentrating seedling-picking claw was designed. A three-dimensional complex root system model of chrysanthemum plug seedlings was generated using L-system theory, incorporating root reinforcement effects typically neglected in substrate-only models. An EDEM-RecurDyn coupling model of the root-substrate-claw system was constructed and validated against extraction tests. The effects of needle configuration, extraction depth, extraction speed, and push-plate stroke on mechanical characteristics and damage were analyzed. Response surface methodology established multivariate regression equations for substrate breakage rate and seedling integrity, yielding optimal working parameters. Results show that extraction depth, extraction speed, and push-plate stroke significantly affect seedling damage. At an extraction depth of 20 mm, extraction speed of 200 mm/s, and push-plate stroke of 5 mm, seedling integrity was optimal, with an extraction success rate of 84.3% and substrate integrity of 93.10%. Compared with the initial parameters (stroke 5 mm, depth 25 mm, speed 200 mm/s), the optimized settings reduced Bond breakage count by 510 and increased seedling integrity by 8.48 percentage points. The three-needle claw exhibited superior grasping stability and interference resistance versus two- and four-needle configurations under center offset conditions. Field trials validated the optimization, providing a reference for automatic seedling-picking mechanism design in chrysanthemum transplanters.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Optimal parameters: extraction depth 20 mm, speed 200 mm/s, push-plate stroke 5 mm yield 84.3% extraction success and 93.10% substrate integrity.
- Optimized settings reduce Bond breakage count by 510 and raise seedling integrity by 8.48 percentage points versus initial parameters.
- Three-needle claw maintains structural integrity under 0-2 mm center offset, outperforming two- and four-needle claws.
- EDEM-RecurDyn coupled model achieves average error of only 8.16 percentage points versus grasping tests.

abstract_en: The formation of food flavor highly depends on the release and perception of volatile odor molecules, whose functional group structures directly influence their recognition patterns with human olfactory receptors. To investigate the binding characteristics of odor molecules with different structures at the molecular level, this study focused on three common types of odor functional groups in food: aldehydes, phenols, and sulfur/alcohol compounds. Nine representative odorant molecules were selected, including trans-2-nonenal, trans,trans-2,4-nonadienal, (2E,4E)-deca-2,4-dienal, 2-methoxy-4-methylphenol, 2-methoxy-4-propylphenol, isoeugenol, dimethyl sulfide, 1-butanol, and methanethiol. These were docked to three human olfactory receptors (OR2W1, OR10K1, OR10S1) and subjected to 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations. The results showed that phenolic and aldehyde odor molecules can form relatively stable hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interaction networks within the binding pockets of olfactory receptors, exhibiting high binding affinity and conformational stability. Among them, (2E,4E)-deca-2,4-dienal and 2-methoxy-4-methylphenol showed the most prominent binding performance. In contrast, sulfur-containing compounds such as dimethyl sulfide and methanethiol, as well as small alcohol molecules like 1-butanol, primarily rely on weak van der Waals interactions for transient binding with the receptors, lacking stable hydrogen bond formation. As a result, these complexes display higher binding free energy (i.e., lower affinity) and greater conformational fluctuations. Comparative analysis across all groups indicates that the functional group structures of odor molecules have a significant influence on olfactory receptor recognition patterns. This study provides a theoretical basis for sensory recognition mechanisms of food flavor substances.

This study decodes the molecular recognition mechanisms between nine representative food odorants and human olfactory receptors (OR2W1, OR10K1, and OR10S1) using molecular docking and 100 ns all-atom molecular dynamics under the CHARMM36 force field. The findings reveal that volatile functional groups dictate receptor binding affinity and conformational stability. Phenolic compounds achieve superior binding energies (-6.4 to -5.5 kcal/mol) through coordinated hydrogen bonds and aromatic pi-pi stacking, maintaining tight receptor compactness (RMSD 0.15-0.45 nm). Aliphatic aldehydes display intermediate affinities (-5.0 to -4.8 kcal/mol) primarily driven by hydrophobic cavity insertion. Conversely, sulfur and alcohol volatiles exhibit weak dispersion interactions (-1.9 to -1.6 kcal/mol), lacking stable hydrogen bonding and triggering marked conformational instability.

## Molecular Docking Configurations and Functional Group Energetics in Olfactory Receptor Cavities

Docking calculations executed using AutoDock 4.2.6 with Lamarckian genetic algorithms across 250,000 evaluations revealed distinct receptor interaction profiles governed by ligand functional group polarity. Phenolic volatiles containing hydroxyl and methoxy substituents exhibited the highest receptor binding affinities. Specifically, 2-methoxy-4-methylphenol docked into OR10K1 with a binding energy of -6.4 kcal/mol, anchoring via a 2.89 Å hydrogen bond with Tyr278, pi-pi stacking with Tyr73, and hydrophobic contacts with Pro283, Glu70, and Phe170. Similarly, 2-methoxy-4-propylphenol engaged OR2W1 with -5.9 kcal/mol through an Asn155 hydrogen bond (3.28 Å), while isoeugenol bound OR10K1 at -5.5 kcal/mol via Leu144 (3.08 Å).

Aldehyde odorants representing fresh and fruity aroma profiles bound with intermediate affinities ranging from -5.0 kcal/mol to -4.8 kcal/mol. In OR2W1, (2E,4E)-deca-2,4-dienal embedded deeply into the hydrophobic cavity, establishing a 3.07 Å hydrogen bond to achieve -5.0 kcal/mol. Trans-2-nonenal docked with -4.9 kcal/mol supported by a 2.87 Å hydrogen bond to Ser217, whereas trans,trans-2,4-nonadienal recorded -4.8 kcal/mol through non-polar packing against Tyr120 and Phe123.

In contrast, pungent and off-flavor sulfur-containing volatiles demonstrated weak interactions. Dimethyl sulfide docked into OR2W1 at -1.9 kcal/mol, and methanethiol docked into OR10K1 at -1.6 kcal/mol, both failing to form directional hydrogen bonds. Meanwhile, 1-butanol utilized its primary hydroxyl group to engage Tyr290 and Asp194 in OR10S1, achieving -3.2 kcal/mol.

- Phenolic odorants formed synergistic hydrogen bonds and aromatic packing, producing binding energies from -6.4 to -5.5 kcal/mol.

- Aliphatic aldehydes balanced alkyl chain hydrophobic insertion with carbonyl hydrogen bonding, yielding energies from -5.0 to -4.8 kcal/mol.

- Small sulfur compounds relied on non-specific van der Waals contacts, resulting in poor binding affinities (-1.9 to -1.6 kcal/mol).

## Conformational Dynamics and Structural Integrity: RMSD, RMSF, and Radius of Gyration Profiles

All-atom 100 ns molecular dynamics trajectories simulated in GROMACS under the CHARMM36 force field demonstrated how functional group contacts govern complex stability. Backbone root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) profiles showed that phenolic complexes maintained superior structural integrity, fluctuating within 0.15-0.45 nm before plateauing around 0.4 nm after 60 ns. Their radius of gyration (Rg) remained restricted between 2.2 nm and 2.35 nm throughout the 100 ns duration, confirming tight receptor fold retention without pocket relaxation.

Aldehyde-bound OR2W1 complexes displayed moderate structural rearrangements, with RMSD values spanning 0.2-0.8 nm before equilibrating at approximately 40 ns. Their Rg trajectories varied within 2.2-2.45 nm, reflecting minor pocket adjustments to accommodate aliphatic chains. Residue fluctuation analysis (RMSF) showed that aldehydes induced slight mobility localized only at the C-terminus beyond residue 280.

Conversely, sulfur-containing systems exhibited pronounced dynamic destabilization. Dimethyl sulfide prompted a sharp RMSD surge near 80 ns alongside marked Rg expansion. Furthermore, dimethyl sulfide triggered severe RMSF fluctuations across residues 200 to 280, indicating that transient dispersion forces fail to stabilize the seven-transmembrane olfactory receptor bundle.

- Aldehyde systems underwent early structural equilibration within 40 ns, displaying low overall RMSF except at the flexible C-terminus.

- Dimethyl sulfide induced late-stage RMSD elevation and severe residue fluctuations across residues 200-280.

## Dynamic Hydrogen Bonding Persistence and Principal Component Trajectory Projection

Dynamic hydrogen bonding monitoring throughout the 100,000 simulation frames elucidated the physical basis of binding stability. Phenolic ligands consistently maintained 1 or 2 actual hydrogen bonds throughout the 100 ns trajectory, accompanied by dense sub-0.35 nm contact frequencies. In contrast, aldehydes oscillated between 0 and 1 active hydrogen bond. Sulfur compounds formed zero hydrogen bonds and exhibited sparse sub-0.35 nm contact density, explaining their tendency toward pocket dissociation.

Principal component analysis (PCA) computed across the equilibrated trajectories (60-100 ns) captured the dominant collective motions. For phenolic complexes, the cumulative variance explained by PC1 and PC2 ranged between 26.06% and 31.52%, characterized by diffuse two-dimensional projections. This pattern reflects fine-grained conformational sampling, including aromatic ring rotation and side-chain rearrangements, without structural breakdown.

In contrast, non-phenolic complexes generally exhibited lower collective variance contribution and constrained projection distributions. These findings confirm that phenolic ligands establish versatile multi-point contact networks that permit flexible side-chain adjustments while preserving overall receptor fold stability.

- Phenolics maintained continuous 1-2 active hydrogen bonds and dense sub-0.35 nm contact frequencies across 100 ns.

- Sulfur compounds formed zero hydrogen bonds throughout the simulation, showing sparse ligand-protein contact frequencies.

- PCA cumulative contribution rates of 26.06% to 31.52% in phenolics reflected localized aromatic adjustments rather than unfolding.

## Simulation Constraints and Scope of Application

This study provides a functional group framework for understanding olfactory receptor recognition but operates within defined in silico boundaries.

- Simulations evaluated monomeric receptor models in aqueous 0.15 mol/L NaCl solution without full lipid bilayer membrane environments or intracellular G-protein coupling complexes.

- The investigation focused on three human olfactory receptors (OR2W1, OR10K1, and OR10S1) and nine volatile ligands, representing a targeted subset of the approximately 400 functional human olfactory GPCRs.

- Trajectories were modeled up to 100 ns; microsecond-scale conformational transitions or receptor activation/deactivation cycles were not captured.

Detailed process conditions, instrument calibrations, and complete supplementary datasets beyond the core quantitative benchmarks are preserved in the Peer-Reviewed PDF Edition below.

# Molecular Simulation Study on Recognition Mechanism Between Typical Volatile Odor Molecules in Food and Human Olfactory Receptors: A Case Study of Aldehydes, Phenols, and Sulfur Compounds

---

**DOI:** `10.13995/j.cnki.11-1802/ts.043033` | **Journal:** Food and Fermentation Industries (食品与发酵工业) | **Year:** 2026  
**Authors:** CHEN Menghan, LAI Keqiang, MIAO Junjian  
**Affiliation:** College of Food Science and Technology, Shanghai Ocean University, Shanghai 201306, China

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

The formation of food flavor highly depends on the release and perception of volatile odor molecules, whose functional group structures directly influence their recognition patterns with human olfactory receptors. To investigate the binding characteristics of odor molecules with different structures at the molecular level, this study focused on three common types of odor functional groups in food: aldehydes, phenols, and sulfur/alcohol compounds. Nine representative odorant molecules were selected, including trans-2-nonenal, trans,trans-2,4-nonadienal, (2E,4E)-deca-2,4-dienal, 2-methoxy-4-methylphenol, 2-methoxy-4-propylphenol, isoeugenol, dimethyl sulfide, 1-butanol, and methanethiol. These were docked to three human olfactory receptors (OR2W1, OR10K1, OR10S1) and subjected to 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations. The results showed that phenolic and aldehyde odor molecules can form relatively stable hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interaction networks within the binding pockets of olfactory receptors, exhibiting high binding affinity and conformational stability. Among them, (2E,4E)-deca-2,4-dienal and 2-methoxy-4-methylphenol showed the most prominent binding performance. In contrast, sulfur-containing compounds such as dimethyl sulfide and methanethiol, as well as small alcohol molecules like 1-butanol, primarily rely on weak van der Waals interactions for transient binding with the receptors, lacking stable hydrogen bond formation. As a result, these complexes display higher binding free energy (i.e., lower affinity) and greater conformational fluctuations. Comparative analysis across all groups indicates that the functional group structures of odor molecules have a significant influence on olfactory receptor recognition patterns. This study provides a theoretical basis for sensory recognition mechanisms of food flavor substances.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Phenolic volatiles exhibited the lowest binding free energies: 2-methoxy-4-methylphenol reached -6.4 kcal/mol with OR10K1 via a 2.89 Å Tyr278 hydrogen bond and pi-pi stacking with Tyr73.
- Aliphatic aldehydes demonstrated intermediate binding affinities (-5.0 kcal/mol for (2E,4E)-deca-2,4-dienal, -4.9 kcal/mol for trans-2-nonenal, and -4.8 kcal/mol for trans,trans-2,4-nonadienal) driven by hydrophobic core insertion.
- Sulfur compounds exhibited weak binding governed solely by dispersion forces, yielding elevated binding energies of -1.9 kcal/mol for dimethyl sulfide and -1.6 kcal/mol for methanethiol.
- Phenolic complexes sustained narrow backbone RMSD fluctuations (0.15-0.45 nm) and constrained radii of gyration (2.2-2.35 nm), stabilizing after 60 ns.
- Principal component analysis indicated that top principal components captured subtle local adjustments, such as aromatic ring reorientation, rather than receptor unfolding.

abstract_en: The Maillard reaction generates extensive arrays of heterocyclic compounds during thermal food processing; however, prior evaluations have predominantly concentrated on aromatic flavor contributions rather than comprehensive structural profiling or toxicological hazards. In this work, model Maillard reaction systems comprising D-glucose coupled with either L-serine or L-methionine were reacted at 180 ℃ for 0.5 h. Reaction mixtures were analyzed using Q-Exactive Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) across m/z 50 to 750 at 60,000 FWHM resolving power, followed by Van Krevelen diagram visualization and in silico toxicity prediction via Discovery Studio TOPKAT. The serine-glucose system generated 198 heterocyclic products, divided into CHON (27 species) and CHON1+x (171 species). In contrast, the methionine-glucose system yielded 159 heterocyclic products across four distinct compositional classes: CHON (12 species), CHONS (5 species), CHON1+x (114 species), and CHON1+xS (28 species). Both reaction systems were dominated by multi-nitrogen CHON1+x heterocycles, primarily pyrrole, imidazole, and pyrazine derivatives, while methionine uniquely mediated the formation of sulfur-containing heterocycles such as thiazoles and thiophenes. Toxicological screening revealed 16 heterocyclic compounds exhibiting marked mutagenicity, developmental toxicity, or dermal sensitization probabilities exceeding 0.7, alongside low oral LD50 and inhalation LC50 thresholds. These findings delineate how amino acid side-chain architecture directs heterocyclic reaction pathways, providing empirical benchmarks and computational methodologies for assessing thermal processing safety.

analysis_markdown_en:
This study establishes an integrated analytical and computational toxicology workflow to identify and assess heterocyclic compounds formed during thermal Maillard reactions between D-glucose and distinct amino acid precursors (L-serine and L-methionine) heated at 180 ℃ for 0.5 h. Using Q-Exactive Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry coupled with Van Krevelen graphical analysis, 198 heterocyclic compounds were characterized in the serine-glucose system and 159 in the methionine-glucose system. Precursor side-chain architecture strongly governed heteroatom incorporation: serine facilitated multi-nitrogen heterocycle synthesis via dehydration and nucleophilic addition, while methionine drove the formation of sulfur-containing rings such as thiazoles and thiophenes. Discovery Studio TOPKAT quantitative structure-toxicity relationship modeling identified 16 high-risk heterocyclic compounds exhibiting mutagenicity, developmental toxicity, or skin sensitization probabilities exceeding 0.7, highlighting latent food processing hazards.

## High-Resolution Mass Spectrometric Profiling and Van Krevelen Elemental Classification

Thermal interactions between reducing sugars and free amino acids initiate complex non-enzymatic browning cascades that yield polyfunctional heterocyclic scaffolds. Aqueous model solutions of D-glucose combined with either L-serine or L-methionine were sealed in KH-50 autoclaves and heated at 180 ℃ for 0.5 h, followed by rapid quenching in an ice-water bath. Diluted reaction mixtures were analyzed using a Q-Exactive Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometer operated in positive electrospray ionization mode across a scan range of m/z 50 to 750 at 60,000 FWHM resolving power. Accurate mass measurements within a 5 ppm error window enabled definitive formula assignments and structural identification against ChemSpider and mzCloud fragmentation libraries via Compound Discoverer 3.3.

Elemental composition analysis confirmed distinct reaction divergence directed by amino acid side-chain functionalities. The serine-glucose system generated 198 heterocyclic products classified strictly into mononitrogen CHON (27 products) and multi-nitrogen CHON1+x (171 products). The abundance of CHON1+x species is mechanistically attributable to the beta-hydroxyl group of serine, which promotes repeated intramolecular dehydration, nucleophilic condensation, and ring closure. Conversely, the methionine-glucose system produced 159 heterocyclic products spanning four classes: 12 CHON, 5 CHONS, 114 CHON1+x, and 28 CHON1+xS. The steric hindrance imposed by the longer thioether chain slightly suppressed total heterocyclic yield while introducing sulfur-containing cyclization pathways.

- Serine-glucose heterocyclic products clustered tightly in Van Krevelen space across O/C ratios of 0.0 to 0.4 and H/C ratios of 0.8 to 1.6, confirming high structural homology.

- Methionine-glucose heterocycles showed broader Van Krevelen dispersion, reflecting structural diversity introduced by thioether bond cleavage and sulfur heteroatom cyclization into thiazole and thiophene cores.

- Both systems were quantitatively dominated by rings bearing two nitrogen atoms and structures bearing three or more nitrogen atoms, primarily five-membered and six-membered rings.

## Precursor Consumption Kinetics and Conjugated Fluorophore Generation Dynamics

Quantitative monitoring of precursor depletion revealed mutual kinetic acceleration between amino acids and D-glucose under thermal treatment. High-performance liquid chromatographic analyses demonstrated that at amino acid-to-glucose molar ratios of 1:1 and 1:2, residual unreacted serine dropped to 18% and 11% of initial concentrations, whereas residual methionine fell to 14% and 7%, demonstrating that excess reducing sugar strongly drives amino acid consumption. Conversely, when examining sugar depletion across 1:1 and 2:1 ratios, serine lowered residual glucose to 26% and 23%, whereas methionine reduced glucose to 43% and 17%, indicating that serine consumes glucose more efficiently under equimolar conditions.

Fluorescence spectrophotometry with excitation at 347 nm captured the assembly of conjugated aromatic fluorophores across the 400 to 600 nm emission window. Unreacted glucose and methionine standards showed no detectable fluorescence emission, while pure serine exhibited faint background emission with a shifted peak, likely arising from thermal self-condensation into diketopiperazine intermediates. Following Maillard coupling, both reaction mixtures generated intense emission maxima centered near 450 nm. Notably, the fluorescence emission intensity of the serine-glucose system was twice that of the methionine-glucose system, confirming accelerated amino-carbonyl condensation, Strecker degradation, and aromatic heterocyclic ring closure driven by serine.

- Hydroxyl-promoted nucleophilic reactivity on serine resulted in greater glucose consumption at equimolar stoichiometry compared to methionine.

- Emission at 450 nm serves as an optical marker for conjugated heterocyclic chromophore accumulation and advanced Maillard aromatization cascades.

## In Silico TOPKAT Toxicological Characterization of High-Risk Scaffolds

Computational toxicology screening was executed on all identified heterocyclic products using the TOPKAT module in Discovery Studio. Predicted endpoints encompassed Ames mutagenicity, developmental toxicity potential, rat oral LD50, rat inhalation LC50, rat chronic oral LOAEL, and rat skin sensitization. Probability scores exceeding 0.7 were defined as indicating significant toxicological hazard. Among the 357 cumulative heterocyclic products identified across both systems, 16 individual compounds exhibited severe hazard profiles, comprising 10 compounds from the serine system and 6 from the methionine system.

Within the serine series, 9 compounds exhibited concurrent mutagenicity and developmental toxicity probabilities approaching 1.000, including N-(dicyclopropylmethyl)-4,5-dihydro-2-oxazolamine, 2-formamidopiperazine, and N-nitrosoproline. In the methionine series, compounds such as 3-allyl-5-isobutyl-2-thioxoimidazolidin-4-one presented combined liabilities across mutagenicity (1.000), developmental toxicity (0.997), and skin sensitization (1.000). Mechanistically, the elevated toxicity of these heterocyclic byproducts is associated with rigid planar conjugated ring frameworks and electrophilic nitrogen atoms that promote DNA intercalation, adduct formation, and reactive oxygen species generation.

- Ten high-risk serine-derived heterocycles showed oral LD50 values from 0.05 g/kg to 10.0 g/kg and inhalation LC50 values from 0.101 g/(m3·H) to 10.0 g/(m3·H).

- Six high-risk methionine-derived heterocycles exhibited oral LD50 values from 0.10 g/kg to 2.1 g/kg and inhalation LC50 values from 2.7 g/(m3·H) to 10.0 g/(m3·H), confirming slight-to-moderate systemic toxicity.

## Methodological Synthesis of Mass Spectrometry and Computational In Silico Bioassays

The experimental and in silico pipeline developed in this study provides an integrated framework for uncovering and ranking trace chemical hazards generated during thermal food manufacturing. High-resolution Orbitrap mass spectrometry resolves complex isomeric and isobaric mixtures, while molecular formula modeling through Van Krevelen coordinates provides chemical classification across reaction parameters. Integrating Discovery Studio TOPKAT modeling immediately identifies which reaction byproducts exhibit actionable liabilities regarding genetic toxicity, organ toxicity, or contact sensitization.

This integrated workflow demonstrates that non-volatile heterocyclic intermediates, historically overlooked in favor of volatile aroma compounds such as pyrazines, can carry substantial toxicological relevance. Applying this dual analytical-predictive platform allows food safety scientists to optimize thermal processing parameters—such as precursor concentrations, heating duration, and temperature regimes—to mitigate the formation of deleterious multi-nitrogen and sulfur-containing heterocyclic toxicants while preserving desirable organoleptic qualities.

- Cross-referencing high-resolution mass spectra against mzCloud and ChemSpider spectral libraries enabled rigorous compound identification under 5 ppm mass tolerance.

- In silico QSAR models provided rapid high-throughput screening benchmarks for emerging thermal processing contaminants without requiring immediate live animal bioassays.

## Analytical Constraints and Dietary Applicability Scope

This study provides detailed structural catalogs and predictive toxicological endpoints using aqueous model Maillard reactions, but practical dietary implications require further matrix validation and in vivo empirical testing.

- Reaction conditions utilized simplified aqueous precursor mixtures at 180 ℃ for 0.5 h, omitting lipid, polyphenol, and mineral matrices present in complex foods that alter Maillard cyclization kinetics.

- Toxicity assessments were established through in silico QSAR modeling (Discovery Studio TOPKAT) without complementary bacterial reverse mutation assays (Ames test) or animal toxicological bioassays.

- Quantitation of identified high-risk heterocycles in commercially processed thermal food commodities was not conducted and warrants targeted chromatographic monitoring.

Detailed process conditions, instrument calibrations, and complete supplementary datasets beyond the core quantitative benchmarks are preserved in the Peer-Reviewed PDF Edition below.

# High-Resolution Mass Spectrometry Analysis and Toxicity Prediction of Heterocyclic Products in the Serine/Methionine-Glucose Maillard Reaction

---

**DOI:** `10.13995/j.cnki.11-1802/ts.045791` | **Journal:** Food and Fermentation Industries (食品与发酵工业) | **Year:** 2026  
**Authors:** LIU Di, LIU Xia, ZHAO Xiaolei, HE Jinxing, HAN Zhonghui  
**Affiliation:** School of Food Science and Engineering, Qilu University of Technology (Shandong Academy of Sciences), Jinan 250353, China

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

The Maillard reaction generates extensive arrays of heterocyclic compounds during thermal food processing; however, prior evaluations have predominantly concentrated on aromatic flavor contributions rather than comprehensive structural profiling or toxicological hazards. In this work, model Maillard reaction systems comprising D-glucose coupled with either L-serine or L-methionine were reacted at 180 ℃ for 0.5 h. Reaction mixtures were analyzed using Q-Exactive Orbitrap high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) across m/z 50 to 750 at 60,000 FWHM resolving power, followed by Van Krevelen diagram visualization and in silico toxicity prediction via Discovery Studio TOPKAT. The serine-glucose system generated 198 heterocyclic products, divided into CHON (27 species) and CHON1+x (171 species). In contrast, the methionine-glucose system yielded 159 heterocyclic products across four distinct compositional classes: CHON (12 species), CHONS (5 species), CHON1+x (114 species), and CHON1+xS (28 species). Both reaction systems were dominated by multi-nitrogen CHON1+x heterocycles, primarily pyrrole, imidazole, and pyrazine derivatives, while methionine uniquely mediated the formation of sulfur-containing heterocycles such as thiazoles and thiophenes. Toxicological screening revealed 16 heterocyclic compounds exhibiting marked mutagenicity, developmental toxicity, or dermal sensitization probabilities exceeding 0.7, alongside low oral LD50 and inhalation LC50 thresholds. These findings delineate how amino acid side-chain architecture directs heterocyclic reaction pathways, providing empirical benchmarks and computational methodologies for assessing thermal processing safety.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Thermal reaction at 180 ℃ for 0.5 h generated 198 heterocyclic products in the serine-glucose model system and 159 in the methionine-glucose system.
- Serine products separated into 27 CHON and 171 CHON1+x species, while methionine generated 12 CHON, 5 CHONS, 114 CHON1+x, and 28 CHON1+xS compounds.
- Substrate depletion assays showed serine reduced glucose residual levels to 26% and 23% at 1:1 and 2:1 ratios, whereas methionine left 43% and 17% residual glucose.
- Fluorescence emission intensity at 450 nm was twice as intense in the serine-glucose reaction mixture compared to the methionine-glucose mixture.
- Discovery Studio TOPKAT screening identified 16 high-risk heterocycles exhibiting mutagenicity, developmental toxicity, or cutaneous sensitization probabilities exceeding 0.7.

## Pedological Stratification and Profile Redistribution Dynamics

Continuous flooded co-culture in IRCC fields establishes extended hydrologic saturation exceeding 320 days annually. This sustained anaerobic condition coupled with crayfish burrowing bioturbation promotes deep translocation of nutrients. Consequently, total phosphorus (TP) and Olsen-P in IRCC exhibit uniform profile behavior with mild increases in deeper horizons, peaking at 20-30 cm depth (699.6±34.8 mg/kg TP and 657.5±45.9 mg/kg inorganic P).

Conversely, restoring paddy-upland rotation through winter oilseed rape cultivation introduces cyclic redox dynamics and seasonal aerobic dry phases. In IRCC-PR systems, double-crop agronomic management applies chemical fertilization during both the rice phase (75 kg/hm2 P2O5) and rapeseed phase (60 kg/hm2 P2O5). Because phosphorus fertilizers are applied as basal dressings into highly sorptive silt loam matrixes, exogenous phosphorus concentrates predominantly within the 0-20 cm plow layer.

Surface accumulation is further reinforced by crop biomass return, where phosphorus absorbed during vegetative stages concentrates in topsoil post-residue incorporation. In IRCC-PR, surface 0-5 cm TP reaches 810.4±102.3 mg/kg, contrasting sharply with 545.4±11.8 mg/kg at 30-50 cm depth. Soil organic matter in IRCC-PR surface horizons similarly increases to 51.8±11.0 g/kg, supporting microbial immobilization in the topsoil.

- Surface 0-5 cm Olsen-P in IRCC-PR is 5.1 times higher than the 30-50 cm subsoil layer.

- IRCC plow layer (0-5 cm) TP is 636.8±31.9 mg/kg, whereas 20-30 cm subsoil reaches 699.6±34.8 mg/kg.

- Rapeseed and rice dual-cropping under IRCC-PR applies two seasonal fertilizer cycles, whereas IRCC receives fertilization solely during the rice cycle.

Transitioning continuous integrated rice-crayfish co-culture (IRCC) back to traditional rice-upland rotation (IRCC-PR) alters soil phosphorus dynamics across the 0-50 cm soil profile. While Moderate-P constitutes the primary fraction (57.2%-72.7%) across systems, IRCC-PR elevates the relative proportions of Labile-P and Residual-P while decreasing Moderate-P. Crucially, IRCC-PR establishes steep vertical stratification, exhibiting 5.1-fold higher Olsen-P and 3.0-fold higher alkaline phosphatase activity in surface soils (0-5 cm) relative to deep subsurface layers (30-50 cm). Consequently, agronomic runoff and surface erosion supersede subsoil leaching as primary phosphorus loss pathways under rotation restoration.

## Modified Hedley Fractionation and Bioavailability Shifts

Sequential chemical fractionation indicates that inorganic phosphorus (Pi) forms constitute the vast majority of both Moderate-P and Labile-P across all treatments. In IRCC-PR, the mean proportion of Labile-Pi rises to 2.7±1.4% and Residual-P reaches 35.0±3.8%, while Moderate-Pi drops to 57.8±1.7%. Under continuous IRCC, Moderate-Pi remains higher at 63.9±0.7% with Residual-P at 31.1±0.7%.

The expansion of Labile-P pools under IRCC-PR elevates instantaneous bioavailability for crop uptake during the active growing season. However, this shift simultaneously depletes intermediate buffering capacity represented by moderately labile pools. Over extended crop cycles, depletion of Moderate-P constrains long-term soil phosphorus replenishment capacity, requiring calibrated supplementary fertilizer inputs to prevent exhaustion.

Enzymatic analysis reveals that alkaline phosphatase activity (APA) closely tracks Olsen-P stratification in rotation fields (r = 0.65, P < 0.01). Surface APA in IRCC-PR reaches 554.6 mg/(kg·h) before declining to 183.5 mg/(kg·h) at depth, whereas continuous submergence in IRCC suppresses overall extracellular enzyme activity across the profile.

- Mean Olsen-P across tested treatments remains 6.1 mg/kg (range 1.8-12.4 mg/kg), reflecting general phosphorus deficiency.

## Methodological Scope and Geochemical Limitations

This empirical evaluation characterizes short-term rotation restoration in Jianghan Plain silt loam paddies under specific fertilization and hydrology.

- Field sampling was conducted at a single geographical site in Yanwo Town, Honghu City, which restricts direct generalization to non-calcareous or acidic paddy soils.

- Restoration observations encompass a two-year window (October 2020 to May 2022); multi-decadal recovery rates and long-term legacy phosphorus drawdown require extended monitoring.

- Average Olsen-P across experimental plots measured 6.1 mg/kg (range 1.8-12.4 mg/kg), maintaining the site in a phosphorus-deficient regime relative to typical agronomic benchmarks.

## Agronomic Nitrogen Coupling and Photosynthetic Capacity

In high-latitude cold agricultural zones, low spring soil temperatures decelerate crop residue decomposition. When rice straw is incorporated into albic soils, initial microbial decomposition triggers intense biological nitrogen immobilization, competing directly with juvenile rice seedlings during the critical tillering phase. To resolve this nutrient deficit, side-deep nitrogen fertilization deposits fertilizer precisely 3 cm lateral to the seedling row at a depth of 5 cm. This mechanical placement concentrates available inorganic nitrogen within the rhizosphere, accelerating early seedling root uptake and compensating for microbial immobilization.

Functional leaf diagnostics confirmed that photosynthetic physiological activity responded dynamically across phenological stages. Under straw returning conditions, split side-deep nitrogen fertilization (B2) elevated tillering functional leaf SPAD readings by 22.97% over conventional broadcast fertilization (B3). During heading and grain-filling phases, deep-placed fertilizer sustained higher flag-leaf transpiration rates, stomatal conductance, and intercellular carbon dioxide concentrations, counteracting late-stage senescence and maintaining active photosynthetic dry matter accumulation.

- Straw incorporation at 7,500 kg·hm-2 typically induces early microbial nitrogen starvation in cold albic soils.

- Precision placement at 3 cm lateral offset and 5 cm depth establishes a concentrated root-zone fertility reservoir.

- Maintained leaf SPAD values during the reproductive phase support extended photosynthetic assimilatory capacity.

This study examines the agronomic impacts of combining rice straw returning with optimized nitrogen placement modes in a cold-region rice production system over two consecutive cultivation seasons (2021-2022). Evaluating straw incorporation (7,500 kg·hm-2) against straw removal across three nitrogen management schemes, researchers identified that pairing straw returning with side-deep fertilization featuring split base-tiller applications mitigates early-stage nitrogen competition. This specific coupling significantly improves leaf chlorophyll SPAD values, photosynthetic gas exchange, antioxidant peroxidase activity, spikelet numbers per panicle, and grain protein content, providing an actionable fertilization regime for cold-region paddy management.

## Antioxidant Enzyme Regulation and Panicle Architecture

Environmental stress and metabolic shifts during grain filling accelerate reactive oxygen species generation, prompting cellular lipid peroxidation. Enzymatic assays revealed that straw returning paired with side-deep fertilization distinctly upregulated flag-leaf antioxidant defense systems. In 2021, heading-stage peroxidase activity under straw returning exceeded straw removal by 40.03%, with the A2B2 combination achieving a 507.37% increase over A2B3, facilitating rapid peroxide clearance and preserving cellular membrane integrity.

Panicle architectural metrics reflected these physiological adaptations. While straw returning reduced total panicle density by 6.64% in 2022 due to early thermal and nutrient constraints, it significantly elevated grains per panicle by 6.26%. Within the straw returning matrix, the B2 nitrogen mode produced the highest individual panicle grain count, outperforming conventional broadcast application by 1.95% and preserving total yield stability across both experimental seasons.

- Peroxidase activity under A2B2 at heading stage was 507.37% higher than under A2B3 in 2021.

- Straw incorporation increased overall grains per panicle by 6.26% while decreasing panicle count by 6.64% in 2022.

- Enhanced reactive oxygen scavenging minimized structural cellular damage during critical carbohydrate translocation windows.

## Milling Quality Attributes and Nutritional Tradeoffs

Straw returning and localized nitrogen placement exerted multidimensional effects on post-harvest grain quality. In 2022, straw returning significantly improved head rice yield by 4.30% relative to straw removal, indicating reinforced structural grain resilience during mechanical milling. Concurrently, chalkiness incidence responded strongly to the nitrogen split: within straw-returned pots, the B2 regime recorded higher chalkiness rates and chalkiness degrees compared to simultaneous single-dose side-deep placement (B1).

Nutritional and palatability evaluations displayed inverse correlations typical of high-latitude japonica varieties. Straw returning increased grain crude protein content by 6.91% in 2021 and 12.73% in 2022 compared to straw removal. While increased protein accumulation under A2B2 bolstered nutritional density, it reduced rice taste scores by 2.17% in 2021 and 2.38% in 2022, highlighting the operational necessity of balancing nitrogen partitioning between yield components and premium eating quality.

- Head rice rate improved by 4.30% under straw incorporation during the 2022 evaluation cycle.

- Crude protein content was enhanced by 6.91% in 2021 and 12.73% in 2022 through straw returning.

- Taste evaluation scores decreased by 2.17% to 2.38% under straw returning as grain protein levels increased.

## Regional Boundary Constraints and Experimental Limitations

This study was conducted under controlled outdoor pot-culture conditions in Daqing, Heilongjiang Province, utilizing albic soil with an organic matter baseline of 28.98 g·kg-1 and a fixed straw return dosage of 7,500 kg·hm-2.

- The empirical observations were derived from pot trials simulating field geometry; multi-hectare mechanized field validations are required to quantify actual farm-scale spatial soil temperature fluctuations.

- The 7,500 kg·hm-2 incorporation rate was evaluated as a single constant level, leaving variable straw dosage interactions with side-deep fertilization unexamined.

- The biological responses reflect the specific genetic architecture of japonica cultivar Kenjing 8 and may exhibit differing phenological responses in longer-duration indica varieties.

# Effects of Straw Returning and Nitrogen Application on Physiological Characteristics, Yield and Quality of Rice in Cold Area

---

**DOI:** `10.13304/j.nykjdb.2024.0429` | **Journal:** Journal of Agricultural Science and Technology (中国农业科技导报) | **Year:** 2026  
**Authors:** MENG Xianzhe, LI Zhuoran, LI Hongyu, ZHANG Hanxue, XIA Yuying, WANG Zhijun, LIU Jiachun, GAO Shengnan  
**Affiliation:** College of Agriculture, Heilongjiang Bayi Agricultural University

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

In order to examine the effects of straw returning and nitrogen application methods on rice in cold regions and provide technical support for efficient nutrient utilization, a two-factor completely randomized experiment was conducted using the japonica cultivar Kenjing 8 during 2021 and 2022. Factor A evaluated straw removal (A1) and straw returning (A2, 7,500 kg·hm-2), while Factor B assessed three fertilization regimes: side-deep nitrogen placement with simultaneous base-tiller fertilization (B1), side-deep placement with separate base-tiller fertilization (B2), and conventional broadcast nitrogen management (B3). Over two seasons, paddy yields showed no significant divergence between straw removal and straw returning main effects. However, in 2022, the A1B2 treatment generated the highest yield, surpassing A1B3 by 8.87%, while the A2B2 regime yielded the greatest grain number per panicle, exceeding A2B3 by 1.95%. Under A2B2, chalkiness rate and chalkiness degree increased by 158.89% and 143.75% relative to A2B1, and grain protein content peaked at a level 4.40% higher than A2B3. Furthermore, leaf SPAD values during the tillering stage peaked under A2B2, exceeding A2B3 by 22.97%. Coupling straw returning with split side-deep nitrogen application effectively alleviates early microbial nitrogen competition, enhances functional leaf photosynthesis, and increases panicle spikelets.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Under straw returning (A2), split side-deep nitrogen placement (B2) increased tillering-stage leaf SPAD values by 22.97% compared with conventional fertilization (A2B3).
- The A2B2 regime maximized grains per panicle in 2022, achieving a 1.95% significant enhancement over the conventional nitrogen practice (A2B3).
- Straw removal paired with split side-deep application (A1B2) yielded the highest overall output in 2022, improving yield by 8.87% relative to A1B3.
- Grain protein content reached its highest concentration under A2B2, demonstrating a 4.40% significant increase compared to A2B3.
- Two-year grain yields demonstrated no statistically significant differences between the overall main effects of straw returning (A2) and straw removal (A1).

analysis_markdown_en:
This study establishes an enzymatic extraction protocol using response surface methodology to recover soluble dietary fiber (SDF) from the discarded fruit pulp of Ziziphus jujuba var. Spinosa. Operating at an optimal cellulase dosage of 10 g / L, pH 4. 7, and 107 min extraction time, the verified experimental SDF yield reached 13. 12%. Comprehensive characterization revealed distinct functional divergence between SDF and insoluble dietary fiber (IDF). While IDF exhibited higher water-holding (23. 03 g / g) and oil-holding (5. 40 g / g) capacities driven by its folded surface morphology, SDF demonstrated superior in vitro hypoglycemic activity with a glucose adsorption capacity of 74. 65 mg / g and 84. 39% alpha-amylase inhibition.

## Response Surface Optimization and Reaction Kinetics

Sour jujube pulp represents an underutilized agricultural residue generated during the processing of Ziziphus jujuba var. Spinosa seeds for traditional pharmacopeia. To extract functional soluble dietary fiber, a Box-Behnken design evaluated three independent variables: cellulase dosage (5 to 15 g / L), pH (4. 5 to 5. 5), and extraction duration (60 to 120 min). Quadratic regression analysis established an empirical model with high statistical significance (P = 0. 001 8) and a determination coefficient of R2 = 0. 933 2 (adjusted R2 = 0. 847 4), with a non-significant lack of fit (P = 0. 095 5).

Linear and quadratic effects of all three variables exhibited significant influences on SDF yield, with relative impact order ranked as pH > cellulase concentration > extraction duration based on variance F-values. Under the optimized conditions of 10 g / L cellulase, pH 4. 7, and 107 min at 50 degrees Celsius, the experimental SDF yield reached 13. 12%, matching the predicted value of 12. 77%. Total dietary fiber purity was confirmed at 60. 75% for SDF and 78. 80% for IDF.

- Optimal extraction coordinates: 10 g / L cellulase dosage, pH 4. 7, 107 min at 50 degrees Celsius.

- Model validity: F-value of 11. 88, regression P-value of 0. 001 8, and lack-of-fit P-value of 0. 095 5.

## Macromolecular Architecture and Monosaccharide Fingerprinting

Morphological examination by scanning electron microscopy revealed marked structural divergences between the two fractions. SDF exhibited a relatively smooth exterior with dispersed microscopic pores and loose fibrillar texture resulting from enzymatic degradation. Conversely, IDF exhibited a highly folded, rough surface with deep convolutions, providing an expansive specific surface area suitable for mechanical entrapment of liquids and lipids.

Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy confirmed typical polysaccharide absorption bands in both fractions, including broad O-H stretching at 3 400 cm-1, C-H stretching at 2 800 to 3 000 cm-1, and carbonyl C=O vibrations at 1 700 to 1 750 cm-1 denoting uronic acids or esterified groups. Molecular weight determination of SDF identified two primary distribution peaks at 48. 5 and 762 kDa, representing fragmented oligosaccharide chains and high-mass polysaccharide polymers. Monosaccharide profiling revealed identical building blocks across both fractions, though IDF had higher proportions of arabinose (7. 81) and xylose (3. 23) relative to glucose (1. 00), whereas SDF possessed enriched galacturonic acid (1. 06).

- Dual molecular weight populations in SDF resolved at 48. 5 and 762 kDa.

- X-ray diffraction displayed crystalline reflection peaks at 19. 1 degrees and 21. 4 degrees, with sharper intensities observed in native IDF.

## In Vitro Hypoglycemic and Hypolipidemic Mechanisms

Hydration and oil-binding assays demonstrated that IDF surpassed SDF in physical retention properties, achieving a water-holding capacity of 23. 03 g / g, oil-holding capacity of 5. 40 g / g, and swelling expansion of 11. 00 g / mL. In contrast, SDF exhibited functional advantages in glycemic moderation. When evaluated across glucose concentrations from 0. 2 to 1. 2 mg / mL, the glucose adsorption capacity of SDF reached 74. 65 mg / g, surpassing IDF at elevated substrate concentrations due to viscous gel network formation.

Enzymatic inhibition assays confirmed that SDF markedly suppressed alpha-amylase activity, scaling positively with fiber mass up to a maximum inhibition rate of 84. 39%, substantially exceeding IDF across all test concentrations. In lipid adsorption assessments, the fibers displayed complementary gastrointestinal behavior. In an acidic gastric environment (pH = 2), SDF bound 79. 65 mg / g of cholesterol compared to 29. 80 mg / g for IDF. In neutral intestinal conditions (pH = 7), IDF bound 81. 09 mg / g of cholesterol compared to 38. 46 mg / g for SDF.

- Glucose adsorption capacity achieved 74. 65 mg / g for SDF at 1. 2 mg / mL glucose concentration.

- Alpha-amylase inhibition reached 84. 39% for SDF, demonstrating strong in vitro antidiabetic potential.

## Process Scale Limitations and Translation Boundary Conditions

The findings establish precise benchmark parameters for laboratory-scale enzymatic extraction of sour jujube fiber, but industrial adoption requires verification across continuous processing systems and in vivo metabolic pathways.

- Optimization was conducted using batch water-bath shaking with 34 g pulp aliquots, requiring validation in pilot-scale bioreactors where mass transfer and shear forces differ.

- Biological activities such as alpha-amylase suppression (84. 39%) and glucose adsorption (74. 65 mg / g) were quantified via in vitro assays without validation in living animal models.

- Ethanol precipitation recovery (4 volumes of ethanol) introduces solvent recycling energy costs that require techno-economic modeling prior to commercial deployment.

Detailed process conditions, instrument calibrations, and complete supplementary datasets beyond the core quantitative benchmarks are preserved in the Peer-Reviewed PDF Edition below.

This study evaluates the agronomic and biochemical feasibility of recycling agricultural chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum × morifolium Ramat) stems as a partial or full replacement for corn cobs in Pleurotus ostreatus cultivation substrates. Incorporating chrysanthemum stems across 6 gradient ratios (10% to 100%) significantly modified substrate aeration, carbon-to-nitrogen ratios, and enzymatic transformation. A 40% substitution (T3) accelerated mycelial colonization to 0.758 cm·d-1, whereas a 60% substitution (T4) yielded the maximum fresh mushroom harvest of 866.09 g per bag and a peak biological efficiency of 86.61%. Furthermore, enriched substrates elevated soluble protein, crude polysaccharides, flavonoids, total phenolics, and free radical scavenging performance while reducing crude lipid accumulation.

## Substrate Physical Properties and Mycelial Colonization Kinetics

Chrysanthemum cultivation generates substantial post-harvest residue, where non-medicinal stems represent 77.8% of total plant biomass. Direct field return of these residues is severely constrained by phytotoxic autotoxicity, microbial nitrogen starvation, and pest transmission. Pulverizing chrysanthemum stalks to 0.5 to 1.0 cm particle size establishes an advantageous balance between bulk porosity and moisture retention when blended with traditional corn cob substrates. The native chrysanthemum stem substrate contained 70.41% organic carbon, 0.76% total nitrogen, 0.077% total phosphorus, and 0.875% total potassium, offering superior nitrogenous nutrition compared to conventional corn cob.

Hyphal vegetative extension exhibited pronounced stimulation under intermediate stem loadings. Mycelial growth velocity followed the hierarchy T3, T4 > T2, T5 > T1 > CK, T6. In the 40% stem treatment (T3), hyphae achieved an optimal linear growth velocity of 0.758 cm·d-1, forming dense, bright white colonies. However, total replacement with 100% chrysanthemum stems (T6) depressed mycelial elongation rates down to parity with the control, caused by the progressive accumulation of antimicrobial volatile oils and flavonoids alongside substrate compaction.

- Dry pulverization of chrysanthemum stems to 0.5-1.0 cm maintains optimal aeration and hyphal anchorage.

- Substrate C:N ratio was modified from 100:1 in pure corn cob toward 76:1 in an 80% chrysanthemum stem blend.

- Excessive stem inclusion beyond 60% triggered hyphal growth deceleration due to concentrated antimicrobial allelochemicals.

## Bioactive Phytochemical Translocation and Radical Scavenging Capacity

Chrysanthemum stem supplementation triggered striking compositional shifts in basidiocarp secondary metabolites and macronutrients. Crude fat content declined from 2.27% in control mushrooms to 1.30% in T5, as enhanced nitrogen availability directed primary carbon fluxes toward structural peptide synthesis rather than lipid storage droplets. Soluble protein culminated at 33.70% in T4 (a 28.72% enhancement over CK), while crude polysaccharides and reducing sugars rose to 13.05 g·100 g-1 (T6) and 51.29 mg·g-1 (T5), driven by the 47.13% cellulose fraction present in chrysanthemum stems.

Total phenolics and flavonoids accumulated in direct proportion to substrate chrysanthemum content, reaching 4.35 mg·g-1 and 0.45 mg·g-1 in T6, representing 1.38-fold and 1.73-fold elevations over CK. Concomitantly, ABTS radical scavenging capacity climbed by 82.36% in T5 and 78.32% in T4 compared with CK. DPPH radical quenching capacity peaked in T3 at 16.19%, aligning with peak ferric reducing antioxidant power. Principal component analysis confirmed that PC1 and PC2 accounted for 88.154% of cumulative variance across 6 major nutritional indices.

- Total phenolic concentration scaled steadily from 3.14 mg·g-1 in CK to 4.35 mg·g-1 in pure chrysanthemum stem substrate.

- ABTS radical scavenging efficiency surged by 82.36% in T5 relative to pure corn cob controls.

- Essential amino acid pool reached 81.30 mg·g-1 in T5, representing a 38% elevation above control basidiocarps.

## Operational Boundary Conditions and Agronomic Constraints

While replacing up to 60% corn cobs with chrysanthemum stalks improves productivity and nutritional profile, higher inclusion rates incur biological penalties linked to chemical and physical substrate properties.

- Substrate ratios exceeding 60% chrysanthemum stem content (T5 and T6) suppressed total yields to 818.67 g and 804.77 g per bag, caused by suboptimal carbon-to-nitrogen balance (around 76:1) and accumulation of natural antimicrobial terpenoids and flavonoids.

- Investigation was restricted to Pleurotus ostreatus strain 7887 cultivated under indoor bag environments; performance across differing commercial macrofungal cultivars or outdoor bed systems remains unverified.

- Mechanical pre-processing requires crushing stalks to 0.5-1.0 cm dimensions and solid-state pre-fermentation for 5-7 d to alleviate structural compaction and optimize fungal enzymatic access.

## Phenotypic Variation and Multivariate Trait Correlations Across Introgression Lines

Wild relatives of tomato provide essential genetic diversity to counteract the narrow genetic base of modern commercial cultivars. Solanum pimpinellifolium accession LA1598 was introgressed into the elite Solanum lycopersicum cultivar Taikonghongzuan to assemble a stabilized BC2F1 population. Whole-genome tracking using a 50K tomato SNP array and KASP genotyping confirmed that 19 selected lines harbored donor chromosomal segments covering the donor genome across 12,183 polymorphic SNP markers. Agronomic characterization encompassed 53 parameters, comprising 35 qualitative and 18 quantitative traits measured under plastic greenhouse cultivation in Ping'an District, Haidong City, Qinghai Province.

Begonia fruit (Calophyllum inophyllum L.) exhibits strong postharvest perishability due to high initial moisture content (85.0 +/- 1)%. Convective hot-air drying serves as a primary preservation technique, yet prolonged heat exposure often degrades product quality. Ultrasonic pretreatment generates acoustic cavitation in liquid media, subjecting plant tissue to localized tension and compression cycles. This physical action produces micro-channels and cellular micro-fissures without macroscopic collapse, dramatically lowering internal mass transfer resistance.

Drying rate curves demonstrated distinct acceleration and falling-rate periods, with the falling-rate stage dominating total dehydration duration. Untreated control slices required 1110, 510, and 300 min to reach the target wet-basis moisture content (<=10%) at 40, 60, and 80 deg C, respectively. Ultrasonic pretreatment at 384 W for 30 min reduced these durations to 600, 450, and 240 min. - Pretreatment at 384 W for 30 min elevated corresponding drying rates to 1.96 x 10^-4, 3.88 x 10^-4, and 1.77 x 10^-3 g/(g*min), yielding gains of 391.23%, 101.34%, and 206.75%.

Paraffin sectioning combined with safranin and fast green double staining captured the progressive deformation of parenchyma cells across dehydration stages. Fresh parenchyma cells exhibited cross-sectional areas of 10000 to 30000 um^2 (peak at 18771.49 um^2), perimeters of 460 to 1000 um (peak at 615.79 um), and equivalent diameters of 130 to 210 um (peak at 154.60 um). As moisture ratio declined from 1.0 to 0.2, removal of free and bound water induced cell wall folding, rupture, and significant leftward shifts in probability density distributions, contracting terminal equivalent diameter peaks to 61.90 um.

To correlate macroscopic moisture loss with microscopic cellular shrinkage, a cubic polynomial model (Y = a*X^3 + b*X^2 + c*X + d) was implemented, where X represents the moisture ratio and Y represents the structural parameter ratio. Regression analysis revealed strong fitting accuracy across all thermal and ultrasonic treatments, with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.9899. The model exhibited exceptionally high fidelity for cell perimeter and equivalent diameter ratios (R^2 reaching 1.0000), confirming their utility as representative microscopic indicators for monitoring moisture transport.

## Operational Boundaries and Implementation Constraints

While ultrasonic cavitation accelerates dehydration, inappropriate power or exposure can impair capillary structure. Mathematical models remain constrained to specific sample geometries and laboratory convective setups.

- Excessive sonication duration (45 min at 384 W) elevated final sample hardness to 13.00 N and extended drying time to 840 min due to internal structural compaction.

- Empirical microstructural models were calibrated on uniform slices of 6 mm thickness and 60 mm diameter, requiring recalibration for varying fruit dimensions.

## Database Heterogeneity and In Vivo Assay Discrepancies

Formulating low-protein, low-soybean meal diversified diets in monogastric livestock production depends entirely on the precision of ingredient nutritional matrices. In current practice, feed manufacturers and researchers rely on distinct compendia, including the Dutch CVB, US NRC, Brazilian Tables, and Chinese national standards. Cross-comparison reveals substantial inter-database divergence for identical feed ingredients. In growing pigs, the range between the lowest and highest published net energy values spans 0.52 MJ·kg-1 for corn, 1.46 MJ·kg-1 for soybean meal, 0.82 MJ·kg-1 for cottonseed meal, 1.16 MJ·kg-1 for canola meal, 2.77 MJ·kg-1 for sunflower seed meal, 1.32 MJ·kg-1 for peanut meal, and 1.56 MJ·kg-1 for corn distillers dried grains with solubles (DDGS). For poultry apparent metabolizable energy, cross-database disparities reach 1.16 MJ·kg-1 for corn, 1.68 MJ·kg-1 for soybean meal, and 2.29 MJ·kg-1 for peanut meal.

These divergences stem from fundamental methodological inconsistencies across compiling organizations. Literature-aggregated compendia aggregate experiments conducted under heterogeneous protocols, animal physiological stages, and assay methodologies. In vivo metabolic studies demonstrate that pre-fasting regimens can alter energy, ether extract, and crude protein digestibility values by 3.5%, 18.56%, and -8.1%, respectively, resulting in a 1.59% shift in apparent metabolizable energy. Chemical analytical discrepancies further distort energy estimates: interlaboratory comparisons across three research institutions analyzing 15 corn DDGS samples demonstrated bomb calorimetry gross energy differences reaching 1.35 MJ·kg-1 due to differing sample encapsulation techniques, while neutral detergent fiber and acid detergent fiber values diverged by 20% to 40% between facilities.

- In vivo fasting vs. non-fasting protocols induce up to 18.56% shifts in ether extract digestibility measurements.

- Calorimetric sample containment variations cause interlaboratory gross energy differences up to 1.35 MJ·kg-1.

- Static regression models suffer target mismatch when fed chemical values derived from unaligned analytical pipelines.

Feed represents 60% to 70% of total costs in swine and poultry operations. Establishing diversified low-protein and low-soybean meal diets requires precise nutritional characterization of diverse feedstuffs. Discrepancies across major international databases (CVB, NRC, Brazilian Tables, and Chinese standards) highlight the severe limitations of static literature-derived values and variable laboratory protocols. Researchers developed an automated monogastric bionic digestion system integrating physiological intestinal parameters, standardized endogenous digestive enzyme kits, and dynamic fluid automation.
