## Soil Acidity Mitigation and Nutrient Availability Dynamics

Intensive vegetable cropping in southern China relies heavily on nitrogen inputs exceeding 300 kg hm-2 a-1, causing annual soil pH declines of 0.3 to 0.5 units and severe soil structural degradation. In this field evaluation conducted on acidic purple clay loam (baseline pH 5.0), single applications of organic fertilizer or potassium humate did not significantly alter pH, exchangeable acidity (ExA), or exchangeable aluminum (ExAl), because early organic matter decomposition produces organic acids and releases protons. In contrast, treatments containing calcium carbonate significantly neutralized acidity, raising non-rhizosphere pH by 0.53 to 1.22 units and rhizosphere pH by 0.51 to 0.95 units while drastically depleting ExAl.

Sole addition of calcium carbonate introduced notable nutrient trade-offs: although it suppressed soil acidity, it decreased non-rhizosphere available phosphorus from 48.48±8.52 mg kg-1 to 35.56±4.97 mg kg-1, and reduced rhizosphere available potassium from 230.0±6.0 mg kg-1 to 161.7±13.6 mg kg-1. This decline stemmed from elevated calcium-potassium competitive leaching and phosphate precipitation onto hydroxy-aluminum polymers. Combining calcium carbonate with organic fertilizer and potassium humate counteracted these losses, maintaining non-rhizosphere available phosphorus at 40.91±6.10 mg kg-1 and increasing available potassium to 276.0±55.0 mg kg-1 in the full-dose MPC regime.

- Sole calcium carbonate increased non-rhizosphere exchangeable Ca2+ from 10.43±0.27 cmol kg-1 to 25.43±6.25 cmol kg-1.

- Non-rhizosphere exchangeable acidity dropped from 5.62±0.70 cmol kg-1 in CK to 0.69±0.23 cmol kg-1 under half-dose co-amendment (mpc).

- Rhizosphere alkali-hydrolyzable nitrogen dropped across all amended regimes compared to the unamended control level of 320.8±19.8 mg kg-1.

Intensive vegetable cultivation with high nitrogen inputs accelerates soil acidification and degrades biological functionality. This field study evaluates calcium carbonate, bio-organic fertilizer, potassium humate, and their combined applications across acidic purple clay-loam soils. While isolated calcium carbonate raised pH, it decreased available phosphorus and rhizosphere organic carbon pools. Conversely, combined treatments containing full-dose calcium carbonate (4,500 kg hm-2), organic fertilizer (3,000 kg hm-2), and potassium humate (450 kg hm-2) significantly neutralized acidity, elevated labile organic carbon fractions, expanded microbial biomass, and increased Chinese cabbage fresh yield by up to 10,500 kg hm-2.

## Organic Carbon Fractionation and Microbial Community Regulation

Labile organic carbon pools responded rapidly to amendment regimes. Microbial community profiling via phospholipid fatty acid analysis demonstrated that non-rhizosphere total PLFA, bacteria, fungi, and Gram-positive bacteria were strongly enhanced by organic inputs, whereas solitary calcium carbonate altered fungal-to-bacterial proportions. Redundancy analysis indicated that non-rhizosphere microbial community variance was explained primarily by alkali-hydrolyzable nitrogen (axis 1 and 2 explaining 58.09% of total variation). ## Structural Equation Modeling of Crop Productivity Drivers

Fresh Chinese cabbage yield increased across all treated plots by 2,745 kg hm-2 to 10,500 kg hm-2 relative to the untreated control. Correlation analyses confirmed that cabbage yield correlated positively with non-rhizosphere pH, rhizosphere exchangeable Ca2+, and exchangeable Mg2+, while correlating negatively with soil exchangeable acidity and exchangeable aluminum. A notable negative correlation was observed between cabbage yield and rhizosphere alkali-hydrolyzable nitrogen, resulting from intensified crop nutrient uptake and vegetative assimilation under remediated pH conditions.

Structural equation modeling exhibited robust data fit in both non-rhizosphere (chi-square/df = 1.260, df=5, P=0.939, CFI=1.000, SRMR=0.013, RMSEA=0) and rhizosphere soils (chi-square/df = 5.299, df=6, P=0.506, CFI=1.000, SRMR=0.047, RMSEA=0). In non-rhizosphere domains, cabbage yield was primarily driven by exchangeable Ca2+, with alkali-hydrolyzable nitrogen modulated by easily oxidizable carbon and Gram-negative bacteria. In the rhizosphere, yield was directly influenced by alkali-hydrolyzable nitrogen, available phosphorus, and Gram-positive bacteria, while Gram-negative bacteria contributed indirectly through organic phosphorus mineralization.

## Field Experimental Scope and Management Caveats

This investigation examines single-season response dynamics within subtropical purple soil under specific application rates of inorganic and organic amendments.

- Evaluation was conducted over a single cropping cycle (October 2022 to January 2023) in subtropical purple clay loam, necessitating multi-year seasonal validation across diverse soil textures.

- Solitary application of full-dose calcium carbonate (4,500 kg hm-2) induced nutrient antagonism, significantly reducing non-rhizosphere available phosphorus and rhizosphere available potassium.

- High application rates of calcium carbonate without organic matter accelerated rhizosphere organic carbon mineralization, decreasing rhizosphere SOC by 14.03% relative to the untreated control.

## 1. Executive Abstract

Vegetable production is frequently associated with high nitrogen fertilizer application and intensive crop rotation, resulting in soil acidification, structural degradation, and proliferation of harmful microorganisms. This study investigated the short-term effects of organic fertilizer, potassium humate, calcium carbonate, and their combinations on soil properties, organic carbon components, and microbial community structure in acidic vegetable fields with an untreated control (CK). Redundancy analysis indicated that non-rhizosphere microbial communities were primarily driven by alkali-hydrolyzable nitrogen, whereas available potassium and DOC governed rhizosphere communities. Structural equation modeling revealed that exchangeable Ca2+, available phosphorus, and alkali-hydrolyzable nitrogen exerted significant positive effects on cabbage yield, demonstrating that co-application balances acidity remediation with nutrient retention.

This study decodes the genetic architecture of alkali tolerance in Brassica napus during seed germination using a 189-line recombinant inbred line population derived from APL01 and Holly. Seeds were evaluated under gradient alkaline stress of 35, 37.5, and 40 mmol·L-1 Na2CO3-NaHCO3 (2:1 molar ratio, pH 10.4). Across six environmental regimes, composite interval mapping identified 49 consensus QTLs, including six major loci on chromosomes A03 and A09 accounting for 10.01% to 22.80% of phenotypic variation. Eight candidate genes governing glutathione detoxification, ubiquitination, and kinase cascades were prioritized, establishing 37.5 mmol·L-1 Na2CO3-NaHCO3 at day 6 as the optimal screening standard.

## Phenotypic Variation and High-Density Linkage Mapping Architecture

Natural inland saline-alkali environments impose compounded stress through high pH coupled with sodium ion toxicity. To resolve the genetic foundations of alkali tolerance during initial seedling emergence, a high-density genetic map comprising 11,458 single nucleotide polymorphism markers and 57 simple sequence repeat markers across 2,755 bins spanning 2,027.53 cM with an average spacing of 0.72 cM was paired with phenotypic screening of 189 recombinant inbred lines. Seed germination was challenged under 35, 37.5, and 40 mmol·L-1 Na2CO3-NaHCO3 (2:1 molar ratio, initial pH 10.4) across cumulative 3-day and 6-day intervals.

The relative germination rate demonstrated normal distribution patterns across all 6 stress regimes, reflecting typical quantitative polygenic inheritance. Female parent APL01 exhibited superior tolerance compared to male parent Holly across all concentrations, while the progeny displayed extensive transgressive segregation ranging from 15.27% to 92.86%. Under 37.5 and 40 mmol·L-1 exposures, the population coefficient of variation reached 22.26% to 27.70%, with broad-sense heritability estimates spanning 0.50 to 0.60, confirming abundant genetic variation for linkage resolution.

- Initial composite interval mapping detected 80 identified QTLs across 17 chromosomes, which integrated via meta-analysis into 49 consensus QTLs.

- Chromosomes A03 and A09 harbored 6 stable major-effect QTLs satisfying single-environment PVE ≥ 20% or multi-environment PVE ≥ 10% criteria.

- Major QTLs clustered continuously across 12.50 to 21.68 cM on chromosome A09, demonstrating distinct alkali specificity compared to neutral salt loci.

## Candidate Gene Prioritization Within Chromosome A03 and A09 Major Loci

Genomic inspection of the confidence intervals underlying the 6 major-effect QTLs combined parental resequencing with Arabidopsis functional orthology. This delimited 8 primary candidate genes orchestrating cellular detoxification, reactive oxygen species buffering, and signal transduction cascades during germination under severe soda alkaline conditions.

Two prominent glutathione S-transferase genes were identified across distinct chromosomal clusters: BnaA03G0270500ZS encodes a Phi-class GST (GSTF3) within cqAlk.A03-1, while BnaA09G0171400ZS encodes a Tau-class GST (GSTU16) within cqAlk.A09-1. Both enzymes mediate glutathione conjugation to counter oxidative injury, though they deploy divergent catalytic actions. Plasma membrane aquaporin BnaA03G0280400ZS (orthologous to PIP1;4) coordinates water balance and hydrogen peroxide mobilization, whereas BnaA03G0260700ZS encodes an E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase (UPL5) targeting senescence transcription factors.

- BnaA09G0176600ZS encodes a serine/threonine protein kinase with an N-terminal myristoylation motif for membrane-anchored kinase signaling.

- BnaA09G0182400ZS encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor (BHLH96) operating in transcriptional stress regulation.

- BnaA09G0182300ZS encodes a late embryogenesis abundant domain protein governing cellular osmotic stabilization.

- BnaA09G0187500ZS encodes inositol-pentakisphosphate 2-kinase (IPK1), mediating phytic acid biosynthesis and phosphoinositide cascades.

## Germplasm Clustering and Evaluation Standard Verification

Two-step cluster analysis based on mean relative germination rates across all 6 environmental treatments classified the 189 lines into two distinct clusters with a silhouette cohesion measure of 0.5. The primary group encompassed 171 lines (90.47%), while the secondary tolerant cluster comprised 18 lines (9.52%) that sustained superior germination capacity across every dosage tier.

Cumulative stress using 37.5 mmol·L-1 Na2CO3-NaHCO3 for 6 days provided optimal phenotypic differentiation without inducing seedling necrosis. Imposing a stringent secondary filter of relative germination rate ≥ 70% under 40 mmol·L-1 exposure for 6 days isolated 6 elite alkali-tolerant lines: AH107, AH24, AH124, AH177, AH192, and AH182. Concurrently, sensitive lines AH25 and AH45 were designated as contrasting physiological controls.

- Cluster 2 accessions maintained relative germination rates of 76.57%~95.83% at 35 mmol·L-1, 67.13%~89.94% at 37.5 mmol·L-1, and 53%~76.68% at 40 mmol·L-1.

- Six elite accessions showed consistent performance exceeding 74.74% relative germination under 37.5 mmol·L-1 stress for 6 days.

- Cumulative stress of 37.5 mmol·L-1 Na2CO3-NaHCO3 for 6 days proved the most reliable phenotypic screening benchmark.

## Methodological Constraints and Physiological Context

This investigation utilized closed filter paper germination assays where medium pH shifted slightly over time, requiring cautious extrapolation to heterogeneous field soils.

- In the non-replenished petri dish filter paper assay, medium pH decreased by 0.2 to 0.6 from the initial value of 10.4 over 6 days due to seed imbibition and metabolic exudates.

- The genetic mapping utilized linkage map centimorgan coordinates, precluding exact physical basepair alignment with previously reported association mapping loci lacking common markers.

- Identified candidate genes were predicted via in silico homology and parental resequencing, requiring subsequent functional knockout or overexpression validation to confirm biological roles under field conditions.

analysis_markdown_en:
Ecological soilification of graphite mine tailings is hindered by excessive bulk density, poor water retention, deficient aggregate structure, and severe nutrient starvation. This investigation evaluates multi-component composite amendments—integrating fly ash, bentonite, cattle manure, and biochar—to systematically rehabilitate graphite tailings into viable soil substrates. Through orthogonal incubation experiments and principal component analysis, the synergistic treatments reduced bulk density by 4.68% to 26.32% and increased total porosity by 1.27% to 15.44%. The optimal formulation (30 g/kg fly ash, 60 g/kg bentonite, 60 g/kg cattle manure, and 75 g/kg biochar) established dominant water-stable macroaggregates while elevating available phosphorus and potassium.

## Synergistic Modification Mechanisms Across Soil Physical Architecture

Unamended graphite tailings exhibit a sandy loam texture (82.59% sand, 15.12% silt, and 2.29% clay) characterized by an unfavorable bulk density of 1.71 g/cm3 and a minimal total porosity of 39.50%. These physical constraints severely restrict gas exchange, root elongation, and moisture percolation. Single-modifier pre-trials established that corn straw biochar exerted the strongest individual effect on compaction alleviation, whereas alkaline fly ash exerted the strongest upward pressure on substrate pH. When co-formulated into composite matrices, the multi-component amendments engineered an interconnected structural skeleton that reduced tailings bulk density down to 1.26 g/cm3 and elevated total porosity up to 45.60%.

The remediation of pore geometry fundamentally altered matrix moisture dynamics. Saturated water holding capacity increased by up to 19.22% (reaching 387.73 g/kg in treatment T4 compared to 325.21 g/kg in the control), while field capacity improved by 22.14% to 53.52% across composite treatments. Mechanistically, biochar particles (0.25 to 0.50 mm) functioned as skeletal spacers preventing compaction of ultra-fine tailings grains, and their microporous networks (specific surface area 13.90 to 60.50 m2/g) provided substantial capillary suction. Concurrently, calcium bentonite formed surface skins that sealed excessive macro-voids, while fly ash contributed micro-aggregate packing and pozzolanic mineral hydration, collectively optimizing water retention without triggering waterlogging.

- Biochar micro-networks and skeletal spacing reduced matrix bulk density by up to 26.32%.

- Field water retention surged by 22.14% to 53.52% through combined capillary and hydrophilic binding.

## Aggregate Restructuring Dynamics and Chemo-Fertility Enhancement

The raw tailings substrate possessed an impoverished aggregate architecture, with water-stable macroaggregates (>0.25 mm) accounting for less than 10% of total mass and unstable microaggregates (<0.053 mm) dominating the matrix. Incorporation of the composite modifier initiated a pronounced phase transition from microaggregates to water-stable macroaggregates. Specifically, particles in the 0.25 to 2 mm fraction increased by 15.17% to 50.82%, while the sub-0.053 mm fraction contracted by 17.55% to 57.63%. This structural agglomeration is mediated by organic bridging from manure humic carboxyl (-COOH) and hydroxyl (-OH) functional groups, calcium ion (Ca2+) displacement of exchangeable sodium reducing repulsive zeta potential, and the precipitation of secondary iron/aluminum phosphates that physically cement mineral particles into durable organo-mineral complexes.

Chemical and nutritional rejuvenation was equally substantial across all experimental cohorts. Untreated tailings exhibited low organic matter (44.2 g/kg), low cation exchange capacity (3.41 cmol/kg), and severe deficiencies in available phosphorus (4.0 mg/kg) and available potassium (74.0 mg/kg). Composite amendments elevated organic matter by 29.19% to 112.90% and cation exchange capacity by 15.25% to 90.03%. Available phosphorus climbed to 7.38-24.48 times baseline values, driven by decomposed manure inputs, while available potassium surged to 6.01-17.58 times baseline levels due to potassium release from straw biochar. Although fly ash and biochar tended to elevate alkalinity, composite treatments stabilized matrix pH between 7.93 and 8.60, remaining safely below the secondary alkalization hazard threshold (pH >= 9.00).

- Water-stable macroaggregate formation was driven by polyvalent cation bridging and humic chelation.

- Soil fertility metrics saw up to 24.48-fold gains in available phosphorus and 17.58-fold gains in available potassium.

## Orthogonal Optimization and Multi-Criteria Index Evaluation

To resolve trade-offs among divergent soil quality endpoints, a two-principal-component model (eigenvalues of 5.89 and 1.81, accounting for 77.05% cumulative variance) was integrated with an extreme variance range methodology. Factor sensitivity rankings derived from the integrated soil quality index (ISQI) demonstrated that cattle manure served as the primary driver of overall soil reconstruction (R = 0.45), exerting dominant control over aggregate stability, organic matter, cation exchange capacity, and available phosphorus. Biochar ranked second (R = 0.41), governing physical compaction, total porosity, water retention, and potassium supply. Bentonite (R = 0.14) and fly ash (R = 0.09) acted as secondary physical and mineral stabilizers.

Evaluation across the orthogonal array positioned treatment T3 as the highest-performing experimental group, recording an ISQI of 2.98 compared to -4.12 for the untreated control. Extreme range analysis of factorial levels confirmed that the theoretical optimum configuration corresponds to level 3 across all amendments (A3B3C3D3): 30 g/kg fly ash, 60 g/kg bentonite, 60 g/kg cattle manure, and 75 g/kg biochar. This calibrated recipe simultaneously satisfies physical soil structure requirements, optimizes water and nutrient retention, and averts excessive alkalization, providing a robust operational pathway for solid-waste-derived mine tailings reclamation.

## Boundary Conditions, Heavy Metal Thresholds, and Field Scalability

The findings reflect controlled 3-month laboratory incubation trials evaluating graphite tailings from Jixi, Heilongjiang. Practical scaling requires strict adherence to ingredient pretreatment standards and environmental monitoring.

- Raw fly ash must undergo leaching pretreatment to reduce Cd content from 0.9 mg/kg to 0.4 mg/kg, ensuring compliance with agricultural environmental safety limits (GB 15618-2018).

- Fly ash application rates must not exceed 30 g/kg to prevent substrate alkalization beyond the threshold of pH 9.00.

- Biochar incorporation rates should be restricted to <=100 g/kg to prevent over-loosening of the matrix and loss of root-anchoring stability (bulk density <= 1.10 g/cm3).

- The evaluation focuses on short-term abiotic soilification; long-term rhizosphere microbial succession, enzymatic dynamics, and outdoor weather-driven leaching remain uncharacterized.

analysis_markdown_en:
The study addresses the bottleneck of low and unstable rice yields in high-latitude and high-altitude regions where cold stress at the booting stage causes severe spikelet sterility. By using SSR markers, which are more practical than RFLP for breeding, the authors mapped QTLs for cold tolerance and relative cold tolerance in an indica/japonica population. The identified QTLs individually explain only 5.6–10.3% of phenotypic variance, indicating that cold tolerance at booting is a complex quantitative trait controlled by multiple minor genes. This limits the immediate utility of linked markers for marker-assisted selection, as the authors note.

The practical relevance lies in the genetic resources and QTL intervals identified. 'Jileng 1' contributed most increasing alleles, confirming its value as a cold-tolerance donor. The tight linkage between qCTB4 and qRCTB4, and between qCTB11 and qRCTB11, suggests pleiotropy or close linkage, which could be exploited after fine-mapping. However, the low coverage of the SSR map (97 markers, 1,357.3 cM) likely underestimates the number of QTLs. Future work requires denser maps and multi-environment testing to identify stable QTLs for effective marker-assisted breeding.

### Abstract

Quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for cold tolerance and relative cold tolerance at the booting stage were identified using an F2:3 population of 200 lines derived from a cross between indica 'Milyang 23' and japonica 'Jileng 1'. Cold stress was applied in a cold-water irrigation nursery in Chuncheon, Korea, from 25 days after transplanting until maturity with 17 °C water at 5 cm depth. Seed setting rate under cold stress defined cold tolerance at the booting stage (CTB), while relative cold tolerance (RCTB) was the ratio of cold-stressed to control seed setting. A genetic linkage map of 97 SSR markers spanning 1,357.3 cM (average interval 13.99 cM) was constructed. Five QTLs for CTB were detected on chromosomes 1, 2, 4, 11, and 12, explaining 5.6–8.2% of phenotypic variance. Four QTLs for RCTB were mapped on chromosomes 1, 3, 4, and 11, explaining 5.9–10.3% of phenotypic variance. Six of the nine QTLs had increasing alleles from 'Jileng 1'. Gene action modes included additive, partial dominance, dominance, and overdominance. The correlation between CTB and RCTB was 0.837 (P<0.01). These results provide a basis for marker-assisted selection and cloning of cold-tolerance genes in rice.

## SSR-Based Linkage Map and QTL Detection for Booting-Stage Cold Tolerance

A linkage map was constructed from 200 F2 individuals using 97 polymorphic SSR markers selected from 196 primer pairs. The map covered 1,357.3 cM across 12 linkage groups with an average interval of 13.99 cM. QTL analysis was performed with MAPMAKER/QTL using a LOD threshold of 2.0. For cold tolerance at the booting stage (CTB), five QTLs were detected on chromosomes 1, 2, 4, 11, and 12, with LOD scores ranging from 2.07 to 3.18 and phenotypic variance explained (PVE) from 5.6% to 8.2%. The QTL with the largest effect was qCTB12 (LOD 2.83, PVE 8.2%), with increasing allele from 'Jileng 1'.

For relative cold tolerance at the booting stage (RCTB), four QTLs were identified on chromosomes 1, 3, 4, and 11, with LOD scores from 2.21 to 3.39 and PVE from 5.9% to 10.3%. qRCTB11 showed the highest LOD (3.39) and PVE (10.3%), with the increasing allele from 'Milyang 23'. Gene action was classified based on the dominance ratio (DR): additive (DR<0.2), partial dominance (0.2<DR<0.8), dominance (0.8<DR<1.2), and overdominance (DR>1.2). Among the nine QTLs, six had increasing alleles from 'Jileng 1', and three from 'Milyang 23'. The modes included additive (qRCTB3), partial dominance (qCTB2, qCTB12), dominance (qCTB1, qRCTB1, qRCTB4), and overdominance (qCTB4, qCTB11, qRCTB11).

## Phenotypic Evaluation under Cold-Water Irrigation and Correlation Analysis

The F3 lines were evaluated in a cold-water irrigation nursery at the Chuncheon Experiment Station, Korea, in 2002. Cold stress was applied from 25 days after transplanting until maturity using 17 °C water at 5 cm depth. A control plot with natural irrigation was maintained. Seed setting rate under cold stress (CTB) and relative cold tolerance (RCTB, calculated as cold-stressed seed setting divided by control seed setting ×100%) were measured. Under cold stress, the tolerant parent 'Jileng 1' had 62.9% seed setting, while the sensitive parent 'Milyang 23' had 10.5%. The F3 population averaged 34.2% under stress and 70.3% under control, with RCTB averaging 47.2%.

The frequency distributions of CTB and RCTB in the F3 population were continuous, approximating normal distributions, consistent with polygenic inheritance. The correlation coefficient between CTB and RCTB was 0.837, highly significant (P<0.01, critical value 0.208 at df=150). This strong correlation suggests either pleiotropy or tight linkage of QTLs affecting both traits. Indeed, qCTB4 and qRCTB4 were closely linked, as were qCTB11 and qRCTB11. However, no single QTL interval was found to affect both traits simultaneously. The authors note that the relatively low coverage of the SSR map may have limited QTL detection, and denser maps are needed to identify additional loci.

# Identification of QTLs for Cold Tolerance at the Booting Stage in Rice

---

**DOI:** `10.3724/SP.J.1006.2026.39.3435` | **Journal:** Acta Agronomica Sinica (Acta Agronomica Sinica (作物学报)) | **Published:** 2026 (Vol 46 39)  
**Authors:** HAN Longzhi, QIAO Yongli, ZHANG Yuanyuan, CAO Guilan, YEA Jong-Doo, KOH Hee-Jong  
**Institution:** Institute of Crop Germplasm Resources, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences  
**Portal:** `https://sinoagritech.com/paper/identification-of-qtls-for-cold-tolerance-at-the-booting-stage-in-rice-165975`

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

Quantitative trait loci (QTLs) for cold tolerance and relative cold tolerance at the booting stage were identified using an F2:3 population of 200 lines derived from a cross between indica 'Milyang 23' and japonica 'Jileng 1'. Cold stress was applied in a cold-water irrigation nursery in Chuncheon, Korea, from 25 days after transplanting until maturity with 17 °C water at 5 cm depth. Seed setting rate under cold stress defined cold tolerance at the booting stage (CTB), while relative cold tolerance (RCTB) was the ratio of cold-stressed to control seed setting. A genetic linkage map of 97 SSR markers spanning 1,357.3 cM (average interval 13.99 cM) was constructed. Five QTLs for CTB were detected on chromosomes 1, 2, 4, 11, and 12, explaining 5.6-8.2% of phenotypic variance. Four QTLs for RCTB were mapped on chromosomes 1, 3, 4, and 11, explaining 5.9-10.3% of phenotypic variance. Six of the nine QTLs had increasing alleles from 'Jileng 1'. Gene action modes included additive, partial dominance, dominance, and overdominance. The correlation between CTB and RCTB was 0.837 (P<0.01). These results provide a basis for marker-assisted selection and cloning of cold-tolerance genes in rice.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Five QTLs for cold tolerance at booting stage explained 5.6-8.2% of phenotypic variance each.
- Four QTLs for relative cold tolerance explained 5.9-10.3% of phenotypic variance, with qRCTB11 explaining 10.3%.
- Six of nine QTLs had increasing alleles from cold-tolerant parent 'Jileng 1'; gene actions included additive, partial dominance, dominance, and overdominance.
- CTB and RCTB correlated at r=0.837 (P<0.01), indicating shared genetic control or tight linkage.

analysis_markdown_en:
Accurate detection of carrot seedlings in natural field environments is impeded by leaf mutual occlusion, weed interference, and restricted compute on agricultural edge devices. This investigation introduces CD-YOLO, an optimized detector built upon YOLOv11s. The architecture integrates depthwise separable convolutions to diminish computational complexity, embeds an efficient multi-scale attention mechanism into the C3k2 block to aggregate fragmented spatial cues, and equips a dynamic detection head to adaptively weight multi-scale spatial representations. Operating with 15.3 GFLOPs and a compact 14.4 MB model footprint, CD-YOLO achieves 84.0% mAP0.5 and demonstrates robust inference on edge hardware.

## Architectural Decoupling and Lightweight Attention Integration

In intensive carrot cultivation, accurate seedling emergence auditing governs yield forecasting and robotic thinning. Natural field vision faces severe challenges: foliage self-overlap disrupts leaf contours, while co-occurring weeds display identical color characteristics. Standard two-stage and dense single-stage vision models demand excessive compute budgets that exceed the power constraints of field edge terminals. CD-YOLO addresses these constraints through a three-stage architectural progression balancing efficiency, feature recovery, and adaptive classification.

The backbone replaces standard CBS convolution operations with depthwise separable convolutions (DWConv). By splitting spatial filtering and pointwise cross-channel expansion, convolution arithmetic is curtailed substantially. Because independent spatial convolutions eliminate immediate cross-channel interactivity and risk representational attenuation, an Efficient Multi-Scale Attention (EMA) mechanism is embedded directly within the C3k2 blocks to yield C3k2_EMA. The EMA construct routes input tensors into three parallel branches (two 1x1 convolutions for cross-channel interdependencies and one 3x3 convolution for spatial receptive field coverage), re-establishing global and local pixel relationships across occluded leaf patches.

- Depthwise separable convolutions minimize redundant cross-channel matrix multiplication across early feature extractors.

- C3k2_EMA restores contextual semantic relationships across fragmented leaf segments via parallel 1x1 and 3x3 spatial pooling paths.

- A unified DynamicHead combines scale-aware and spatial-aware attention to dynamically adjust detection weights across non-uniform seedling layouts.

## Ablation Progression and Comparative Detector Benchmarks

Systematic ablation experiments demonstrate the mutual reinforcement of the lightweight backbone, attention-driven feature restoration, and multi-scale detection heads. Introducing DWConv exclusively (Trial 2) drops model complexity to 14.8 GFLOPs and 13.8 MB, but causes mAP0.5 to slip by 0.2 percentage points due to inter-channel information degradation. Integrating C3k2_EMA (Trial 3) independently increases mAP0.5 to 82.9% while cutting processing time to 11.7 ms. Implementing DynamicHead alone (Trial 4) elevates mAP0.5 to 83.7% with 12.3 ms processing time.

Combining all three modules in CD-YOLO (Trial 8) achieves peak operational balance: 81.2% precision, 76.4% recall, and 84.0% mAP0.5 at 15.3 GFLOPs and 14.4 MB storage footprint. When benchmarked against alternative lightweight backbones such as MobileNetv3 (79.9% mAP0.5), ShuffleNetv2 (77.8% mAP0.5), and EfficientVit (79.7% mAP0.5), CD-YOLO demonstrates superior feature preservation. Compared with established detectors including SSD (72.2% mAP0.5, 63.5 GFLOPs), Faster R-CNN (77.7% mAP0.5, 142.6 GFLOPs), YOLOv5s (80.5% mAP0.5), and YOLOv8s (81.6% mAP0.5), CD-YOLO provides superior accuracy alongside the lowest computational overhead.

- Ablation confirms DWConv provides computational headroom, allowing C3k2_EMA and DynamicHead to restore discriminative representation without latency penalties.

- CD-YOLO outperforms the YOLOv11s baseline across precision (+3.0 percentage points), recall (+1.5 percentage points), and mAP0.5 (+2.4 percentage points).

- Single-image processing latency drops from 14.3 ms in YOLOv11s to 9.6 ms in CD-YOLO on standard GPU hardware.

## Occlusion Quantification and Edge Inference Validation

To rigorously quantify seedling masking, the authors established a bounding-box overlap metric Oi, partitioning images into light (Oi < 10%), moderate (10% <= Oi < 40%), and severe (40% <= Oi) occlusion categories. An explicit occlusion test subset comprising 122 images (1 652 targets) was evaluated. On this subset, CD-YOLO achieved 79.6% precision, 75.1% recall, and 80.6% mAP0.5, outperforming YOLOv11s by 3.7, 4.0, and 5.1 percentage points, respectively. Absolute missed targets dropped from 315 in YOLOv11s to 221 in CD-YOLO, reducing the occlusion missed rate from 19.1% to 13.4%.

Physical edge deployment was verified on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX processor (6-core Arm Cortex-A78AE CPU, 1024-core Ampere GPU, 8 GB RAM). Operating at an input resolution of 640x640 with batch size 1, the untuned model delivered 12.9 frames/s. Applying TensorRT 8.5.2 acceleration elevated throughput by 2.5 times to 32.5 frames/s (30.7 ms total pipeline processing time). Field test verification confirmed an edge missed detection rate of 5.1% and a false detection rate of 2.7%, meeting real-time requirements for mobile tractor-mounted weeders and counters.

- Quantitative occlusion partitioning categorizes seedling targets across light, moderate, and severe overlapping strata.

- TensorRT execution accelerates embedded inference on Jetson Orin NX hardware from 12.9 frames/s to 32.5 frames/s.

- Field trials on edge hardware establish error metrics of 5.1% missed detections and 2.7% false classifications under ambient outdoor conditions.

## Operational Boundary Conditions and Motion Vulnerabilities

While CD-YOLO exhibits resilient detection under stationary and moderate field occlusions, performance degrades under rapid platform vibration, high-velocity motion blur, and extreme weed density where weed dimensions match seedling profiles.

- Image capture using cameras capped at 30 frames/s and 33.3 ms maximum exposure introduces 2 cm linear smear when vehicle transit speeds reach 0.6 m/s, suppressing high-frequency spatial gradients and increasing missed detections.

- Extremely small weeds with green chromatic signals that lack distinct leaf serration can trigger false positives when feature scales bypass receptive-field thresholds.

- The empirical dataset was gathered across a single experimental station during September 2024, requiring additional geographic and multi-seasonal validation before universal field deployment.

Detailed process conditions, instrument calibrations, and complete supplementary datasets beyond the core quantitative benchmarks are preserved in the Peer-Reviewed PDF Edition below.

abstract_en: This study investigated the effects of different application time and rates of bud-promoting fertilizer on the quality of main crop rice and annual yield of ratoon rice to lay a basis for optimizing nitrogen management in ratoon rice cultivation for the coordination of high yield and high quality. A field experiment was performed using two rice varieties (Liangyou 6326 and Yongyou 4949), with two application time of bud-promoting fertilizer (early application at heading stage and normal application 15 days after heading) and two rates of fertilizer application (normal nitrogen rate of 75 kg/hm² and reduced nitrogen rate of 30 kg/hm²), to examine the growth of ratoon buds, dry matter accumulation, grain filling characteristics of the main crop, yield and rice quality. When applied at the normal time, the reduced rate led to a decrease in both ratoon and annual yields for both varieties, primarily due to reduced panicle number per unit area in the ratoon crop. Under early application with reduced rate, the effective panicle number and both ratoon and annual yields showed no significant differences compared to the normal application practice of bud-promoting fertilizer. Compared to the normal application practice, early application with reduced application rate of bud-promoting fertilizer lowered the grain filling rate in the main crop of both varieties, extended the active grain filling period of superior spikelets, increased the head rice percentage, decreased the percentage of chalky grains and chalkiness, and improved the appearance and processing quality of main crop rice. However, early application with the normal (high) rate of bud-promoting fertilizer resulted in a decrease in amylose content in Liangyou 6326 and an increase in grain protein content, reducing cooking and eating quality. analysis_markdown_en:
Optimizing nitrogen management in ratoon rice cultivation is essential to harmonize main crop milling quality with annual grain productivity. This study evaluated two rice cultivars (Liangyou 6326 and Yongyou 4949) across distinct bud-promoting fertilizer timing regimes (full heading stage vs. 15 days after heading) and application rates (75 kg/hm² vs. 30 kg/hm² pure nitrogen). Advancing nitrogen application to the heading stage under a reduced rate of 30 kg/hm² sustained annual grain yields comparable to conventional high-nitrogen practices (reaching 14.46 t/hm² in Liangyou 6326), while lowering main crop chalkiness and extending active grain filling duration.

## Agronomic Nitrogen Timing and Annual Yield Balance

In ratoon rice production systems, bud-promoting fertilizer applied during the late reproductive phase of the main crop determines dormant axillary bud vitality on remaining stubble. Standard agronomic practices apply 75 kg/hm² of pure nitrogen approximately 15 to 20 days after full heading. However, when fertilizer rates are cut to 30 kg/hm² under this delayed schedule, insufficient nitrogen reserves induce significant yield penalties. For Liangyou 6326 and Yongyou 4949, ratoon season yields fell by 13.5% and 8.3%, and annual productivity dropped by 8.1% and 6.7%, respectively, primarily caused by reduced effective panicle numbers.

Advancing the fertilizer application to the full heading stage successfully overcomes this nitrogen restriction. Under early application with 30 kg/hm² nitrogen, annual yields reached 14.46 t/hm² for Liangyou 6326 and 14.37 t/hm² for Yongyou 4949, exhibiting no statistically significant difference from conventional high-rate regimes (14.61 t/hm² and 14.88 t/hm²). The early timing stimulates canopy photosynthetic efficiency, minimizing excessive remobilization of stored non-structural carbohydrates from stem sheaths to main crop panicles and preserving crucial basal reserves.

- Main crop grain yields remained stable across all timing and rate regimes, ranging between 8.69 t/hm² and 9.65 t/hm².

- Ratoon season panicle density reached 357.64 per m² in Liangyou 6326 under early reduced fertilizer, preventing canopy gaps.

## Grain Filling Dynamics and Stubble Biomass Partitioning

The timing of bud-promoting fertilizer strongly influences post-heading dry matter partitioning and grain filling kinetics in both superior and inferior spikelets. Conventional fertilization late in grain filling accelerated starch deposition rates, which frequently correlates with loose packing of amyloplasts and increased grain chalkiness under high summer temperatures. Conversely, early application combined with reduced nitrogen moderated the maximum and mean grain filling rates, thereby prolonging the active grain filling phase of superior spikelets.

Correlation analysis confirmed that mature stubble dry weight exhibits a significant positive correlation with viable bud number (r = 0.643, p < 0.01) and subsequent ratoon panicle density (r = 0.502, n = 24). Post-heading dry matter accumulation showed significant negative correlations with chalkiness rate (r = -0.633) and chalkiness degree (r = -0.723). By maintaining higher stubble biomass and reducing post-heading stem-sheath dry matter translocation, the early reduced treatment mitigates nutrient starvation in developing ratoon buds.

- Dry matter translocation of stem and sheath after heading was reduced to 1.11 t/hm² in Liangyou 6326 under early reduced nitrogen.

- Viable axillary bud numbers reached 248.83/m² on upper nodes and 243.38/m² on lower nodes for Liangyou 6326 under early reduced treatment.

## Main Season Rice Processing and Physicochemical Properties

Main crop milling, appearance, and cooking traits respond sensitively to bud-promoting nitrogen regimes. High nitrogen input applied early (75 kg/hm² at heading) adversely impacted grain composition, causing grain protein content in Liangyou 6326 to surge to 12.57% and reducing amylose content to 12.29%, which stiffens cooked rice texture and lowers palatability. Under normal timing with 30 kg/hm², chalkiness rate escalated to 8.95% in Liangyou 6326.

In contrast, early application of reduced nitrogen (30 kg/hm²) optimized grain quality attributes. In Liangyou 6326, head rice rate increased to 55.48%, while chalkiness rate and chalkiness degree dropped to 4.96% and 8.35%, respectively. In Yongyou 4949, head rice rate reached 66.20%, accompanied by an amylose content of 18.05% and protein content of 9.83%. Thus, synchronizing fertilizer reduction with heading-stage timing protects grain appearance and milling recovery without sacrificing yield.

## Agronomic Boundary Conditions and Cultivar Specificity

The field trials were conducted across two hybrid varieties under ecological conditions in central China, requiring careful verification before extrapolation to different climatic zones or planting models.

- Cultivar physiological responses varied notably: Yongyou 4949 maintained stable panicle numbers under rate shifts, whereas Liangyou 6326 showed significant panicle sensitivity.

- The experimental design evaluated nitrogen split ratios specific to mechanically harvested stubble heights of 40 cm, which may interact with basal tiller morphology under shorter cutting regimes.

- Early high-nitrogen applications (75 kg/hm² at heading) demonstrated risks of grain protein accumulation up to 12.57%, necessitating strict rate moderation.

Detailed process conditions, instrument calibrations, and complete supplementary datasets beyond the core quantitative benchmarks are preserved in the Peer-Reviewed PDF Edition below.

# Effects of Application Time and Rate of Bud-promoting Fertilizer on Main Crop Quality and Annual Yield of Ratoon Rice

---

**DOI:** `10.16819/j.1001-7216.2026.241009` | **Journal:** Chinese Journal of Rice Science (中国水稻科学) | **Year:** 2026  
**Authors:** XIAO Wuwei, ZHANG Yuqing, ZHU Chenguang, TIAN Guisheng, CAI Yuehong, WANG Fei, XIONG Dongliang, HUANG Jianliang, PENG Shaobing, CUI Kehui  
**Affiliation:** National Key Laboratory of Crop Genetic Improvement, Huazhong Agricultural University

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

This study investigated the effects of different application time and rates of bud-promoting fertilizer on the quality of main crop rice and annual yield of ratoon rice to lay a basis for optimizing nitrogen management in ratoon rice cultivation for the coordination of high yield and high quality. A field experiment was performed using two rice varieties (Liangyou 6326 and Yongyou 4949), with two application time of bud-promoting fertilizer (early application at heading stage and normal application 15 days after heading) and two rates of fertilizer application (normal nitrogen rate of 75 kg/hm² and reduced nitrogen rate of 30 kg/hm²), to examine the growth of ratoon buds, dry matter accumulation, grain filling characteristics of the main crop, yield and rice quality. When applied at the normal time, the reduced rate led to a decrease in both ratoon and annual yields for both varieties, primarily due to reduced panicle number per unit area in the ratoon crop. Under early application with reduced rate, the effective panicle number and both ratoon and annual yields showed no significant differences compared to the normal application practice of bud-promoting fertilizer. Compared to the normal application practice, early application with reduced application rate of bud-promoting fertilizer lowered the grain filling rate in the main crop of both varieties, extended the active grain filling period of superior spikelets, increased the head rice percentage, decreased the percentage of chalky grains and chalkiness, and improved the appearance and processing quality of main crop rice. However, early application with the normal (high) rate of bud-promoting fertilizer resulted in a decrease in amylose content in Liangyou 6326 and an increase in grain protein content, reducing cooking and eating quality. Early application with reduced bud-promoting fertilizer achieves high annual yield while enhancing main crop appearance and milling quality.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Applying reduced bud-promoting fertilizer (30 kg/hm²) at heading maintained annual yields at 14.46 t/hm² for Liangyou 6326 and 14.37 t/hm² for Yongyou 4949.
- Conventional timing with reduced nitrogen led to ratoon yield declines of 13.5% in Liangyou 6326 and 8.3% in Yongyou 4949 due to lower panicle counts.
- Early reduced fertilization improved milling quality, raising head rice rates to 55.48% in Liangyou 6326 and 66.20% in Yongyou 4949.
- Early timing significantly stimulated dormant bud survival, generating 248.83 upper-node viable buds/m² in Liangyou 6326 under 30 kg/hm² nitrogen.
- Applying high nitrogen (75 kg/hm²) early lowered amylose content and elevated grain protein to 12.57% in Liangyou 6326, compromising eating quality.

abstract_en: Sugars regulate nitrogen transformation processes in arable soils, yet the structural influence of carbohydrate degree of polymerization on urea nitrogen conversion remains insufficiently characterized. In this study, modified urea formulations were prepared by incorporating 1% mass fractions of glucose (monosaccharide, GU), maltose (2-poly, MU), oligomeric maltose (≈5-poly, OU), and polydextrose (≈20-poly, PU) into molten urea at 130 °C. A 28-day laboratory incubation experiment in calcareous fluvo-aquic soil compared unfertilized control (CK), conventional urea (U), and the four modified urea variants under identical nitrogen input (0.3 g N·kg-1 dry soil). Dextran-modified urea generated Schiff base (C=N) complexes, which mitigated urease activity and delayed its kinetic peak from 1 d to 2 d. Consequently, dextran-modified urea delayed urea hydrolysis, increasing soil amide nitrogen residues by 15.3%-37.1% relative to U, with OU maintaining the highest residue. Cumulative ammonia volatilization was reduced by 2.2%-12.9%, with the lowest volatilization observed in GU and volatilization increasing as polymerization degree increased. By day 28, soil nitrate nitrogen content increased by 14.1%-30.5% in modified treatments, demonstrating a non-linear relationship with polymerization degree that reached an optimum at 3.35.

analysis_markdown_en:
This study evaluates the soil nitrogen transformation dynamics of dextran-modified urea formulations synthesized via molten urea incorporation across distinct degrees of polymerization: glucose (GU, monomer), maltose (MU, dimer), oligomeric dextran (OU, ≈5-mer), and polydextrose (PU, ≈20-mer). In calcareous fluvo-aquic soil incubations, dextran-modified formulations generated Schiff base (C=N) functional groups, delayed the peak of soil urease activity from day 1 to day 2, and increased soil amide nitrogen residues by 15.3%-37.1%. Cumulative ammonia volatilization decreased by 2.2%-12.9%, with GU exhibiting the strongest mitigation, while late-incubation nitrate nitrogen increased by 14.1%-30.5%, peaking at an optimal polymerization degree of 3.35.

## Chemical Structure Formation and Enzymatic Peak Modulation

Incorporation of dextrans into molten urea at 130 °C for 30 s induced reactive condensation, yielding functional Schiff base (C=N) complexes verified through 13C nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Spectroscopic quantification revealed that the relative concentration of Schiff base structures decreased progressively as the carbohydrate degree of polymerization increased from monomeric glucose to ≈20-mer polydextrose. These unsaturated C=N double bonds functioned as competitive urease inhibitors within the soil matrix.

Under 25 °C closed incubation, conventional urea triggered an immediate surge in soil urease activity, reaching its initial peak at 1 d. In contrast, all four dextran-modified urea formulations successfully suppressed enzyme induction during initial dissolution, shifting the primary urease activity peak to 2 d. At 1 d, urease activity was suppressed by 20.8% in GU, 24.8% in MU, 33.0% in OU, and 17.0% in PU relative to U. This delay extended amide nitrogen persistence, enabling a 15.3%-37.1% increase in average residual amide nitrogen and mitigating abrupt spikes in soil alkalinity.

- 13C-NMR spectroscopy confirmed the formation of Schiff base (C=N) motifs, whose relative content correlated inversely with carbohydrate chain length.

- Soil urease induction was deferred by 24 hours across all modified formulations, moderating the rapid hydrolytic surge characteristic of conventional urea.

## Ammonium Hydrolysis Dynamics and Gaseous Volatilization Loss

The enzymatic delay directly regulated the accumulation of mineral nitrogen species in the alkaline fluvo-aquic soil environment (baseline pH 8.29). During the critical early period of 0.25 to 1 d, soil ammonium nitrogen accumulation proceeded slowly, followed by a rapid surge between 1 and 3 d that peaked at 3 d. On day 1, ammonium concentrations under GU, MU, OU, and PU were reduced by 12.46%, 7.3%, 5.6%, and 13.7% relative to conventional urea (73.92 mg·kg-1). On day 2, ammonium levels in modified treatments were 1.6%-38.6% lower than U (141.85 mg·kg-1).

Because ammonia volatilization in calcareous systems is driven by high dissolved ammonium concentrations and transient pH increases, suppressing early ammonium release minimized gaseous losses. Across the 7-day gaseous capture period, dextran-modified formulations decreased cumulative ammonia volatilization by 2.2%-12.9%. Monomeric glucose modification (GU) achieved the lowest emission rates, while increasing dextran polymerization resulted in a progressive recovery of cumulative ammonia volatilization toward conventional levels.

- Soil ammonium accumulation at 1 d was curtailed to 64.71 mg·kg-1 in GU and 63.79 mg·kg-1 in PU, compared with 73.92 mg·kg-1 in conventional urea.

- Peak soil pH elevation at day 1 was attenuated by 0.21, 0.13, and 0.20 pH units in GU, MU, and OU treatments compared to conventional urea (pH 8.30).

## Nitrate Accumulation Profiles and Degree-of-Polymerization Optimization

Following the transition from ammonium depletion (days 5 to 7) to active nitrification, soil nitrate nitrogen levels rose consistently across all fertilized systems. Between days 3 and 28, nitrate pools in dextran-modified soils consistently exceeded those in conventional urea soils, establishing statistically significant divergence by day 7. At the conclusion of the 28-day incubation, dextran-modified formulations elevated nitrate concentrations by 14.1%-30.5% relative to conventional urea.

The ultimate nitrification benefit was non-linearly governed by carbohydrate polymerization degree. Regression analysis linking Schiff base relative content and polymerization degree (modeled by y = 1.08x - 0.62) against nitrate yield established an optimum at a Schiff base relative content of 0.5%, corresponding to a dextran degree of polymerization of 3.35. Oligomeric maltose (OU, ≈5-poly) delivered the greatest absolute nitrate availability among empirical treatments, outperforming both low-molecular monomers and hyper-polymerized polydextrose.

- Final soil nitrate nitrogen content reached maximum levels under intermediate-chain oligomeric modification, surpassing conventional urea by up to 30.5%.

- Regression modeling established an optimal polymerization degree threshold of 3.35 for maximizing late-stage nitrate conversion in calcareous fluvo-aquic soil.

## Pedological Boundary Conditions and Kinetic Explanatory Limits

The empirical findings are grounded in controlled microcosm conditions within calcareous fluvo-aquic soil and require field validation across divergent edaphic conditions.

- The linear regression between Schiff base content and cumulative ammonia volatilization exhibited a modest determination coefficient of R2 = 0.22, indicating that additional chemical and microbial variables influence gaseous nitrogen loss beyond Schiff base concentration alone.

Sugars regulate nitrogen transformation processes in arable soils, yet the structural influence of carbohydrate degree of polymerization on urea nitrogen conversion remains insufficiently characterized. analysis_markdown_en:
This two-year field study investigates water-salt dynamics, root physiology, and agronomic productivity under alternate wetting and drying (AWD) regimes in salinized paddy soils in Ningxia, China. Conventional continuous flooding was benchmarked against three AWD moisture depletion thresholds: -10 kPa (W1), -20 kPa (W2), and -30 kPa (W3). The mild -10 kPa AWD treatment decreased irrigation water requirements by 12.21% while raising grain yield by 3.96% to 4.75% and water use efficiency by 18.30% to 19.77%. In contrast, severe moisture deficits intensified soil salt accumulation, suppressed root morphological vitality, and caused yield declines reaching 20.00% to 46.46%.

## Soil Water-Salt Spatial Redistribution Under Cyclic Irrigation Regimes

In arid and semi-arid irrigation areas, continuous flooding has traditionally served as the primary mechanism for leaching excessive soluble salts from the crop root zone. However, mounting freshwater constraints demand irrigation regimes that conserve water without triggering secondary soil salinization. Over two cropping cycles, soil moisture and electrical conductivity (EC) across five depth strata down to 100 cm demonstrated that the 0-40 cm layer serves as the primary zone for salt dynamic exchange.

Under the W1 treatment (-10 kPa threshold), soil moisture content within 0-40 cm decreased by 11.46% relative to CK, yet sustained an average moisture level of 56.93% during critical vegetative periods. Although topsoil (0-20 cm) electrical conductivity increased by 8.43% under W1 due to evaporative concentration during drying phases, subsequent cyclic re-flooding established an effective downward hydraulic gradient, delivering a net desalination rate of 6.14% in the crucial 20-40 cm sublayer. In contrast, under the severe drying thresholds of W2 (-20 kPa) and W3 (-30 kPa), capillary rise exceeded downward percolation, causing marked subsoil salt accumulation with negative desalination rates reaching -5.96% and -11.21%.

- The cyclic re-flooding pattern of W1 creates a repeated pulsed leaching effect that flushes mobile ions out of the 20-40 cm root stratum.

- Extended soil drying under W2 and W3 disrupts soil structural aggregates and accelerates capillary upward salt migration from shallower groundwater tables.

## Root Morphophysiological Adaptation and Canopy Photosynthetic Regulation

Root system architecture and physiological activity serve as direct interfaces mediating crop adaptation to concurrent moisture and osmotic stresses. The moderate drying cycles under W1 stimulated adventitious root growth and structural expansion. At heading and grain-filling stages, W1 maintained significantly greater total root length and volume than CK, with heading root volume exceeding CK by 27.09%. Enhanced root oxygenation during brief drying phases stimulated metabolic activity, resulting in superior triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) reducing power and elevated active absorption surface areas.

Conversely, severe water stress under W2 and W3 induced cellular dehydration and root apical senescence, drastically diminishing both total root length and active absorbing area. The physiological vitality established under W1 supported superior canopy performance. Flag leaf SPAD readings and net photosynthetic rates (Pn) peaked at heading and remained significantly elevated through grain filling under W1, whereas W2 and W3 prompted premature canopy chlorosis and substantial declines in leaf carbon assimilation capacity.

- W1 increased root volume at heading to 102707.10 mm3/plant in 2023 and 86082.73 mm3/plant in 2024, providing robust structural support for nutrient uptake.

- Root-shoot ratio under W1 was enhanced by 55.06% at heading, maintaining balanced resource allocation between belowground acquisition and aboveground panicle development.

## Agronomic Yield Components and Structural Equation Modeling Drivers

Yield component evaluation revealed that W1 increased total grain yield to 7085 kg·hm-2 in 2023 and 6922 kg·hm-2 in 2024, outperforming continuous flooding by 3.96% and 4.75%. This yield improvement was primarily underpinned by elevated spikelet setting percentages, which reached 93.09% and 93.30%, alongside well-maintained spikelets per panicle. Mild moisture deficits effectively curbed unproductive tillers during vegetative growth while preserving high productive tiller conversion rates (54.95% in 2023 and 54.82% in 2024).

Partial least squares path modeling (PLS-PM) unraveled the hierarchical causal network linking irrigation regimes to final agronomic output. Irrigation practices exerted direct regulatory control over soil water-salt equilibrium, which directly governed root morphological and physiological indices. Root vigor subsequently steered leaf photosynthetic activity, which acted as the predominant direct driving variable dictating grain filling and yield.

- W2 and W3 treatments suffered significant reductions across panicle count, spikelets per panicle, and thousand-grain weight, dropping yields to 3605-5287 kg·hm-2.

- PLS-PM path coefficients demonstrated that optimizing root-zone salinity and morphology translates directly into sustained canopy photosynthesis during grain filling.

## Soil Specificity, Deficit Threshold Boundaries, and Hydrological Constraints

The experimental validation is specifically contextualized to the continental semi-arid climate and irrigated warp soils of the Yinchuan plain in Ningxia.

- The positive effects of AWD are strictly confined to a mild water potential threshold of -10 kPa; exceeding this boundary to -20 kPa or -30 kPa triggers severe root restriction, soil salinization, and yield declines between 20.00% and 46.46%.

- Field experiments were conducted using a single regional japonica rice cultivar (Ningjing 52) on moderately salinized warp soils (initial total salt 2.83 to 4.69 g·kg-1, pH 8.78 to 9.11), necessitating further calibration across differing soil textures and salt chemistry.

- The irrigation regime requires precise field monitoring instruments, such as tensiometers and automated water meters, which may encounter deployment barriers in broadacre smallholder agricultural contexts.

## Laminar Expansion Dynamics and Application Timing

In flue-cured tobacco cultivation, upper canopy leaves represent 35% to 45% of total plant dry biomass. However, these leaves frequently suffer from narrow lamina architecture, tightly packed cellular organization, and high nicotine accumulation, leading to restricted inclusion rates in commercial cigarette formulations. Topping eliminates apical dominance and redirects source-sink photoassimilate partitioning, but the abrupt shift in endogenous hormone equilibrium often halts further laminar cell division.

Field evaluations in Dehong demonstrated that exogenous hormone intervention immediately on the day of topping was critical. Single-agent treatment with 20 mg/L KT stimulated pronounced lateral expansion, with width gains of 23.34% to 41.27% outpacing longitudinal length increases of 9.85% to 32.90% by 1.3 to 2.1 times. Conversely, delayed application at 7 days post-topping produced attenuated responses (7.18% to 24.83% width increase). While zeatin (ZT) at 1 mg/L suppressed leaf expansion when applied on the day of topping (width gain of -20.47% to 1.49%), it switched to moderate promotion at 7 days post-topping (12.29% to 28.83%), underscoring divergent hormonal sensitivities across distinct post-topping developmental windows.

- Day-of-topping spraying aligns with active cellular division prior to secondary cell wall thickening.

- Tank-mixed compound regulators induced lamina width shrinkages between 5.2% and 19.7% relative to control.

Upper leaves account for 35% to 45% of total plant dry weight in flue-cured tobacco, yet poor leaf expansion, narrow lamina geometry, and elevated nicotine limit industrial usability. This dual-site investigation across Dehong and Lijiang evaluated the exogenous application of forchlorfenuron (KT), zeatin (ZT), and brassinolide (BR) on 'Yunyan 87'. Single-agent foliar application at topping demonstrated superior agronomic efficacy over tank mixtures and delayed applications. Specifically, 20 mg/L KT maximized lateral laminar expansion and decreased nicotine concentration by 3.80% to 15.50%, while 1 mg/L BR markedly improved appearance score, combustibility, and sensory smoking quality.

Flue-cured tobacco processing suitability requires strict chemical harmony among nitrogenous fractions, reducing sugars, and mineral ions. Brassinolide at 1 mg/L achieved the highest sensory score increase of 11.17%, generating marked gains in aroma quality, aroma volume, and aftertaste purity. This study provides practical foliar spraying protocols for improving upper leaf morphology and sensory quality, though several agronomic limitations should be considered prior to widespread multi-region adoption.

- Field trials were conducted across two locations during a single calendar year (2020), which limits verification across long-term interannual climate fluctuations.

- Investigation focused exclusively on the cultivar 'Yunyan 87', leaving responsiveness across alternative cultivars such as KRK26 unverified.

- Evaluations lacked profiling of specific volatile neutral aroma constituents and pyrolysis degradation compounds.

- Spray volume was fixed at 450 L/hm 2 targeted at the top 1 to 6 leaf positions, requiring re-calibration for mechanized misting booms.

This two-year field investigation (2022-2024) evaluates the synergistic application of fermented sheep manure (27 t·hm-2) and gradient dosages of wood vinegar (0, 270, 540, and 810 kg·hm-2) for reclaiming inland saline-alkali soils in the low plain of Hebei. Incorporating sheep manure with 540 kg·hm-2 wood vinegar (T2) decreased 0-20 cm soil bulk density by an average of 8.03% and electrical conductivity by 13.17% compared with conventional fertilization. T2 elevated available nutrients, flag leaf antioxidant enzyme activities, stomatal aperture, and aboveground nutrient accumulation, driving winter wheat grain yield gains of 5.93% to 17.29%.

## Pedological Edaphic Property Optimization and Nutrient Desorption Dynamics

Inland saline-alkali soils within the alluvial Hebei plain exhibit severe soil physical degradation, compacted structural horizons, and excessive sodium ion accumulation, resulting in physiological drought and restricted crop establishment. The field trial demonstrated that integrating porous sheep manure with acidic wood vinegar altered soil physical indices. Across the 0-20 cm topsoil horizon, the T2 intervention (27 t·hm-2 sheep manure paired with 540 kg·hm-2 wood vinegar) lowered bulk density by an average of 8.03% and dropped soil electrical conductivity by 13.17% compared with conventional fertilization. Soil total porosity expanded, facilitating aeration and downward salt leaching while mitigating capillary upward salt migration.

Chemical nutrient bioavailability responded strongly to the combined organic regimen. Low-molecular-weight organic acids (such as acetic acid at 253 g·kg-1) and phenolic components within wood vinegar actively chelate polyvalent soil cations, accelerating the mobilization and release of fixed mineral phosphorus and potassium. In the 0-20 cm layer, T2 maintained available phosphorus at 19.63±0.42 mg·kg-1 in 2023 and 20.41±1.15 mg·kg-1 in 2024, outperforming CK and sole manure. Furthermore, significant mobilization extended into the 20-40 cm subsoil profile, where T2 elevated available phosphorus to 6.47±0.28 mg·kg-1 and 6.91±0.68 mg·kg-1 in respective seasons.

- Electrical conductivity dropped from 892.67±44.24 μS·cm-1 in CK to 775±52.72 μS·cm-1 in T2 during 2023.

- Available potassium in topsoil reached 139±4.39 mg·kg-1 in 2023 and 144.9±8.28 mg·kg-1 in 2024 under T2.

- Nitrate nitrogen under T2 increased to 20.84±0.26 mg·kg-1 (2023) and 21.04±0.97 mg·kg-1 (2024).

Osmotic shock and oxidative injury induced by reactive oxygen species represent primary physiological constraints on winter wheat cultivated under saline-alkali environments. Flag leaf biochemical assays demonstrated that the T2 amendment enhanced protective metabolic cascades throughout the reproductive grain filling stages. Superoxide dismutase (SOD) and peroxidase (POD) activities were significantly upregulated during early and middle filling phases, suppressing harmful superoxide anion radical accumulation as verified by lighter nitroblue tetrazolium and diaminobenzidine histochemical tissue staining.

In parallel, flag leaf osmotic regulation was bolstered by sustained increases in soluble sugar, soluble protein, and free amino acid concentrations, delaying premature monocarpic senescence. Optical micromorphology of epidermal impressions revealed that T2 expanded flag leaf stomatal length to 60.26±1.27 μm, width to 28.07±0.78 μm, perimeter to 143.4±2.0 μm, and total stomatal area to 1 327.7±28.5 μm2. ## Allometric Nutrient Partitioning and Spike-Driven Agronomic Productivity

Nutrient bioaccumulation across vegetative and reproductive wheat organs governs final harvest index and grain yield formation. Total plant accumulation of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium across husk, stem, leaf, and kernel compartments increased by 8.30% to 25.79% under T2 relative to CK, T0, and T1. Enhanced organ-level nitrogen concentration was particularly prominent within grain and glume tissues, confirming that root uptake and translocational efficiency were safeguarded from sodium ion antagonism.

Yield component dissection indicated that agronomic gains were predominantly governed by effective spike density per hectare rather than kernel weight variations. In 2023, effective spike number rose to 592.8±6.6 × 10^4 hm-2 in T2 compared with 527.7±13.1 × 10^4 hm-2 in CK; in 2024, spike density achieved 647.5±16.4 × 10^4 hm-2. Consequently, total winter wheat grain yield reached 6 782±140 kg·hm-2 and 7 072±183 kg·hm-2 across the two consecutive cropping seasons, confirming that balanced organic-acid co-application remediates yield gaps in saline-alkali farmland.

- Effective spikes increased by 5.66% to 7.89% over sole sheep manure (T0) and 5.06% to 5.39% over low wood vinegar (T1).

- Grain number per spike and thousand kernel weight exhibited stable trends without significant treatment depressions.

- Simulated optimal application thresholds identified a narrow operational window between 535.46 and 551.03 kg·hm-2 wood vinegar.

## Experimental Scope and Regional Ecological Boundary Conditions

This study evaluated a winter wheat-summer maize rotation over a two-year experimental timeframe on inland salinized fluvo-aquic soils in Hebei province.

- Findings reflect a two-year field trial (2022-2024); prolonged cumulative effects of recurring sheep manure and wood vinegar co-application on soil microbial dynamics and subsoil salinization warrant long-term monitoring.

- Field trials utilized supplementary micro-brackish surface river water containing 1.4 g·L-1 salt; hydrological responses may vary under deeper saline irrigation or coastal saline-alkali environments.

- Wood vinegar raw material composition was derived from pyrolyzed pear and apple wood (pH 2.97, organic acids 323 g·kg-1, organic carbon 31.14 g·kg-1); variations in feedstock pyrolysis byproducts require local calibration.

analysis_markdown_en:
This study evaluated six formulated nursery substrates against field soil control (CK) to enhance seed germination and seedling vigor in Panax japonicus (Zhaoshen). Compounded volumetric treatments utilized coir dust, fermented medicinal herb residue, and field soil in standardized plug trays. While high-porosity mixtures like A2 (coir:residue:soil = 1:3:5) and A6 (coir:residue:soil = 3:1:5) maximized 40-day seedling emergence at 83.3% and 82.5%, the binary mixture A4 (coir:soil = 5:5) generated superior vegetative development. A4 elevated root count by 88.17%, rhizome diameter by 41.26%, rhizome length by 31.36%, and seedling fresh weight by 94.3% while curtailing seedling mortality by 65.09%. Comprehensive fuzzy membership function analysis established A4 (0.810) and A6 (0.735) as the optimal substrate configurations.

## Substrate Aeration Dynamics and Germination Kinetics

Panax japonicus seeds display intense morphophysiological dormancy, requiring up to 180 d under natural stratification to achieve physiological maturity. In traditional field soil nursery beds, high soil bulk density and insufficient aeration restrict radical penetration and favor soil-borne pathogens like Rhizoctonia damping-off. Incorporating lightweight organic matrices alters mechanical impedance and moisture tension within the root zone.

Emergence dynamics over 40 d demonstrated that adding coir dust and composted Chinese herbal residue significantly accelerated germination velocity. By day 20, formulation A6 exhibited the fastest germination at 18.9%, significantly surpassing CK (8.3%, P<0.05). By day 40, cumulative emergence stabilized, ranking A2 (83.3%) > A6 (82.5%) > A3 (80.0%) > A5 (78.3%) > A1 (72.5%) > A4 (68.3%) > CK (55.8%). The porous texture of coir and residue composites facilitated gas exchange while maintaining moisture levels necessary to trigger embryo elongation.

Coloration of emerging seedlings also reflected nursery microenvironments. Seedlings reared in A1, A4, A6, and CK retained dark green foliage, whereas high medicinal residue ratios without sufficient field soil buffers (such as A2, A3, and A5) yielded light green shoots, pointing to potential minor nutrient imbalances or altered pH regimes during early autotrophic transition.

- Day 20 germination in A6 reached 18.9%, more than doubling the 8.3% recorded in unamended field soil.

- Day 40 final emergence reached 83.3% in A2 and 82.5% in A6 compared to 55.8% in control soil.

## Rhizome Morphogenesis and Post-Emergence Biomass Partitioning

While germination was highest in ternary mixtures rich in herbal residue, seedling vegetative vigor exhibited different physical substrate requirements. Because the primary commercial and medicinal organ of Panax japonicus is its subterranean rhizome, subterranean root expansion and lodging resistance serve as crucial benchmarks for transplant viability.

Substrate A4 (coir dust:field soil = 5:5) promoted notable underground development. Mean rhizome diameter in A4 reached 9.86 mm, followed by A6 at 8.94 mm, surpassing CK (6.98 mm) by 41.26% and 28.08%, respectively (P<0.05). Root proliferation similarly favored A4, yielding 3.50 roots per plant compared to 1.86 in CK. This robust root architecture supported superior single-plant fresh weight (1.03 g in A4 vs 0.53 g in CK).

Seedling lodging mortality, recorded in September, demonstrated substantial divergence across treatments. Field soil control seedlings suffered from compacted, saturated conditions, whereas A1 experienced severe damping-off losses reaching 72.9%. Conversely, A4 restricted seedling lodging to 31.8%, representing a 65.09% decline relative to CK. The balanced 1:1 volumetric ratio of coir dust and loam provided an elastic structure that averted moisture logging while sustaining anchor stability.

- A4 produced the thickest rhizomes (9.86 mm) and highest lateral root count (3.50 roots per plant).

- A4 and A6 produced individual seedling fresh weights of 1.03 g and 0.96 g, respectively, compared to 0.53 g in CK.

- Lodging mortality was curtailed to 31.8% in A4, contrasting sharply with 72.9% observed in A1.

## Comprehensive Fuzzy Membership Evaluation and Nursery Strategy

Because individual growth parameters favored differing substrate formulations, single-metric screening fails to capture holistic nursery quality. To reconcile trade-offs between initial emergence percentage, morphological vigor, and lodging resistance, subordinate function values were calculated across ten vegetative indicators.

Positive trait indicators (plant height, stem diameter, leaflet dimensions, root count, rhizome length, rhizome diameter, fresh weight, and emergence rate) and the inverse negative indicator (lodging rate) were normalized. The resulting mean subordinate values ranked treatments as follows: A4 (0.810) > A6 (0.735) > A1 (0.699) > A2 (0.607) > A3 (0.541) > A5 (0.431) > CK (0.033).

The evaluation reveals that coir dust is distinctly superior to medicinal herbal residue as a primary conditioning agent for Panax japonicus. Coir provides an acidic buffering environment consistent with the species' adapted pH range (5.5-7.0), slow structural degradation, and elevated capillary water-holding capacity. For commercial nursery production, A4 (coir:soil = 5:5) serves as the primary recommendation for root development, while A6 (coir:residue:soil = 3:1:5) offers an effective alternative that couples high germination velocity with strong seedling growth.

- A4 scored the highest comprehensive membership index (0.810), driven by root expansion and survival.

- A6 secured second rank (0.735), demonstrating balanced agronomic performance across emergence and biomass.

- Pure field soil control achieved an index of only 0.033, confirming the necessity of structured organic substrates.

## Methodological Scope and Field Translation Constraints

This investigation establishes effective nursery formulations for Panax japonicus, but several empirical boundaries qualify its direct commercial extrapolation across multi-year production cycles.

- Substrate physicochemical properties including bulk density (optimum range 0.1-0.8 g/cm3), total porosity, aeration porosity, EC, and dynamic nutrient depletion were not directly measured across the cultivation period.

- The trial was conducted in 50-hole nursery plug trays within a controlled greenhouse at Yongfeng Base, requiring multi-location field validation across distinct alpine microclimates.

- Evaluations were restricted to first-year seedlings; subsequent transplant establishment, overwinter survival, secondary saponin accumulation, and multi-year yield trajectories remain unassessed.

Detailed process conditions, instrument calibrations, and complete supplementary datasets beyond the core quantitative benchmarks are preserved in the Peer-Reviewed PDF Edition below.

analysis_markdown_en:
Robotic fruit harvesting requires real-time, high-precision detection under complex natural orchard conditions characterized by leaf occlusions, fluctuating illumination, background color camouflage, and small object scales. This study introduces an enhanced perception model built upon the lightweight YOLOv10 baseline for tomato picking robots. By designing a multi-branch Feature Enhancement Module (FEM), an improved BiFPN-derived Feature Fusion Module (FFM) with channel reweighting concatenation, and a tri-branch Spatial Context Aware Module (SCAM), the network captures fine local details and global semantic relationships while suppressing cluttered foliage backgrounds. Across natural orchard benchmarks, the architecture achieves a mean average precision of 0.910 at 88.4 frames per second, driving a field picking success rate of 95.59%.

## Tri-Tier Architectural Feature Extraction and Context Modeling

In orchard environments, early-stage green tomatoes and immature fruit clusters exhibit close color similarity to foliage, severe foliage occlusion, and restricted pixel areas, with small objects (pixel area below 32x32) constituting 32% of natural canopy targets. To address these visual perception bottlenecks on resource-constrained platforms, the proposed network modifies the YOLOv10 architecture through three structural units: the Feature Enhancement Module (FEM), the Feature Fusion Module (FFM), and the Spatial Context Aware Module (SCAM).

The FEM expands the receptive field of the backbone while preserving fine spatial structures. It splits feature maps into four parallel paths: a residual 1x1 convolution path that preserves raw small-target geometries, and three paths utilizing 1x3, 3x1, and 3x3 standard and dilated convolutions (dilation rate of 5). This multi-branch setup captures diverse semantic contexts and fine local boundaries before cross-scale aggregation.

The FFM refines multi-scale aggregation over deep features (X4 at 40x40), mid-level features (X3 at 80x80), and shallow features (X2 at 160x160). Departing from standard BiFPN architectures that assign equal weights across channels, FFM incorporates Channel Reweighting Concat (CRC), applying normalized learnable parameters to recalibrate concatenated feature maps across spatial scales. Downstream, SCAM applies global average and maximum pooling alongside 1x1 query-key projections, using broadcast Hadamard products to build spatial-channel attention maps that filter cluttered canopy backgrounds.

- Receptive field expansion via FEM employing dilated convolutions at dilation rate 5 for dense foliage penetration.

- Cross-scale feature alignment via FFM with learnable channel-reweighted concatenation (CRC2).

- Long-range dependency modeling via tri-branch SCAM global pooling and batched matrix multiplication.

- Loss formulation integrating Normalized Wasserstein Distance (NWD) with CIoU at trade-off weight lambda = 0.5 to reduce sensitivity to small bounding box boundary shifts.

## Quantitative Benchmark Comparisons and Component Ablation

Empirical evaluation was conducted on an expanded 3,640-image orchard dataset collected in Xiangcheng, Henan Province under varying illumination angles and natural canopy occlusions. Object annotations were assigned based on surface color coverage: green tomatoes (<30% red area), semi-ripened (30% to 90% red area), and fully-ripened (>90% red area). Across independent testing, the improved algorithm recorded an overall mAP50 of 0.910, exceeding baseline YOLOv10 by 0.041 and transformer-based Co-DETR by 0.016.

The performance gain was most pronounced in green tomato detection, where the model reached an AP50 of 0.911 compared to 0.862 for baseline YOLOv10, 0.857 for YOLOv11, and 0.836 for DETR. This validates the effectiveness of dilated receptive field expansion and spatial context filtering in resolving severe foliage-fruit camouflage. Concurrently, model complexity remained compact at 7.79 M parameters and an operational speed of 88.4 frames·s-1 on desktop GPU hardware, outperforming heavyweight architectures such as DETR (62.95 M, 36.1 frames·s-1) and Co-DETR (80.43 M, 24.8 frames·s-1).

Component-wise ablation experiments demonstrated progressive contributions from each engineered unit. Adding FEM alone boosted mAP50 from 0.869 to 0.900 while improving precision from 0.901 to 0.927. The addition of FFM improved recall from 0.827 to 0.838 with negligible parameter growth (0.01 M). The complete configuration combining FEM, FFM, and SCAM achieved peak metrics across precision (0.930), recall (0.856), mAP50 (0.910), and mAP50:95 (0.351).

- FFM integration contributed +0.011 to recall with virtually zero computational overhead.

- Evaluation of neck reweighting confirmed CRC2 (mAP50: 0.910) outperforming SENet-based CRC1 (0.904) and ECANet-based CRC1 (0.898).
