## Field Robotic Harvesting Deployment and Closed-Loop Validation

To test the practical viability of the vision pipeline, the trained weights were embedded into an integrated agricultural harvesting robot. The hardware assembly comprises a Warthog UGV mobile base, a NovAtel PwrPak7D-E1 navigation system, an Ouster OS1-32 LiDAR scanner for orchard canopy mapping and collision avoidance, an Intel RealSense D455 RGB-D camera for near-field perception, an ABB IRB1600-10/1.45 six-axis manipulator, an AKD2G motion controller, and an mGrip Modula soft pneumatic gripper.

All edge inference operations were hosted on an onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin master controller. Real-time bounding box outputs and depth maps were registered with LiDAR point clouds to generate three-dimensional grasping coordinates for tomatoes exhibiting ripeness above 90%. Field trials carried out across seven distinct harvesting locations with 182 total tomato targets (42 green, 72 semi-ripened, and 68 ripe) yielded 176 correct recognitions, 4 missed targets, and 2 false alarms.

Guided by the vision system, the robotic manipulator executed grasping sequences on mature targets, successfully picking 65 of the 68 mature fruits, representing a picking success rate of 95.59%. The vision subsystem sustained an edge inference speed of 48.7 frames·s-1 throughout autonomous operation, proving capable of guiding real-time pneumatic picking cycles without pipeline latency stalls.

- Edge deployment executed on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin host controller at 48.7 frames·s-1.

- Spatial coordinate fusion via Intel RealSense D455 depth streaming and Ouster OS1-32 point cloud scanning.

- Automated pneumatic harvesting driven by an ABB IRB1600 manipulator and mGrip Modula flexible end effector.

- Demonstrated 96.70% detection accuracy and 95.59% harvesting success across natural orchard field trials.

## Operational Scope, Edge Constraints, and Monocular Bottlenecks

While the proposed architecture demonstrates high precision and real-time inference across natural orchard benchmarks, practical limitations persist regarding viewpoint ambiguity, multi-class scaling, and edge throughput trade-offs.

- Inference speed drops from 101.6 frames·s-1 in baseline YOLOv10 to 88.4 frames·s-1 in the full model on desktop hardware, and declines to 48.7 frames·s-1 during embedded edge execution on the Jetson AGX Orin controller.

- Single-perspective 2D camera projections are prone to classification mismatches when fruits display asymmetric ripening, such as showing red coloring on the camera-facing side while remaining green on the rear unexposed surface.

- The dataset and network parameters are currently tailored specifically to Solanum lycopersicum ripeness stages (green, semi-ripened, and fully-ripened), lacking multi-task heads for simultaneous pest, disease, or heterogeneous crop detection.

LiteFocus-Net introduces an efficient tri-point architectural enhancement strategy over baseline YOLOv11n for detecting tiny lesions, insect eggs, and fungal clusters on corn leaves under complex field environments. By integrating an Adaptive Kernel Lightweight Block (AKL-Block) with 3x3, 5x5, and 7x7 dynamic depthwise kernels, a Feature Decomposition and Reconstruction (FDR) module for targeted sub-pixel detail recovery, and a continuous Scale-Aware Gradient Boosting Loss (SAGB-Loss), the architecture resolves deep spatial attenuation and small-target gradient starvation. LiteFocus-Net attains 74.97% mAP@0.5 and 32.77% AP_s on a field dataset of 10,324 images while trimming compute overhead to 5.3 GFLOPs across 2.52 M parameters.

## Tri-Point Architectural Paradigm for Scale Adaptation and Detail Recovery

Field-based computer vision models for agricultural pathology frequently degrade when encountering early fungal clusters or tiny insect eggs whose bounding areas span fewer than 32x32 pixels. In traditional downsampling pipelines, repetitive strided operations eliminate local textures and high-frequency boundaries, while standard fixed receptive fields fail to encompass both micro-lesions and broad foliar chlorosis. LiteFocus-Net addresses these structural vulnerabilities by dividing enhancements across receptive field selection, deep feature recovery, and gradient backpropagation.

The Adaptive Kernel Lightweight Block replaces static convolutional kernels with a lightweight channel-gated selection between 3x3, 5x5, and 7x7 depthwise separable operations. During training, Gumbel-Softmax routing allows end-to-end differentiable optimization across kernel branches, whereas execution collapses onto the single highest-probability kernel per input to eliminate multi-branch compute latency. To mitigate severe signal loss across deep P5 stages, the Feature Decomposition and Reconstruction module splits channel representations into a C/4 global structural branch handled via non-parametric bilinear interpolation and a 3C/4 detail branch processed via sub-pixel PixelShuffle upsampling. This deliberate bifurcation restricts parameter-heavy learnable upsampling strictly to local lesion contours, avoiding the computational explosion associated with full-channel deconvolution.

- Dynamic single-path execution in AKL-Block lowers feature extraction compute to 5.0 GFLOPs while matching multi-branch feature diversity.

- Channel division in FDR (1:3 structural-to-detail ratio) adds a negligible 0.02 M parameter overhead relative to full sub-pixel implementations.

In supervised object detection, bounding-box regression signals are predominantly governed by medium and large spatial ground truths, marginalizing tiny annotations and destabilizing boundary convergence. Hard-threshold weighting strategies induce gradient discontinuities near scale boundaries, deteriorating intermediate-scale accuracy. LiteFocus-Net overcomes this via the Scale-Aware Gradient Boosting Loss, incorporating stride-dependent layer coefficients with a smooth exponential area enhancement factor.

Across a benchmark cohort of 10,324 field images, LiteFocus-Net attained 75.0% mAP@0.5 and 32.8% AP_s in comparative evaluations against contemporary lightweight and dense detectors. It outperformed models such as YOLO-MSM (74.0% mAP@0.5, 30.2% AP_s), MA-YOLO (73.9% mAP@0.5, 32.1% AP_s), and YOLO-LCE (73.9% mAP@0.5, 30.1% AP_s). Real-world field validation requires deterministic deployment on embedded hardware without exceeding tight thermal dissipation budgets. Symmetric INT8 quantization mapped to [-128, 127] was implemented on the Rockchip RK3588 NPU and NVIDIA Jetson Orin platforms. While LiteFocus-Net provides a calibrated compromise among parameter volume, inference speed, and small-target bounding recall, architectural boundary conditions govern its broader field deployment.

- Image-level kernel arbitration in the AKL-Block applies a single global receptive field choice across the entire spatial feature map, restricting optimal feature capture when microscopic spore clusters and expansive leaf necrosis co-occur within the same frame.

- The Feature Decomposition and Reconstruction module relies on residual P5 feature responses; if micro-targets undergo catastrophic spatial erasure during initial strided downsampling, sub-pixel reconstruction amplifies noise rather than missing structural boundaries.

- The Scale-Aware Gradient Boosting Loss is tuned to fixed pixel distributions; altering optical zoom, mounting distances on unmanned aerial platforms, or camera sensor resolutions shifts target bounding scales and may require re-tuning the enhancement coefficient alpha=2.0 to prevent gradient bias against medium lesions.

This study evaluates gross nitrogen transformation rates across seven representative soils spanning forest, grassland, and upland ecosystems in China. Using 15N paired isotope dilution paired with the numerical NtraceBasic MCMC inversion framework, the authors quantified ten distinct gross nitrogen flux pathways. Nitrogen mineralization, microbial immobilization, and autotrophic nitrification formed the primary internal flux channels. Land-use classifications showed no statistically significant discrepancies in bulk gross transformation rates. Instead, nitrogen retention versus leaching risks were governed by individual soil physicochemical factors, notably soil organic carbon, bulk density, and salinity, which dictated the ratio of nitrification to microbial ammonium immobilization.

## Isotopic Inversion Across Pedological Gradients

Quantifying the discrete mechanisms governing terrestrial nitrogen turnover requires disaggregating simultaneous production and consumption fluxes. In this investigation, seven representative Chinese soils covering red soil, brown soil, purple soil, fluvo-aquic soil, chestnut soil, and alpine meadow soil were examined. The sampling sites captured extensive climatic gradients, ranging in mean annual temperature from -4.8 ℃ at Bayanbulak to 18.3 ℃ at Chongqing, and annual precipitation from 282 mm to 1 330 mm. Laboratory micro-incubations were implemented using dual 15N isotopic labelling (15NH4NO3 and NH415NO3 applied at 20 mg N per kg dry soil with 10% 15N abundance) destructively sampled at 0.5, 12, and 48 h.

The numerical model NtraceBasic, incorporating Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, resolved kinetics across ten gross nitrogen transformations by minimizing divergence from measured inorganic isotopic abundances. Quality optimization was confirmed against the Akaike Information Criterion, accepting model solutions at R2 > 0.80. Across all incubations, autotrophic nitrification and ammonium immobilization accounted for the overwhelming share of inorganic nitrogen flux, whereas dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium remained minimal (0.00±0.00 to 0.02±0.00 mg·kg-1·d-1).

- Dual-label isotopic dilution enabled simultaneous partitioning of labile versus recalcitrant organic nitrogen pools.

- MCMC optimization circumvented localized minima during multi-parameter iterative kinetic optimization.

Statistical evaluations revealed that broad ecosystem classifications (forest, grassland, and upland agriculture) did not exhibit significant divergences in gross mineralization, gross immobilization, or gross nitrification rates. The mean gross immobilization rates recorded were 4.24±3.04 mg·kg-1·d-1 in forest, 6.93±3.79 mg·kg-1·d-1 in grassland, and 5.54±2.00 mg·kg-1·d-1 in upland soils. Total inorganic nitrogen activity clustered around 12 to 13 mg·kg-1·d-1 across most sites, with markedly lower values in Changsha forest (2.05 mg·kg-1·d-1) and Chongqing forest (7.44 mg·kg-1·d-1).

Resistant organic nitrogen mineralization (MNrec) peaked at 1.97±0.61 mg·kg-1·d-1 in Linzhi forest, contrasting with 0.08±0.07 mg·kg-1·d-1 in Chongqing forest. In contrast, labile organic mineralization (MNlab) spanned 0.47±0.25 to 1.41±0.38 mg·kg-1·d-1 without significant inter-site divergence. ## Physicochemical Regulation and Environmental Loss Risks

The direction and retention capacity of mineralized nitrogen were evaluated via the nitrification-to-immobilization ratio (N/I). Soils exhibiting N/I ratios exceeding 1.0 were Quzhou upland (1.71) and Bayanbulak grassland (1.33). These conditions highlight an imbalance where nitrate generation substantially outpaces biological assimilation, predisposing the pedosphere to nitrate leaching and nitrous oxide emissions. Conversely, Duolun grassland (0.25) and Chongqing forest (0.14) displayed robust ammonium retention capacities.

Pearson correlation matrices demonstrated that gross mineralization rates correlated positively with soil organic carbon and negatively with bulk density. Labile nitrogen mineralization correlated positively with total nitrogen and organic carbon, but inversely with mean annual temperature. Autotrophic nitrification exhibited a significant positive correlation with soil salinity. Ammonium adsorption rates correlated negatively with pH (P < 0.001), reflecting mineral surface charge and cation competition phenomena.

- Low C/N ratios across sites (8.5 to 15.0) indicated baseline microbial carbon limitation across investigated soils.

- Elevated soil salinity aligned with enhanced autotrophic nitrification rates across arid and intensive agricultural soils.

## Methodological Constraints and Laboratory Boundary Conditions

This investigation relies on standardized short-term 48 h laboratory micro-incubations conducted under uniform temperature (25 ℃) and moisture (60% water holding capacity) conditions, which exclude real-time plant root uptake, mycorrhizal interactions, and in situ diurnal fluctuations.

- Laboratory incubations maintained static soil moisture at 60% WHC and constant temperature at 25 ℃, conditions that alter microbial metabolic kinetics relative to field conditions.

- The absence of living root systems eliminates plant-microbe competition for inorganic ammonium and nitrate pools.

- Extrapolations across regional scales are constrained by a sample size of seven geographic locations across three ecosystem types.

Detailed process conditions, instrument calibrations, and complete supplementary datasets beyond the core quantitative benchmarks are preserved in the Peer-Reviewed PDF Edition below.

# Gross Nitrogen Transformation Rates and Their Regulation in Soils of Three Typical Ecosystems in China

---

**DOI:** `10.11766/trxb202507290364` | **Journal:** Acta Pedologica Sinica (土壤学报) | **Year:** 2026  
**Authors:** HAO Tianxiang, YANG Meng  
**Affiliation:** Key Laboratory of Ecosystem Network Observation and Modeling, Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, Chinese Academy of Sciences

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

Soil gross nitrogen (N) transformation processes represent fundamental components of terrestrial biogeochemical cycling, yet the primary factors regulating gross transformation kinetics across contrasting ecosystem domains remain inadequately characterized. In this investigation, seven typical topsoils (0 to 20 cm) representing three major Chinese ecosystem types—forest (Changsha, Linzhi, Chongqing), grassland (Duolun, Bayanbulak), and upland cropland (Shangzhuang, Quzhou)—were sampled along atmospheric deposition, climate, and soil physicochemical gradients. Short-term laboratory incubations were conducted using 15N paired isotope dilution (15NH4NO3 and NH415NO3) coupled with the numerical tracing model NtraceBasic based on Markov chain Monte Carlo optimization to resolve ten gross N flux rates. Gross mineralization, microbial immobilization, and autotrophic nitrification dominated internal soil N turnover. Across ecosystem classes, mean gross mineralization rates were 1.40±1.31 mg·kg-1·d-1 for forest, 2.07±1.46 mg·kg-1·d-1 for grassland, and 1.83±0.01 mg·kg-1·d-1 for upland soils. Gross immobilization rates averaged 4.24±3.04, 6.93±3.79, and 5.54±2.00 mg·kg-1·d-1, while gross nitrification rates reached 1.47±1.30, 3.75±1.86, and 5.26±2.52 mg·kg-1·d-1, respectively, exhibiting no significant overall divergences among land-use classes. However, substantial heterogeneity was detected across individual sites. Gross mineralization correlated positively with soil organic carbon and negatively with bulk density, whereas autotrophic nitrification correlated with soil salinity. High nitrification-to-immobilization ratios in Quzhou upland (1.71) and Bayanbulak grassland (1.33) indicated elevated nitrate accumulation and leaching vulnerabilities, underscoring the necessity of multi-factor regulatory assessments.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Mean gross mineralization rates were 1.40±1.31 mg·kg-1·d-1 in forest, 2.07±1.46 mg·kg-1·d-1 in grassland, and 1.83±0.01 mg·kg-1·d-1 in upland soils, showing no significant differences among ecosystem categories.
- Gross immobilization rates averaged 4.24±3.04 mg·kg-1·d-1 for forest, 6.93±3.79 mg·kg-1·d-1 for grassland, and 5.54±2.00 mg·kg-1·d-1 for upland soils, heavily driven by NH4+-N microbial assimilation.
- Autotrophic nitrification (ONH4) ranged widely from 0.60±0.03 mg·kg-1·d-1 in Changsha forest to 7.04±0.07 mg·kg-1·d-1 in Quzhou upland, while heterotrophic nitrification remained negligible at 0.00±0.00 mg·kg-1·d-1 across all sites.
- Gross nitrification-to-immobilization (N/I) ratios exceeded unity in Quzhou upland (1.71) and Bayanbulak grassland (1.33), demonstrating heightened nitrate accumulation and environmental loss potential.
- Gross mineralization rates correlated positively with soil organic carbon (P < 0.05) and negatively with bulk density, while gross nitrification was positively linked to soil salinity.

## Microbial Alpha Diversity and Spatiotemporal Succession

Jiangxiangxing Baijiu manufacturing relies on an open, multi-phase solid-state fermentation process wherein steamed sorghum and wheat starter interact with surrounding ecological niches. In the fourth production round, grain discharged from distillation retorts (ZP1) exhibited initial bacterial richness of 430 OTUs (Shannon index 3.58; Chao 1 index 436.00) and fungal richness of 328 OTUs (Shannon index 3.07; Chao 1 index 377.46). Spreading and mechanical ridge breaking (ZP2) immediately gathered airborne and tool-borne microbiota, expanding bacterial richness to 797 OTUs (Chao 1 of 995.88). However, residual thermal stress during initial cooling temporarily trimmed richness to 512 OTUs (Chao 1 of 566.19) at stage ZP3, before Daqu inoculation (ZP4) replenished richness to 687 OTUs and Chao 1 to 881.53.

During closed stacking heap progression from day 1 (DJ1) to pit-entry readiness (XJ) at temperatures approaching 50 deg C, microbial alpha diversity exhibited targeted functional filtering. Bacterial Shannon diversity peaked at 3.67 on day 3 (DJ3) before stabilizing at 3.14 (510 OTUs, Chao 1 of 542.68) at pit entry. Simultaneously, fungal Shannon diversity declined steadily from 3.07 at discharge to 1.28 at pit entry (250 OTUs, Chao 1 of 296.88). Taxonomically, discharged grains initially harbored unclassified Chloroplast (27.12%), unclassified Caulobacteraceae (11.33%), and unclassified Dipodascaceae (36.63%). Cooling and starter blending induced substantial enrichment of core thermotolerant functional bacilli and actinomycetes, alongside an ecological shift where initial hydrolytic molds yielded dominance to ester-synthesizing yeasts.

- Bacterial OTU richness expanded from 430 in ZP1 to 797 in ZP2, contracted to 512 in ZP3, and stabilized at 510 in terminal XJ.

- Fungal communities transitioned from Thermomyces (46.08% in ZP6) and Aspergillus (20.23% in ZP6) to an absolute dominance of Pichia (90.08% in terminal grain).

- Stacking microenvironments filtered unclassified plant-derived plastid sequences in favor of thermophilic hydrolytic and aroma-synthesizing taxa.

This study decodes the microbial community succession and ecological origin dynamics across the transition from spreading to stacking fermentation during the fourth round of Jiangxiangxing Baijiu production. By integrating Illumina MiSeq high-throughput sequencing of 16S rRNA and ITS regions with gas chromatography and Bayesian SourceTracker analysis across 31 grain, starter, and facility environmental samples, the investigators established that core functional bacteria (Bacillus, Kroppenstedtia, Thermoactinomyces, Virgibacillus) and fungi (Pichia) enrich during grain spreading before reaching dominance during heap fermentation. Source tracking proved that operating tools drive inoculation during initial spreading, whereas Daqu inoculation contributes 68% of bacterial and 73% of fungal succession, supporting modern mechanized transitions.

## Volatile Metabolite Dynamics and Microbial Correlation Networks

Gas chromatographic quantification identified 33 volatile flavor compounds spanning 5 aldehydes, 8 carboxylic acids, 8 esters, 10 alcohols, and 2 miscellaneous components across the operational trajectory. Total volatile content climbed progressively during floor cooling, rising from 1872.10 mg/L in freshly discharged grains (ZP1) to 2547.28 mg/L at heap gathering (ZP6). Carboxylic acids constituted 57.20% of this net accumulation, contributing an additional 386.20 mg/L. Specific short-chain and medium-chain fatty acids, including acetic, isovaleric, heptanoic, isobutyric, and hexanoic acids, expanded by 1.5 to 2.7 fold. At heap gathering, acetic acid represented the predominant volatile constituent at 1002.65 mg/L.

Subsequent heap stacking triggered a shift in volatile chemistry: aldehyde and organic acid fractions contracted while higher polyols expanded significantly. At pit entry (XJ), 1,2-propanediol emerged as the dominant volatile constituent, reaching 1207.72 mg/L alongside elevated meso-2,3-butanediol. Spearman correlation modeling (P < 0.01) coupled with network topology demonstrated that acetic acid was significantly linked to 15 distinct taxa. Acinetobacter, unclassified Caulobacteraceae, Ralstonia, Thermoactinomyces, Aspergillus, Kazachstania, Paecilomyces, and Saccharomyces correlated positively with acetic acid accumulation, whereas Bacillus, Virgibacillus, Weissella, Pichia, Thermoascus, Thermomyces, and unclassified Dipodascaceae exhibited negative associations. Polyol accumulation (1,2-propanediol and meso-2,3-butanediol) correlated positively with Virgibacillus, while Pichia and Thermomyces correlated positively with isovaleraldehyde, isovaleric acid, and ethyl isovalerate.

- Accumulation of organic acids accounted for 386.20 mg/L of the 675.18 mg/L volatile increase during open floor spreading.

- Stacking fermentation elevated 1,2-propanediol to 1207.72 mg/L at pit entry, accompanied by increases in ethyl lactate and ethyl phenylacetate.

- Network analysis highlighted Virgibacillus as the primary bacterial driver of polyol biosynthesis and Pichia as the core driver of branched-chain esters.

## Bayesian SourceTracker Bio-Traceability and Environmental Habitats

Environmental microbiome characterization partitioned surrounding surfaces into operational tools (Group A), ancillary structural fixtures (Group B), raw/auxiliary materials (Group C), and floor surfaces (Group D). Tools harbored an exceptionally high relative abundance of lactic acid bacteria (15.93% to 85.93%), including Weissella (1.14% to 54.38%), Lactobacillus, Lactococcus, Pediococcus, Lactiplantibacillus, and Leuconostoc. Direct-contact floor points before spreading (TLQ) and stacking (DJQ) were dominated by Pediococcus (31.62% to 42.32%). Daqu starter served as the exclusive reservoir for high Kroppenstedtia, Bacillus, Virgibacillus, and Thermomyces (57.43%), whereas auxiliary rice husks primarily supplied Fusarium (36.93%), Dendryphiella (25.76%), and unclassified Chloroplast.

SourceTracker Bayesian modeling revealed that 25% of bacterial taxa in discharged grains originated from rice husks, with the remainder attributed to unknown baseline sources. As cooling commenced, operational tools provided 77% of bacteria in ZP2 and 58% in ZP3, alongside 66% to 88% of fungal taxa during initial spreading. Blending Daqu starter drastically reconfigured community origin, supplying 68% of bacteria and 73% of fungi in ZP4; Daqu-derived bacteria maintained a 34% to 80% presence throughout subsequent stacking. Secondary fungal contributions during heap fermentation derived from tools (9% to 84%) and floor surfaces (3% to 23%). Crucially, manual worker contact accounted for negligible bacterial and fungal colonization, confirming that solid-state inoculations are driven by physical implements, starter dosing, and thermal heap succession rather than direct human handling.

- Operational tools contributed 77% and 58% of grain bacteria during early mechanical handling before Daqu introduction.

- Daqu inoculation provided 68% of bacterial and 73% of fungal community fractions at blending stage ZP4.

- Minimal colonization from manual workers demonstrates the microbiological feasibility of engineering automated spreading machinery.

## Process Constraints and Industrial Generalizability

This empirical investigation tracks microbial succession and environmental reservoirs exclusively within the fourth manufacturing round of a single Jiangxiangxing Baijiu facility in Zunyi, Guizhou.

- Microbial community dynamics and volatile profiles were characterized during the fourth round in 2024; seasonal microclimatic variations across rounds 1 through 7 remain outside the scope of this dataset.

- Traceability relies on Bayesian SourceTracker probabilistic modeling from surface swab samples, which may underestimate contribution pathways from unmonitored ambient bioaerosols.

High-resolution diagnostic imagery, step-by-step methodological settings, and exhaustive dataset tables remain accessible exclusively inside the Archival PDF Viewer.

# Analysis of Distribution Patterns and Sources of Microbial Communities During Fourth-Round Stacking Fermentation of Jiangxiangxing Baijiu

---

**DOI:** `10.13995/j.cnki.11-1802/ts.043024` | **Journal:** Food and Fermentation Industries (食品与发酵工业) | **Year:** 2026  
**Authors:** HUANG Heou, ZHU Anran, WU Cheng, HU Feng, HU Jianfeng, LU Hu  
**Affiliation:** Guizhou Xijiu Co., Ltd.

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

Stacking fermentation represents an open solid-state bio-enrichment phase termed secondary starter-making that governs flavor precursor biosynthesis in traditional Jiangxiangxing Baijiu production. In this study, the microbial community dynamics, environmental habitats, and volatile flavor profiles during the fourth-round production cycle were systematically investigated across the full operational sequence from grain spreading to high-temperature heap fermentation. Using high-throughput sequencing of bacterial 16S rRNA gene V3-V4 and fungal ITS3-ITS4 regions alongside gas chromatography, 31 fermented grain and environmental niche samples were tracked. Operational taxonomic unit richness and alpha diversity metrics demonstrated rapid microbial acquisition during spreading followed by niche filtering during heap heating up to 50 deg C. Bacterial taxa Kroppenstedtia, Bacillus, Thermoactinomyces, and Virgibacillus expanded from baselines under 0.35% up to 22.59%, 13.96%, 4.73%, and 12.33% by heap assembly, while Pichia expanded to 90.08% relative abundance at the completion of stacking. Total volatile flavor compounds increased from 1872.10 mg/L to 2547.28 mg/L during spreading, dominated by a 386.20 mg/L surge in organic acids. In stacking fermentation, aldehydes and acids declined while higher alcohols accumulated, led by 1,2-propanediol reaching 1207.72 mg/L. Bayesian SourceTracker analysis demonstrated that processing tools drive early inoculation, Daqu provides 68% of bacteria and 73% of fungi upon addition, and direct worker contact imparts minimal colonization, confirming the technical feasibility of automated clean brewing platforms.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Total volatile flavor compounds climbed from 1872.10 mg/L in discharged grain (ZP1) to 2547.28 mg/L at heap gathering (ZP6), with acids contributing 386.20 mg/L (57.20%) of the net increase.
- Bacterial functional genera Kroppenstedtia, Bacillus, Virgibacillus, and Thermoactinomyces increased from 0.34%, 0.17%, 0.08%, and 0.13% at discharge to 22.59%, 13.96%, 12.33%, and 4.73% at heap gathering.
- Fungal community succession shifted from initial mold dominance (Aspergillus at 20.23% and Thermomyces at 46.08% in ZP6) to yeast dominance, with Pichia reaching 90.08% at terminal stacking.
- SourceTracker analysis proved that operating tools contributed 77% and 58% of bacteria during early ridge breaking (ZP2, ZP3), whereas Daqu supplied 68% of bacteria and 73% of fungi upon inoculation.
- Manual worker contact contributed minimal microbial loads to fermented grains, verifying the microbiological viability of mechanized cooling and spreading systems.

## Agronomic Yield and Crop Quality Trajectories

Investigating vegetable waste anaerobic digestion slurry applications reveals pronounced positive modulations of vegetative biomass and physiological metabolites in edible dock. In pot trials maintaining identical total liquid volumes of 2 L per pot, increasing biogas slurry from 8 L/m 2 (T1) to 12 L/m 2 (T3) produced progressive biomass accumulation. Fresh weight rose from 375.00±10.61 g/m 2 in clean water controls (CK) to 880.00±11.31 g/m 2 under T1, 1050.00±7.07 g/m 2 under T2, and reached a maximum of 1250.00±7.07 g/m 2 under T3, representing an enhancement of 233.33%. Above this threshold, biomass contracted to 1070.00±4.24 g/m 2 under T4 (14 L/m 2).

Phytochemical quality components mirrored this non-monotonic pattern. Leaf chlorophyll concentrations rose across all treated groups from 36.84±1.00 mg/g in CK to 48.19±1.02 mg/g in T2 and 47.89±0.89 mg/g in T3. Vitamin C concentrations expanded from 2.37±0.22 mg/g in CK to 5.88±0.33 mg/g in T3 and 5.90±0.61 mg/g in T2. Protein content increased from 31.55±1.34% in CK to 45.70±0.99% in T3, driven by active nitrogen assimilation. Total sugar peaked under T1 at 30.16±0.44 mg/g and remained elevated at 28.70±0.09 mg/g in T3 compared to 22.13±0.04 mg/g in CK.

Excessive dosing in T4 depressed reducing sugar to 5.64±0.01 mg/g, down from 6.89±0.06 mg/g in T2 and 6.55±0.12 mg/g in T3, reflecting an 18.1% reduction from T3. High ionic concentration and salinity stress at 14 L/m 2 disrupted plant carbohydrate metabolism pathways.

- Fresh weight reached 1250.00±7.07 g/m 2 under T3 versus 375.00±10.61 g/m 2 in CK.

- Edible dock crude protein content increased from 31.55±1.34% to 45.70±0.99% under T3.

- Reducing sugar declined from 6.55±0.12 mg/g in T3 to 5.64±0.01 mg/g in T4.

Agricultural recycling of anaerobic digestion slurry derived from vegetable residues addresses waste management while providing organic crop nutrition. This controlled pot investigation established quantitative response curves for Rumex patientia-based edible dock under four volumetric slurry irrigation regimes against a water control. Supplying biogas slurry significantly enhanced vegetative biomass and nutrient synthesis, culminating at an optimal application rate of 12 L/m 2 (1.2 L/pot, designated T3), which elevated fresh weight by 233.33% alongside substantial increases in crude protein, vitamin C, and soil enzymatic indices. However, exceeding this threshold at 14 L/m 2 (T4) depressed reducing sugar concentrations and compromised nutrient assimilation efficiency.

## Edaphic Nutrient Stocks and Soil Acidification Amelioration

Application of alkaline vegetable residue slurry (pH 7.72) systematically counteracted soil acidity, transforming the native soil substrate (initial pH 6.52, control final pH 6.94±0.52). Slurry-treated soils recorded significant alkalization, rising to 8.02±0.30 in T1, 8.42±0.42 in T2, 8.21±0.15 in T3, and 8.29±0.14 in T4, representing an overall percentage increase of 15.56% to 21.3%.

Soil organic matter stocks increased from 14.28±0.02% in CK to 16.18±0.25% in T1, 16.34±0.07% in T2, 16.72±0.24% in T3, and 16.62±0.18% in T4, equivalent to gains of 13.3% to 17.09%. Available potassium exhibited substantial enrichment due to the potassium-rich input slurry (317.63 mg/kg native slurry potassium), increasing from 136.63±15.22 mg/kg in CK to 274.33±26.51 mg/kg in T1, 306.63±8.39 mg/kg in T2, and plateauing at 369.90±17.50 mg/kg in T3 and 369.47±11.96 mg/kg in T4.

Total nitrogen advanced from 0.10±0.01% in CK to between 0.14±0.03% and 0.15±0.01% across T1 through T4, denoting a 40% to 50% enrichment. Soil available phosphorus displayed non-linear behavior, declining from 28.39±0.20 mg/kg in CK to 26.77±0.55 mg/kg in T1, 27.49±0.19 mg/kg in T2, and 25.17±0.65 mg/kg in T4, while T3 achieved 29.21±0.34 mg/kg. Phosphorus precipitation with calcium or iron oxides under alkaline pH accounted for the 11.3% reduction observed in T4.

- Soil pH adjusted upwards from 6.94±0.52 to 8.21±0.15 under T3.

## Enzymatic Kinetics and Biogeochemical Correlation Dynamics

Soil urease and beta-glucosidase activities tracked biochemical nutrient cycling throughout a 60 h post-irrigation incubation window. Urease activity, responsible for catalyzing urea conversion into bioavailable ammonium, exhibited a unimodal trajectory that crested at 36 h. Under T3 treatment, urease activity was consistently elevated compared with alternative treatments, accelerating organic nitrogen mineralization. Beta-glucosidase activity, which hydrolyzes cellulose-derived carbohydrates to release labile carbon, increased in direct proportion to slurry dosage, with T3 and T4 exhibiting statistically superior activity levels that also peaked at 36 h.

Statistical Pearson correlation and Mantel evaluations confirmed coordinated carbon-nitrogen coupling within the soil-crop continuum. Soil pH correlated positively with soil organic matter (r=0.62, P<0.01), available potassium (r=0.58, P<0.05), total nitrogen (r=0.61, P<0.01), and plant protein content (r=0.55, P<0.05). Beta-glucosidase activity exhibited positive linkages with available potassium (r=0.63, P<0.01), total nitrogen (r=0.65, P<0.01), and organic matter (r=0.59, P<0.05).

Edible dock protein synthesis demonstrated strong dependence on edaphic nitrogen and potassium availability, correlating significantly with soil total nitrogen (r=0.71, P<0.01), available potassium (r=0.54), organic matter (r=0.59), and plant reducing sugar (r=0.57, P<0.05). Conversely, available phosphorus exhibited loose associations with beta-glucosidase (r=-0.41, P>0.05) and total sugar (r=-0.38, P>0.05), functioning independently in the rhizosphere.

- Soil urease and beta-glucosidase activities peaked simultaneously at 36 h post-irrigation in T3.

- Beta-glucosidase activity correlated strongly with soil total nitrogen (r=0.65, P<0.01) and available potassium (r=0.63, P<0.01).

- Plant crude protein correlated tightly with soil total nitrogen (r=0.71, P<0.01).

## Dosage Boundaries and Methodological Constraints

The study findings derive from a single 30-day potted growth cycle using controlled 10 kg soil units, requiring validation across multi-season open-field environments where precipitation and drainage dynamics operate.

- Heavy metal accumulation in edible dock tissues was not empirically quantified, which warrants attention given the crop heavy metal bioconcentration potential and safety limits for livestock feed or human food.

- The 14 L/m 2 (T4) treatment caused osmotic and alkalization stress (pH 8.29), reducing available phosphorus by 11.3% and reducing sugar by 18.1%, setting an upper boundary for single-cycle application.

## Dehydration Kinetics and Moisture Migration Dynamics

Raw mulberry pomace generated from juice processing possesses an initial moisture content of 71.60%, rendering the matrix vulnerable to rapid microbial spoilage and biochemical degradation. Applying different thermal dehydration methods established distinct moisture dissipation behaviors. Moisture ratios decreased steeply across all groups during the initial 0 to 2 h window due to low internal moisture diffusion resistance and steep internal-to-surface temperature gradients. As dehydration progressed, unfreezable and bound water dominated the internal structure, causing surface crusting and increasing internal diffusion resistance.

Thermal elevation substantially curtailed processing duration across both convective hot air drying (HAD) and heat pump drying (HPD). HAD required 12.0 h at 50 ℃, 5.0 h at 60 ℃, and 4.5 h at 70 ℃ to reach the endpoint moisture threshold below 8%. Under identical operational temperatures, HPD expedited drying to 10.0 h, 3.5 h, and 2.5 h, representing an efficiency enhancement of 16.7% to 44.4% over HAD. Regulating relative humidity at 15% inside the HPD drying chamber magnified internal-to-external moisture gradient driving forces, mitigating internal mass transfer resistance.

- Increasing HAD temperature from 50 ℃ to 60 ℃ reduced drying time by 58.3%, with a further 10% reduction achieved between 60 ℃ and 70 ℃.

- HPD reduced drying time by 65.0% when elevated from 50 ℃ to 60 ℃, and by 28.6% when elevated from 60 ℃ to 70 ℃.

This investigation evaluated vacuum freeze-drying alongside convective hot air drying and closed-loop heat pump drying across thermal regimes of 50, 60, and 70 °C for valorizing high-moisture mulberry juice pomace. While vacuum freeze-drying demonstrated exceptional phytochemical retention, it required 36 h and generated irregular flaky particles with poor bulk powder flowability. Convective and heat pump drying promoted particle spherical contraction, yielding superior powder packing densities and lower repose angles. Specifically, processing at 60 °C under hot air and heat pump configurations preserved antioxidant activities and anthocyanins while shortening dehydration durations by up to 83.3%, identifying an energy-efficient industrial standard.

## Powder Micromorphology and Functional Hydration Behavior

Post-drying mechanical milling (30,000 r / min for 60 s) revealed pronounced divergences in powder micromorphology and bulk flowability governed by initial sublimation versus thermal evaporation dynamics. Powders generated via vacuum freeze-drying (VFD) exhibited irregular flaky fragments and high inter-particle friction, evidenced by a loose bulk density of 0.26 ± 0.03 g / cm3 and an elevated resting angle of 48.52 ± 1.81°, indicating poor powder flowability. However, VFD powders demonstrated superior oil-holding capacity (4.87 ± 0.10 g / g) and solubility (32.36 ± 0.29%) attributable to open, porous cellular architectures that readily exposed hydrophilic and lipophilic functional groups.

Conversely, thermal dehydration induced volumetric shrinkage, resulting in semi-spherical milled granules with diminished inter-particle contact areas and friction. All HAD and HPD powders demonstrated significantly improved flow characteristics, exhibiting uniform bulk densities between 0.44 ± 0.01 and 0.45 ± 0.01 g / cm3 and resting angles spanning 39.74 ± 0.58° to 43.29 ± 0.83°. Water retention capacities showed no statistically significant differences across drying regimes, remaining stable within 3.18 ± 0.31 to 4.08 ± 0.18 g / g.

- HPD50 yielded the finest particle distribution with D10 of 10.90 ± 0.07 μm, D50 of 116.33 ± 1.38 μm, and highest dispersion span of 3.68 ± 0.13.

- VFD displayed larger particle dimensions (D50 of 159.27 ± 5.35 μm) and lower specific surface area (60.10 ± 1.44 m2 / kg) due to low structural hardness.

## Phytochemical Retention and Volatile Fingerprint Discrimination

Thermal and atmospheric exposure directly dictated the degradation profiles of functional polyphenols and anthocyanin monomers. VFD retained maximum total phenolic content (56.3 mg / g) and total flavonoids (59.6 mg / g) due to low-temperature sublimation (condenser at -80 ℃ and vacuum at 81.3 Pa) inhibiting polyphenol oxidase (PPO) and peroxidase (POD). In contrast, HAD and HPD regimens exhibited parabolic retention curves where 60 ℃ preserved higher phenolic levels than 50 ℃ or 70 ℃, because 50 ℃ sustained elevated enzymatic degradation over prolonged dehydration cycles while 70 ℃ promoted thermal breakdown.

High-performance liquid chromatography and electronic nose principal component analysis (PCA) confirmed that intermediate thermal processing closely matched VFD bioactive profiles. Cyanidin-3-O-glucoside (C-3-G) and total anthocyanin concentrations in HPD60 aligned most closely with VFD benchmarks, whereas HAD70 preserved the highest cyanidin-3-O-rutinoside (C-3-R) retention. Principal components PC1 (65.4%) and PC2 (26.4%) captured 91.8% of volatile variance, indicating that HAD60 and HPD60 retained core aroma signatures while offering robust processing economies.

## Process Scale Boundaries and Industrial Considerations

While convective and heat pump drying at 60 ℃ demonstrate high functional retention and operational efficiency, distinct physical boundaries constrain broader industrial deployment.

- Thermal drying cannot replicate the superior solubility of 32.36 ± 0.29% or oil-holding capacity of 4.87 ± 0.10 g / g achieved by low-temperature vacuum freeze-drying.

- Lower thermal drying at 50 ℃ prolonged processing time to 12.0 h in HAD and 10.0 h in HPD, increasing enzyme-mediated polyphenol oxidation.

- The empirical evaluations were confined to laboratory batch drying equipment and a single raw material moisture level of 71.60% before pulverization.

# Effects of Drying Methods and Temperatures on Physicochemical Properties, Bioactive Compound Retention, and Flavor Profile of Mulberry Pomace Powder

---

**DOI:** `10.13995/j.cnki.11-1802/ts.042901` | **Journal:** Food and Fermentation Industries (食品与发酵工业) | **Year:** 2026  
**Authors:** CHEN Zhihua, PENG Jian, XIAO Gengsheng, WU Wanling, YU Yuanshan, LI Lu, LIU Jun, XU Yujuan  
**Affiliation:** Sericultural & Agri-food Research Institute, Guangdong Academy of Agricultural Sciences

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

This study employed vacuum freeze-drying (VFD), hot air drying (HAD) at temperatures of 50, 60, and 70 ℃, and heat pump drying (HPD) at the corresponding temperatures to prepare mulberry pomace powder, yielding seven distinct experimental samples designated as VFD, HAD50, HAD60, HAD70, HPD50, HPD60, and HPD70. The systematic effects of drying regimes and dehydration temperatures on physical powder attributes, bioactive constituent retention, and volatile flavor profiles were thoroughly assessed. Results indicated that while VFD effectively maintained overall physicochemical quality, bioactive polyphenols, antioxidant capacities, and aroma profiles, its microstructure comprised irregular flaky fragments exhibiting inferior powder flowability alongside prolonged drying durations exceeding 30 h (reaching 36 h). Conversely, powders generated through HAD and HPD at varying temperatures displayed no significant discrepancies in color parameters, microstructure, water-holding capacity, oil-holding capacity, bulk density, or repose angle. Notably, HPD50 produced the smallest median particle diameter with the lowest size uniformity, whereas HAD50 yielded the lowest aqueous solubility. Crucially, HAD60 achieved comparable total phenolics, total flavonoids, and radical-scavenging capacities to VFD, alongside superior soluble sugar retention, while reducing total drying time by 83.3%. Overall, processing via HAD or HPD at 60 ℃ provides optimal industrial balance between dehydration efficiency, functional powder flowability, and bioactive retention.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Heat pump drying accelerates moisture removal, completing dehydration in 2.5 h at 70 ℃ compared to 4.5 h for hot air drying and 36 h for vacuum freeze-drying.
- Hot air drying at 60 ℃ reduced drying duration by 83.3% relative to vacuum freeze-drying while maintaining comparable antioxidant capacity and phenolic content.
- Powders processed via hot air and heat pump drying exhibited superior flowability with resting angles between 39.74° and 43.29°, compared to 48.52° for vacuum freeze-drying.
- Vacuum freeze-drying retained the highest total phenolics at 56.3 mg / g and total flavonoids at 59.6 mg / g, but resulted in an irregular flaky matrix and poor packing density of 0.26 g / cm3.
- Dehydration at 60 ℃ under convective hot air or heat pump regimes balances bioactive preservation with industrial energy efficiency for mulberry by-product valorization.

analysis_markdown_en:
The study addresses a critical gap in ecosystem service research: most assessments treat cities as homogeneous units, failing to capture supply-demand heterogeneity along urban-rural gradients in mountainous metropolitan regions. By partitioning Chongqing into four urbanization zones (rural, urban-rural transition, urban expansion, urban) using weighted population, economic, and land urbanization indicators, the analysis reveals that rural areas function as core supply zones while urban cores are persistent deficit zones. The urban expansion zone crossed from supply-demand balance to deficit between 2015 and 2020, with its comprehensive ratio dropping to −0.145 by 2023.

The InVEST-based quantification shows that carbon sequestration demand grew 131.88% while supply rose only 0.28%, and food production was the sole service with a persistent deficit (ESDR −0.18 in 2023). Soil conservation and water yield were the only services with increasing surpluses. The trade-off/synergy analysis indicates that soil conservation–water yield synergy strengthens with urbanization intensity (88.04% in urban areas), while water yield–habitat quality trade-off remains dominant (78.03% in expansion zones). These zone-specific patterns support differentiated management: ecological network enhancement in urban cores, red-line enforcement in transition and expansion zones, and ecological compensation mechanisms in rural areas.

### Study Abstract

To clarify the evolution of ecosystem services in regional development systems and reveal interactions under human disturbance, this study integrated the InVEST model and Spearman correlation analysis to assess six ecosystem services—carbon sequestration, food production, soil conservation, water yield, habitat quality, and recreation and leisure—across urbanization zones in Chongqing from 2005 to 2023, analyzing spatiotemporal supply-demand evolution and trade-off/synergy relationships. Results show that: (1) Although ecosystem services maintained a surplus, the surplus scale contracted, with the comprehensive supply-demand ratio exhibiting a small-amplitude, slowly declining temporal trend. High supply-demand ratio areas for carbon sequestration, water yield, soil conservation, habitat quality, and recreation concentrated in northeastern and southeastern Chongqing, while low-value areas clustered in the core of the main urban metropolitan area. (2) Urbanization displayed a monocentric multi-point pattern, higher in the west and lower in the east, with overall urban expansion and rural contraction. Demand increased from rural to urban areas while supply showed the opposite gradient; rural areas were core supply zones and urban areas were deficit zones. Most service supply-demand ratios declined; urban expansion zones transitioned from balance to deficit, with only soil conservation and water yield surpluses increasing. (3) Static relationships in rural areas were dominated by strong synergies and trade-offs with high stability; urban-rural transition zones showed weak synergies with significant fluctuations; urban expansion zones shifted from trade-off to synergy dominance. Only five service pairs in urban areas exhibited consistent trade-off/synergy with low volatility. Habitat quality and recreation were always synergistic across zones, while water yield and recreation were always in trade-off. Soil conservation and water yield remained synergistic, strengthening with urbanization intensity. These findings support coordinated socioeconomic and ecological development in Chongqing.

## InVEST-Based Quantification of Six Ecosystem Services Across Urbanization Zones

The study quantified supply and demand for six ecosystem services—carbon sequestration, food production, soil conservation, water yield, habitat quality, and recreation and leisure—using the InVEST model and socioeconomic indicators. Carbon sequestration supply was calculated as the sum of aboveground, belowground, soil, and dead organic matter carbon pools multiplied by grid area, while demand was derived from per capita energy consumption and carbon transfer coefficients. Food production supply used NDVI-based cropland weighting, and demand was estimated from per capita food consumption. Soil conservation supply applied the Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) with rainfall erosivity, soil erodibility, topographic, cover, and conservation practice factors, while demand used the same USLE structure. Water yield supply came from InVEST's water yield module, and demand from per capita water consumption. Habitat quality and recreation demand were proxied by construction land area, GDP, and per capita park green space.

Urbanization zoning was established using weighted population (0.292), economic (0.107), and land (0.601) urbanization indicators, classified into four zones: rural areas (comprehensive index 0–0.05), urban-rural transition zones (0.05–0.19), urban expansion zones (0.19–0.46), and urban areas (0.46–1.00). From 2005 to 2023, rural area share declined from 97.56% to 94.13%, while urban-rural transition zones rose from 1.79% to 3.46%, urban expansion zones from 0.51% to 1.81%, and urban areas from 0.13% to 0.59%. The comprehensive urbanization level exhibited a monocentric multi-point pattern, higher in the west and lower in the east, with high-value clusters in the core of the main urban metropolitan area and low-value areas concentrated in northeastern and southeastern Chongqing.

## Supply-Demand Ratio Dynamics and Trade-off/Synergy Analysis (2005–2023)

Between 2005 and 2023, all ecosystem services except food production maintained aggregate supply exceeding demand, but trends diverged. Carbon sequestration supply fluctuated from 9,203.63 t/km² in 2005 to 9,206.21 t/km² in 2023 (0.28% increase), while demand surged 131.88% from 213.53 to 495.15 t/km². Food production supply declined 6.19% (141.73 to 132.96 t/km²) and demand fell 9.95% (43.03 to 38.75 t/km²), yet the service remained in deficit with ESDR at −0.18 in 2023 and deficit area expanding from 54.81% to 55.98%. Soil conservation supply decreased 6.18% (1,677.36 to 1,801.02 t/hm²) while demand rose 7.75% (108.42 to 116.82 t/hm²), but ESDR increased from 0.82 to 0.83. Water yield supply grew 37.14% (618.24 to 847.90 mm/km²) and demand fell 17.75% (74.14 to 60.98 mm/km²), raising ESDR from 0.86 to 0.89. Habitat quality supply declined 0.51% (0.594 to 0.587) and demand rose from 0.004 to 0.020, with ESDR falling from 0.98 to 0.94. Recreation supply fell 1.59% (0.525 to 0.517) and demand rose from 0.001 to 0.005, with ESDR dropping 40.00% from 0.05 to 0.03.

Trade-off/synergy relationships were assessed using Spearman correlation coefficients for static analysis and the ecosystem service trade-off and synergy degree (ESTD) for dynamic analysis. In rural areas, most service pairs were not significant (SC-RL 73.1%), with GP-SC, SC-HQ, and WY-HQ dominated by trade-offs (WY-HQ 61.67%) and GP-WY and SC-WY by synergies (SC-WY 71.00%). Urban-rural transition zones showed similar patterns except GP-HQ (43.60% synergy) and GP-WY (52.43% trade-off). Urban expansion zones had only five non-significant pairs (GP-RL 97.08%), four synergistic pairs (SC-WY 81.42%), and six trade-off pairs (WY-HQ 78.03%). Urban areas had mostly non-significant relationships (SC-RL 95.88%), with CS-WY (49.07%) and WY-HQ (50.31%) as trade-offs and CS-HQ (49.07%) and SC-WY (88.04%) as synergies. Across all zones, SC-WY consistently showed the largest synergy area and WY-HQ the largest trade-off area. Dynamic trade-off strength for WY-HQ ranked: urban (50.31%) < rural (61.67%) < urban-rural transition (75.35%) < urban expansion (78.03%).

## Boundary Constraints and Applicability of Urbanization-Zoned Ecosystem Service Assessment

- Demand quantification relies on socioeconomic proxies (per capita energy consumption, food consumption, water use, GDP, construction land area) with lower precision than process-based supply models.

- The study period spans 2005–2023 with five-year interval snapshots (2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2023), limiting detection of intra-decadal dynamics.

- Urbanization zoning uses a fixed 2023 classification as the spatial base, which may not capture zone boundary shifts over the 18-year study period.

- Findings are specific to Chongqing's mountainous topography (97% hilly/mountainous terrain) and may not transfer directly to flatland metropolitan regions.

- The ESTD dynamic analysis defines significance as area share ≥50% for a service pair, potentially masking localized trade-off/synergy patterns below this threshold.

# Spatiotemporal Evolution of Ecosystem Service Supply-Demand and Trade-off/Synergy Relationships in Chongqing, China Based on Urbanization Zoning

---

**DOI:** `10.11975/j.issn.1002-6819.202510003` | **Journal:** Transactions of the Chinese Society of Agricultural Engineering (Transactions of the Chinese Society of Agricultural Engineering (农业工程学报)) | **Published:** 2026 (Vol 46 12)  
**Authors:** TAN Jia, ZHANG Junyi, WANG Lingzhi  
**Institution:** School of Geography and Tourism, Chongqing Normal University  
**Portal:** `https://sinoagritech.com/paper/spatiotemporal-evolution-of-ecosystem-service-supply-demand-and-trade-offsynergy-relationships-127079`

---

## 1. Executive Abstract

To clarify the evolution of ecosystem services in regional development systems and reveal interactions under human disturbance, this study integrated the InVEST model and Spearman correlation analysis to assess six ecosystem services-carbon sequestration, food production, soil conservation, water yield, habitat quality, and recreation and leisure-across urbanization zones in Chongqing from 2005 to 2023, analyzing spatiotemporal supply-demand evolution and trade-off/synergy relationships. Results show that: (1) Although ecosystem services maintained a surplus, the surplus scale contracted, with the comprehensive supply-demand ratio exhibiting a small-amplitude, slowly declining temporal trend. High supply-demand ratio areas for carbon sequestration, water yield, soil conservation, habitat quality, and recreation concentrated in northeastern and southeastern Chongqing, while low-value areas clustered in the core of the main urban metropolitan area. (2) Urbanization displayed a monocentric multi-point pattern, higher in the west and lower in the east, with overall urban expansion and rural contraction. Demand increased from rural to urban areas while supply showed the opposite gradient; rural areas were core supply zones and urban areas were deficit zones. Most service supply-demand ratios declined; urban expansion zones transitioned from balance to deficit, with only soil conservation and water yield surpluses increasing. (3) Static relationships in rural areas were dominated by strong synergies and trade-offs with high stability; urban-rural transition zones showed weak synergies with significant fluctuations; urban expansion zones shifted from trade-off to synergy dominance. Only five service pairs in urban areas exhibited consistent trade-off/synergy with low volatility. Habitat quality and recreation were always synergistic across zones, while water yield and recreation were always in trade-off. Soil conservation and water yield remained synergistic, strengthening with urbanization intensity. These findings support coordinated socioeconomic and ecological development in Chongqing.

---

## 2. Core Quantitative Takeaways

- Carbon sequestration demand rose 131.88% (213.53 to 495.15 t/km²) from 2005 to 2023, while supply increased only 0.28% (9,203.63 to 9,206.21 t/km²).
- The comprehensive supply-demand ratio in urban expansion zones fell from 0.364 in 2005 to -0.145 in 2023, crossing from balance to deficit between 2015 and 2020.
- Soil conservation-water yield synergy area reached 88.04% in urban areas and 81.42% in urban expansion zones, the strongest synergy pair across all zones.
- Water yield-habitat quality trade-off area was 78.03% in urban expansion zones and 61.67% in rural areas, the most significant trade-off pair.

## Coupled Thermodynamic Modeling and State Constraint Formulation

Circulation counter-flow dryers operate under severe non-linear dynamics and significant transport delays. In the industrial 5HP-20 drying tower, wet grain flows sequentially through tempering, preheating, drying, and discharging stages, with a bucket hoist returning grain to the tower apex for repeated circulation. To establish an accurate predictive framework, mass and energy conservation equations were formulated across all four functional stages. Within the dual counter-flow drying sections, hot air exchanges heat and moisture with downward-flowing paddy. In the preheating zone, heat pipe wall conduction from flue gas warms the grain via Newton cooling formulations without active airflow. The tempering and discharging sections facilitate moisture redistribution and radiative cooling to ambient surroundings.

The control architecture treats grain velocity vg as the single manipulated variable, bounded between 1 m/h and 3.9 m/h around an operational baseline of 2 m/h. Discharged wet basis moisture content is constrained within safe storage boundaries. To suppress kernel fissure formation and preserve sensory palatability, explicit material state constraints enforce that grain remains in the rubbery thermodynamic state throughout desiccation, preventing protein denaturation and uneven starch gelatinization.

- Governing equations incorporate phase interface heat transfer coefficients hτα and mass transfer coefficients μγα based on empirical drying constants.

- Optimization utilizes sequential quadratic programming (SQP) with prediction horizon Np = 4 and control horizon Nc = 4.

- A temporal attenuation coefficient β = 0.3 relaxes control rate constraints in initial prediction intervals to balance responsiveness and actuator wear.

## Disturbance Attenuation and Dynamic Setpoint Trajectory Tracking

Controller robustness was evaluated under steep step changes in initial grain moisture content and ambient relative humidity. When inlet moisture suddenly dropped from 18% to 17.2% at 1 h, the controller exhibited an intentional 0.91 h dead-time delay before elevating grain flow velocity, effectively preventing over-drying of incoming grain while respecting internal convective transport delays. When inlet moisture surged from 17.2% to 19% at 5 h, grain speed was decreased after a 0.77 h delay, yielding an overshoot of 2.30% and settling time of 0.20 h. In contrast, abrupt changes in ambient relative humidity (shifting from 50% to 80%, then plunging to 20%) directly impacted the drying base, eliciting immediate actuator responses that maintained output deviations below 0.01% with zero overshoot.

Setpoint tracking tests demonstrated consistent stability across varied profiles. For step transitions between -0.3% and 0.8%, the controller attained maximum relative deviations of 5.24% and an overall relative average deviation (RAD) of 0.11%. Ramp transitions with slopes of 1%/h exhibited tight profile synchronization with an RAD of 0.07%. Sinusoidal target variations yielded an RAD of 0.01% and maximum deviation of 3.11%, demonstrating effective phase matching and elimination of steady-state tracking error.

- Controlled moisture trajectory remains strictly within operational error bands during inlet grain moisture surges.

- Mechanical malfunction step disturbances of -0.6% and 1% were settled within 0.02 h and 0.12 h respectively.

- Actuator velocity modulation exhibits damped oscillatory behavior, trading small transient rate adjustments for long-term setpoint stability.

## Comparative Benchmarking Under Simulated Operational Faults

To rigorously assess practical industrial viability, synthetic stochastic disturbances of ±40%, ±60%, and ±90% peak amplitudes were injected into grain drying states at the drying section exit. Without active feedback control, unattenuated fluctuations propagated directly to the tower discharge, generating maximum relative deviations up to 11.03% in moisture content and 5.72% in grain temperature. Standard feedback PID and feedforward PID architectures provided partial compensation but struggled against intrinsic process transport dead-time, leaving substantial residual oscillations.

The model predictive controller consistently outperformed both PID configurations across all disturbance levels. By minimizing predicted tracking error over the multi-step horizon, the MPC controller confined maximum moisture deviation to 2.33% and temperature deviation to 1.12% under extreme ±90% upset conditions. The resulting moisture RAD dropped to 0.41%, representing a 30.5% error reduction over uncontrolled operation, 21.2% over standard PID, and 14.6% over feedforward PID.

- Under ±40% disturbances, MPC moisture RAD reached 0.32%, outperforming PID (0.34%) and feedforward PID (0.33%).

- Under ±60% disturbances, MPC moisture RAD reached 0.40%, outperforming PID (0.45%) and feedforward PID (0.43%).

- Discharge grain temperature RAD was held to 0.10% (±40%) and 0.12% (±60% and ±90%), maintaining stable thermal output.

Conventional circulation paddy dryers frequently suffer from moisture deviations and energy inefficiency due to delayed feedback, non-linear drying kinetics, and unmeasured operational disturbances. This study develops a Model Predictive Control (MPC) architecture tailored for an industrial 5HP-20 circulation counter-flow paddy drying system. By solving a constrained rolling-horizon optimization problem using sequential quadratic programming, the controller dynamically adjusts grain flow velocity while maintaining paddy in the rubbery state to prevent crack generation. The control scheme attenuates sudden shifts in inlet grain moisture, ambient relative humidity, and mechanical disruptions, delivering tight setpoint regulation and superior disturbance rejection over classical proportional-integral-derivative baselines.

## Process Boundaries and Operational Considerations

While demonstrating robust tracking and disturbance rejection, the MPC architecture requires accurate real-time parameter identification and computational resources for sequential quadratic programming.

- Computational overhead associated with real-time non-linear optimization may limit deployment on resource-constrained embedded microcontrollers without neural network surrogate approximations.

- Controller performance relies on well-calibrated physical equations and accurate measurements from air velocity sensors (AS8336, precision ±0.01 m/s) and temperature transducers.

- The current implementation manipulates grain discharge velocity while holding stage ventilation parameters at predetermined stepped setpoints (60 ℃ and 2 988 m/h during initial 0 to 3.9 h; 80 ℃ and 2016 m/h thereafter).

This feeding trial evaluates the efficacy and physiological safety of substituting conventional feedstuffs with corn starch sugar residue in male Pekin ducks across a 42-day rearing period. Inclusion levels of 5% to 10% supported growth performance and improved digestive organ development, specifically augmenting gizzard, pancreatic, and duodenal indices while decreasing jejunal crypt depth. ## Phase-Dependent Growth Performance Responses and Metabolic Shifts

Evaluating alternative agro-industrial co-products is essential to alleviate global feed grain supply pressures. Corn starch sugar residue provides 21.98% crude protein, 25.88% ether extract, and an apparent metabolizable energy of 18.09 MJ/kg for meat ducks. In this 42-day trial, graded dietary additions of 0, 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% were assessed in 240 male Pekin ducks. During the starter period from 1 to 21 days of age, dietary inclusion of 5% and 10% corn starch sugar residue exerted no adverse impact on average body weight, average daily gain, average daily feed intake, or feed-to-gain ratio.

In contrast, starter diets containing 15% and 20% residue depressed 21-day average body weight to 1296.72±32.02 g and 1284.34±21.97 g, compared to 1349.69±23.54 g in the control cohort. Average daily gain during the starter phase dropped from 61.91±1.36 g/d in controls to 58.52±1.32 g/d in the 20% group, while feed-to-gain ratio rose to 1.56±0.03. During the 22 to 42 day grower-finisher window, growth performance remained resilient up to 15% inclusion, showing body weights comparable to control (3028.56±99.09 g vs. 3112.07±41.80 g), whereas the 20% group exhibited significantly impaired final body weight at 2977.04±66.84 g.

This study was conducted to investigate the effects of dietary corn starch sugar residue supplementation on growth and development, plasma biochemical parameters, and breast muscle quality of Pekin ducks. Compared with the control group, dietary supplementation with 15% and 20% corn starch sugar residue significantly reduced average body weight (ABW) at 21 days of age and average daily gain (ADG) from 1 to 21 days of age (P<0.05). ## Hydro-Salinity Dynamics Across Spatial Row Configurations

In the chloride-dominated saline soils of Pingluo County within the Hetao Plain, point-source drip irrigation creates pronounced spatial heterogeneity in moisture and salt distribution. Drip emitters stationed along narrow crop rows (40 cm spacing) systematically wash soluble salts toward the wetting front boundaries located in the adjacent unmulched wide rows (70 cm spacing). In unmulched control plots, capillary rise fueled by an annual pan evaporation of 1 755 mm versus 170 mm annual precipitation forces soluble ions to gather densely within the top 0-20 cm layer.

Deploying transparent polyethylene film over the narrow rows provides a physical vapor barrier that suppresses upward capillary transport. Consequently, soil electrical conductivity in narrow rows drops substantially throughout the vegetative phases. At the jointing stage, mulching enhances 0-20 cm soil moisture retention by 15.78%. However, this moisture advantage disappears after tasseling. As maize transpirational demand accelerates, crop water extraction overtakes soil evaporation suppression. By harvest, the absence of rainfall infiltration through the intact plastic film depresses narrow-row subsoil water content relative to unmulched controls.

- Lateral salt displacement forces peak electrical conductivity outward into the 0-20 cm wide-row inter-row zones.

- Average 0-20 cm soil salinity across the growing season is reduced by 22.13% in wide rows and 35.62% in narrow rows under mulched drip conditions.

- Soil pH exhibits minor buffering fluctuations across all growth stages, maintaining moderately alkaline values between 8.49 and 8.85.

In the arid Hetao Plain of Northwest China, agricultural sustainability is constrained by secondary soil salinization and acute irrigation water shortages. This field study evaluated the agronomic and edaphic consequences of mulched drip irrigation versus unmulched drip irrigation in maize across wide and narrow row geometries. While plastic mulching effectively mitigated surface salt accumulation—lowering narrow-row electrical conductivity by 25.29% to 56.90% and elevating early soil moisture retention by 15.78%—it unexpectedly decreased maize grain yield by 12.60% and straw yield by 26.52%. The yield decline stemmed from a steep lateral salinity gradient between mulched narrow rows and unmulched wide rows, which severely restricted root extension and lateral branching.

Mulched drip irrigation reorganizes the spatial distribution of macro-nutrients and microbial enzymatic activity across the soil profile. Under mulching, narrow-row surface total nitrogen in the 0-10 cm horizon decreases by 26.87%, driven by enhanced microbial mineralization and accelerated downward moisture movement. Inorganic nitrogen dynamics are heavily governed by solute leaching and lateral diffusion. Surface nitrate in the narrow row drops by 61.37% under mulching, while subsoil nitrate at 20-40 cm rises by 72.98% alongside substantial lateral accumulation in the wide rows. Concurrently, available phosphorus and available potassium show broad-spectrum profile increases across 0-40 cm depths under mulched management, expanding by 26.73% to 50.37% and 67.22% to 104.17% in the deepest evaluated horizon. This accumulation reflects both reduced crop uptake from stunted root systems and favorable microclimates for microbial mineral solubilization.

Enzymatic catalysts respond directly to local desalinization. Invertase activity in the 0-10 cm and 10-20 cm narrow-row layers increases by 50.31% and 40.06% under mulching, respectively, while urease activity rises by 12.53% and 8.81%. Salt alleviation relieves osmotic pressure on microbial biomass, preserving active enzyme conformations. However, beta-glucosidase activity in the 0-10 cm narrow-row layer drops by 25.81%, reflecting sensitivity to late-season aeration deficits under continuous plastic covering.

## Root Confinement Mechanisms and Agronomic Yield Penalties

Despite creating a desalinated, nutrient-enriched rhizosphere directly beneath the drip tape, mulched drip irrigation produced an agronomic penalty in maize productivity. Grain yield dropped from 8.65 t/hm2 in unmulched controls to 7.56 t/hm2 under mulching, while straw yield fell from 28.58 t/hm2 to 21.00 t/hm2. High-resolution morphological root scans revealed that the decline was directly mediated by architectural confinement of the maize root system.

Total root length collapsed by 33.18%, root surface area contracted by 45.55%, and branching frequency fell by 54.17%. Although the proportion of fine roots with diameters between 0 and 0.5 mm increased by 2.87%, root expansion into inter-row zones was obstructed. During grain filling and harvest, the lateral electrical conductivity disparity between the unmulched wide rows and the mulched narrow rows spanned 1.61 to 2.22 dS/m under mulched plots, compared to only 0.94 to 1.58 dS/m in unmulched plots. This steep salinity gradient established a physiological barrier, confining root proliferation to the narrow band under the film and intensifying intra-root resource competition.

## Management Boundary Conditions and Field Constraints

The findings are derived from a silt loam chloride-saline soil regime in the Hetao Plain irrigated with 250 mm of Yellow River water across ten irrigation events. Results illustrate that unmanaged full-season film coverage induces negative root entrapment under wide-narrow furrow geometries.

- Continuous film retention throughout late grain filling prevents natural rainfall infiltration and intensifies lateral salinity barriers between rows, inducing maize yield depression.

- Applicability is centered on arid continental climates with high evaporation-to-precipitation ratios (1 755 mm versus 170 mm) and silty loam textures, requiring agronomic recalibration under alternative soil textures or sulphate-dominant salinity types.

- Timely manual or mechanized film removal during mid-to-late reproductive stages is critical to unlock root expansion into inter-row zones and capture late-season precipitation.

analysis_markdown_en:
This study evaluated dietary supplementation of Tribulus terrestris by-products (TTB) at 0%, 5%, 10%, and 15% in 68 male Tan sheep lambs over a 60-day trial following a 10-day adaptation. Dietary inclusion of 5% TTB significantly optimized rumen fermentation by increasing the propionate molar ratio from 25.26% to 27.64% and decreasing the acetate-to-propionate ratio from 2.56 to 2.38 while preserving stable total volatile fatty acid levels (65.38 mmol/L vs. 68.04 mmol/L in controls). Furthermore, 16S rDNA sequencing showed that 5% TTB maintained microflora Alpha diversity, elevated the relative abundance of Saccharofermentans, and upregulated functional pathways associated with glycan and energy metabolism without destabilizing rumen homeostasis.

## Dose-Dependent Rumen Fermentation Dynamics and Acid Profiles

Rumen fermentation parameters serve as sensitive bioindicators of digestive health, microbial metabolism, and energy capture efficiency in ruminants. Across all test cohorts, ruminal pH remained within the safe physiological threshold of 6.31±0.18 to 6.74±0.25 (P=0.121), confirming that dietary substitution with Tribulus terrestris by-products did not induce systemic acidosis or compromise luminal buffer capacity. However, distinct dosage divergence emerged across volatile fatty acid fractions and nitrogenous metabolites.

In the 5% TTB cohort, the molar proportion of propionate rose significantly from 25.26±1.54% in controls to 27.64±1.58% (P<0.01), driving a concurrent reduction in the acetate-to-propionate ratio from 2.56±0.23 down to 2.38±0.20. Because propionate provides the principal substrate for hepatic gluconeogenesis, this metabolic shift enhances metabolic energy conversion. Total volatile fatty acid yield in the 5% cohort remained robust at 65.38±1.70 mmol/L compared to 68.04±4.22 mmol/L in controls.

In sharp contrast, elevating TTB inclusion to 10% and 15% triggered unfavorable fermentation shifts. Ruminal ammonia nitrogen increased progressively from 8.70±0.59 mg/dL in controls to 10.96±2.08 mg/dL (5% TTB), 13.91±2.65 mg/dL (10% TTB), and 17.56±1.90 mg/dL (15% TTB). Concurrently, total volatile fatty acids declined sharply to 37.29±0.74 mmol/L in the 10% group, while acetate proportions escalated to 74.06±0.74%, yielding an unfavorable acetate-to-propionate ratio of 4.29±0.25.

- Propionate molar ratio peaked at 27.64±1.58% under 5% TTB inclusion, yielding the lowest acetate-to-propionate ratio (2.38±0.20).

- Ammonia nitrogen accumulated up to 17.56±1.90 mg/dL at 15% TTB inclusion, reflecting accelerated microbial deamination of supplemental crude protein.

- Butyrate molar ratio declined from 8.64±0.85% in controls to 5.83±0.52% in the 5% TTB group.

## Taxonomic Compositional Shifts and Microbial Biomarker Enrichment

High-throughput sequencing of the 16S rDNA V3-V4 hypervariable regions yielded 1,324,632 valid reads across 24 ruminal samples, clustering into 4,661 operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at 97% sequence similarity. Goods coverage exceeded 0.98 for all treatment cohorts, establishing exhaustive sampling depth. Microbial richness and diversity estimators, including Chao1, Shannon, Simpson, and PD whole tree indices, exhibited no statistically significant alterations across groups (P>0.05), verifying that TTB inclusion preserves ecological richness.

Ordination via principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) and non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS, stress=0.107) revealed tight clustering between the control group and the 5% TTB group, demonstrating broad structural stability. At the phylum level, Firmicutes, Bacteroidota, and Proteobacteria dominated the rumen microbiome, jointly comprising over 91.96% of the total microbial abundance. In the 10% TTB group, Bacteroidota increased significantly to 50.46±9.71% while Firmicutes fell to 40.40±9.94% (P=0.035).

Linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe, LDA score > 3.0) identified 41 differentially enriched taxonomic clades across cohorts. Specifically, the 5% TTB group was selectively enriched for the cellulolytic and polysaccharide-fermenting genus Saccharofermentans (rising to 2.86±1.38% vs. 0.96±0.85% in controls, P<0.01), Hungateiclostridiaceae, and Bacteroidales UCG-001. Conversely, higher inclusion levels enriched Succinivibrionaceae UCG-001 in the 10% group and Dialister in the 15% group, while Ruminococcus abundance was broadly suppressed across all TTB treatments.

- Shared core microbiome encompassed 1,407 OTUs across all four experimental cohorts.

- Saccharofermentans abundance expanded nearly threefold in the 5% TTB cohort, supporting enhanced polysaccharide utilization.

- Ruminococcus abundance decreased from 10.92±5.28% in controls to 2.25±1.77% in trial group I and 1.49±1.02% in trial group II.

## Predictive Functional Pathways and Host Metabolic Integration

Metabolic pathway reconstruction via PICRUSt2 mapped primary functional categories predominantly to global metabolism and genetic information processing. Secondary hierarchical pathway evaluations indicated sustained enrichment across cofactor and vitamin metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and carbohydrate metabolism across all cohorts, underscoring functional redundancy within the rumen ecosystem.

Statistically significant divergence occurred within secondary metabolic modules. In lambs receiving 5% TTB, functional gene abundances dedicated to glycan biosynthesis and metabolism increased by 3.43% relative to controls (reaching 66,940.56±3,276.08), accompanied by significant elevations in endocrine systems, terpenoid and polyketide metabolism, and energy metabolism pathways. These metabolic enhancements align with the expanded relative abundances of Bacteroidota and Saccharofermentans, which ferment complex structural carbohydrates into metabolizable short-chain fatty acids.

Conversely, pathways linked to cardiovascular disease and transcriptional stress declined in the 5% and 10% TTB cohorts. Flavonoid and saponin secondary metabolites native to Tribulus terrestris likely exert antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties within the ruminal milieu. However, the enrichment of Dialister at the 15% dosage cautions against excessive inclusion, corroborating that a 5% dietary threshold achieves an optimal balance between volatile fatty acid production and microflora stability.

- Glycan biosynthesis and metabolism pathways rose significantly to 66,940.56±3,276.08 in the 5% group and 74,120.25±5,347.53 in the 10% group.

- Secondary pathways for terpenoids, polyketides, and energy metabolism reached peak relative abundance in the 5% TTB treatment cohort.

- Cardiovascular disease functional orthologs decreased, suggesting secondary bioactivities associated with supplemental phytogenic saponins.

## Nutritional Boundary Conditions and Intake Thresholds

While Tribulus terrestris by-products provide a viable unconventional feed resource, their dietary efficacy follows a strict non-linear dose response. Inclusion rates exceeding 5% impair volatile fatty acid synthesis and risk phytogenic secondary compound accumulation.

- Inclusion rates above 5% severely depressed total volatile fatty acids from 65.38±1.70 mmol/L down to 37.29±0.74 mmol/L at 10% TTB, impairing overall ruminal energy yield.

- High inclusion levels (15% TTB) elevated ruminal ammonia nitrogen to 17.56±1.90 mg/dL and promoted inflammatory biomarkers such as Dialister.

- The experimental cohort was restricted to 3-month-old male Tan sheep lambs weighing 24.68±0.90 kg over a 60-day feeding window, necessitating caution when extrapolating to breeding ewes or mature ruminants.

Detailed process conditions, instrument calibrations, and complete supplementary datasets beyond the core quantitative benchmarks are preserved in the Peer-Reviewed PDF Edition below.

## 1. Executive Abstract

This trial investigated the effects of dietary supplementation with Tribulus terrestris by-products (TTB) on rumen fermentation parameters and microflora structure in Tan sheep. Sixty-eight healthy 3-month-old male Tan sheep lambs weighing 24.68±0.90 kg were randomly allocated into four groups (17 lambs per group, individually penned) and fed diets supplemented with 0 (control), 5% (trial group I), 10% (trial group II), or 15% (trial group III) TTB for a 60-day feeding period following a 10-day adaptation. Furthermore, 5% TTB significantly increased the relative abundance of Saccharofermentans (P<0.01). PICRUSt2 functional predictions revealed enriched pathways for glycan biosynthesis and energy metabolism in trial group I. Overall, 5% dietary TTB enhances glucogenic propionate fermentation without disturbing rumen microflora stability.

- Relative abundance of the cellulolytic genus Saccharofermentans expanded significantly to 2.86±1.38% in the 5% TTB group versus 0.96±0.85% in controls (P<0.01).
